WASHINGTON (Reuters) — U.S. Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke is set to deliver his recommendation to the White House on Saturday regarding whether the Bears Ears monument in Utah should be reduced in size or revoked entirely. This upcoming decision will establish a precedent for the Trump administration's wider examination of protected public lands that could potentially be opened up for commercial development. The exact timing for when this choice will be publicly disclosed remains uncertain. 

Although the 1.35 million acres making up the Bears Ears designation are not thought to hold vast quantities of petroleum, natural gas, or coal, several other protected sites under Zinke's review do harbor such resources, elevating the significance of the Bears Ears verdict for corporate energy interests. Below is an overview of those locations:

BASIN AND RANGE: Established as a 704,000-acre national monument in southeastern Nevada by Barack Obama in 2015, this territory lies within the Chainman Shale formation, viewed by certain sectors of the drilling sector as a high-potential deposit.

BEARS EARS: Formed in late 2016 by Barack Obama just prior to the end of his presidency, this 1.35 million-acre southeastern Utah monument encompasses two well-known buttes and possesses moderate oil and gas prospects. Prior to its protection status, EOG Resources had already secured drilling leases inside the area.

CANYON OF THE ANCIENTS: Set aside by Bill Clinton as a 178,000-acre national monument in southwestern Colorado in the year 2000, this location was already utilized by the petroleum industry. Consequently, the former president permitted existing energy operations to persist under specific restrictions.

CARRIZO PLAIN: Designated by Bill Clinton in 2001, this 204,000-acre site in California sits in a region with a history of petroleum prospecting and holds moderate prospects for commercial extraction. Pre-existing extraction rights belong to the California Resources Corporation within a section of the monument, though a major discovery has not yet been achieved.

GRAND STAIRCASE-ESCALANTE: Established by Bill Clinton in 1996 as a 1.9 million-acre expanse in southern Utah, the Utah Geological Survey indicates that this monument contains an estimated 62 billion tons of coal, alongside coal bed methane and potential commercial reserves of petroleum.

UPPER MISSOURI RIVER BREAKS: Created by Bill Clinton in 2001, this 495,000-acre region in central Montana was evaluated by the U.S. Geological Survey in 1995, which estimated the presence of 58.2 to 719.9 billion cubic feet of natural gas and 14 million to 180 million barrels of oil.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Secretary of State Rex Tillerson announced on Friday that the United States has designated a special representative to spearhead diplomatic efforts concerning the conflict in Ukraine. Tillerson noted that the decision to fill this role came following a prompt from the Russian president. 

Kurt Volker, a veteran diplomat and former U.S. ambassador to NATO, will take charge of pushing forward American objectives outlined in the 2015 Minsk accord, which aims to de-escalate fighting in the Donbass area of Ukraine. According to the State Department, Volker is scheduled to travel alongside Tillerson to Kiev on Sunday. 

The crisis began when Russia took over Crimea in 2014, and the government in Kiev continues to claim that Moscow supports eastern separatist fighters, a charge the Kremlin rejects. The Minsk pact mandates a truce in the east, pulling back heavy weaponry from the combat zones, and institutional changes granting greater self-rule to eastern regions. 

Speaking to journalists in Hamburg, Germany, following a discussion between Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump during the G20 summit, Tillerson stated, “At the request of President Putin, the United States has appointed a special representative for Ukraine, Ambassador Kurt Volker.” 

In Kiev, President Petro Poroshenko expressed approval of the appointment via Twitter, asserting it would aid in stopping what he termed Russian aggression and bringing Crimea back under Ukrainian control. Poroshenko's post called the decision an essential and well-timed step toward safeguarding the country's borders and sovereignty. 

Volker brings a background as a career diplomat, having held the post of permanent representative to NATO through both the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations. At present, he works as a national security and foreign policy specialist at the McCain Institute for International Leadership, which is part of Arizona State University. 

In an official statement, Tillerson praised the selection, expressing total faith in Volker's capability to guide the peace process forward while reaffirming Washington's dedication to the goals of the Minsk accords. 

Meanwhile, Julie Smith, an ex-Pentagon official focused on NATO and European affairs during the Obama presidency, voiced support for Volker specifically, though she expressed confusion over Tillerson's remark that Putin had initiated the appointment. Smith, currently a senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, questioned whether Ukraine had previously been a low priority for the current administration, calling the framing of the announcement a strange choice of words.

Oklahoma House Bill 3098 was passed on Thursday by the state House of Representatives, advancing legislation that permits the open carrying of firearms without requiring a permit or training. Authored by state Representative Jeff Coody, the measure is grounded in the belief that the right to bear arms is granted by both the Constitution and God, intended for the self-defense of Bible-believing Christians. Coody described the legislation as the ultimate freedom bill regarding open carry, while co-author Representative Jeff Bennett emphasized that self-defense is a God-given right.

During the debate, Democratic Representative Emily Virgin questioned the wisdom of allowing individuals to carry weapons without knowing how to operate them or locate the safety mechanism. Coody dismissed the concern, stating that government does not grant permission to exercise freedoms. While the bill bars convicted felons from openly carrying firearms, it does not apply the same restriction to individuals subject to domestic violence protective orders. Furthermore, the legislation contains no mandate for safety courses or training. 

When questioned about the absence of training requirements, Coody contrasted gun ownership with driving, noting that driving is a privilege whereas the Second Amendment is a constitutional right. Another lawmaker, Representative Mike Brown, questioned whether the government held a responsibility to protect citizens, to which Coody responded in the negative, maintaining that a greater prevalence of firearms enhances overall safety. Conversely, critics pointed out that rape rates in Oklahoma reached a ten-year high following the enactment of the state's concealed carry law, and drew comparisons to automobile regulations from 1950 to 2014 that successfully reduced traffic fatalities through reasonable safety standards without infringing on the ability to drive with proper licensing and training.

Prior to passing in a 73-15 vote with 13 abstentions, the legislation had originally proposed eliminating licensing and training requirements for concealed carry as well. The measure now advances to the state Senate for consideration. Representative Virgin issued a warning regarding the potential consequences, stating that the combination of domestic violence and increased firearm access without training or background checks would lead to fatalities.

An outspoken critic of the Affordable Care Act's repeal is blasting conservatives, with a former evangelical pointing out the hypocrisy in supporting such a move. Bruce Horst is intimately familiar with the struggle of securing medical coverage while managing pre-existing conditions. Before the implementation of Obamacare, insurance providers consistently turned him away, leaving his household exposed to the financial devastation of a potential medical emergency. The health law ultimately protected Horst and his relatives from potential medical bankruptcy. 

Despite the legislation providing coverage to upwards of 30 million people, lawmakers in the House and Senate recently pushed through a late-night vote to dismantle it, an action that drew cheers from conservatives. 

This celebration drew sharp criticism from Horst. Now an atheist, he utilized Facebook to heavily chastise these self-described evangelical Christians for celebrating what he characterized as a death sentence for countless individuals. Expressing his views online, Horst stated his belief that determining medical assistance based strictly on an individual's financial capability is immoral, adding that his perspective is informed by biblical teachings. He noted that as of 2010, he had spent his entire adult life as a Conservative Evangelical Christian, eventually observing that fellow believers opposed affordable health insurance for individuals like him. According to Horst, these churchgoers had been misled into believing that extending coverage to others would negatively impact their own access to care.

Reflecting on his past faith, Horst explained that he once felt he would be judged on the Final Judgment Day based on how he treated the "least of these," referencing the twenty-fifth chapter of the book of Matthew. Upon realizing that his fellow Christians lacked similar convictions and seemingly disregarded the words of Jesus, he ultimately lost his belief entirely. 

Observers have noted a decline in church attendance among conservatives, and critics argue that such callousness and hypocrisy help explain why individuals like Horst walk away from the faith. The effort to strip millions of necessary medical care only reinforced his decision to leave the church.

Furthermore, Horst targeted congressional Republicans and criticized the contradiction of conservatives who claim to be "pro-life" while supporting policies that he claims will strip coverage from roughly 18 million Americans at the urging of Conservative Evangelical Christians. Pointing out that friends of his owe their survival to Obamacare, he argued that his former Christian peers are not genuinely pro-life, but are instead manipulated—likely to maintain tithes and secure votes for preferred candidates. 

While uncertain of the immediate legislative future regarding healthcare, Horst expressed that he would be pleasantly surprised if the president persuaded Congress to broaden coverage for everyone. However, he maintained that if his Christian acquaintances continue to insist that medical care should depend on personal wealth, they would face the condemnation attributed to Jesus in Matthew 25. Concluding his thoughts, Horst suggested that conservatives backing these measures are contradicting the teachings of Jesus and merely pretending to follow the faith.

BERLIN (Reuters) — On Friday, members of the digital activism network Avaaz dismantled a temporary barrier close to the historic Berlin Wall. The demonstration was organized to encourage American citizens residing in Germany to cast ballots opposing Donald Trump, the Republican candidate, in the upcoming November 8 U.S. presidential election. Participants drew a parallel to Trump's campaign pledge to construct a massive barrier along the U.S.-Mexico border to block migrants. Furthermore, the protest took place right by the Brandenburg Gate, echoing the historic 1987 moment when U.S. President Ronald Reagan challenged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev to "tear down this wall."

A crowd of cheering campaigners, numbering in the dozens, used their bare hands and rubber mallets to flatten the 2.5-meter (8.2-foot) barrier, which featured a printed likeness of Trump and red and blue signs that read "Stop Trump" and "Tear Down Trump’s Wall." Spectators, numbering around 150, watched the event and shouted slogans such as "The wall must come down!" as the structure collapsed. 

According to information released by Avaaz, roughly 8 million U.S. citizens reside outside the country, though a mere 12 percent participated in the 2012 presidential contest. Emma Ruby-Sachs, who serves as the deputy director for Avaaz, noted that expatriate Americans represent a hidden swing state capable of swinging the current election, with a significant population based in Germany. Meanwhile, a Reuters/Ipsos survey released the previous week indicated that 42 percent of likely voters favored former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, while 38 percent threw their support behind the Republican candidate and businessman.

Representative Luis Gutierrez, a staunch advocate for granting amnesty to undocumented immigrants, has dismissed the tragic death of Kate Steinle as "a little thing," arguing that critics routinely weaponize isolated incidents to push for the complete termination of sanctuary city policies. During a broadcast addressing a Rasmussen Reports survey revealing that sixty-two percent of the American public rejects sanctuary city protocols, Spanish-language broadcaster Telemundo shaped its reporting to support the continuation of these controversial municipal rules. 

Reporting live from Chicago—itself a sanctuary city—Telemundo journalist Janet Rodríguez featured an undocumented individual defending the policy alongside statements from Congressman Gutierrez, who downplayed the killing of Steinle by a repeat offender and five-time deportee in San Francisco. Although Rodríguez did mention the survey data showing widespread public opposition and support for penalizing sanctuary cities by withholding federal dollars, she offered only a single dissenting perspective, highlighting presidential candidate Donald Trump's characterization of sanctuary cities as "a disgrace." 

Furthermore, the broadcast misinformed viewers regarding the broad, cross-party opposition to these measures. Rodríguez claimed during the segment that the poll predominantly reflects Republican viewpoints on eliminating sanctuary cities or cutting their federal funding. In contrast, the actual survey results demonstrate that federal funding cuts are backed by seventy-nine percent of Republicans, sixty-six percent of unaffiliated voters, and forty-six percent of Democrats, while Department of Justice legal actions against sanctuary jurisdictions are supported by seventy-nine percent of Republicans, sixty-five percent of independents, and forty-three percent of Democrats.

United States Attorney General Jeff Sessions appears to have experienced a sudden recollection regarding Russian contacts during the 2016 race, after previously testifying under oath that he had no knowledge of such communications. 

Back in January during his confirmation proceedings, Sessions assured Senator Al Franken (D-MN) that he was unaware of any campaign associates interacting with Moscow officials. Now, however, that stance is shifting following the Monday unsealing of court records. These documents show that former Trump campaign adviser George Papadopoulos proposed organizing a summit between Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin in March 2016, boasting of helpful contacts to make it happen.

Adding to the scrutiny, an archived Instagram post from Trump's official profile places Sessions in the room when Papadopoulos pitched the idea. This development is drawing intense focus from Special Counsel Robert Mueller's ongoing investigation into the Russia scandal. According to an NBC insider, Sessions actually shot down the proposed meeting, although sources indicate it remains ambiguous whether the Attorney General presently remembers turning it down. NBC reporter Ken Dilanian noted on social media that while the proposal was indeed rejected by Sessions, his personal recollection of doing so remains uncertain.

Senator Franken expressed sharp frustration over what he characterized as a recurring trend of misleading statements given under oath regarding interactions with a foreign adversary that meddled in the election. In a formal statement, Franken accused Sessions of repeatedly obscuring the truth about both his own encounters with Russian operatives and his knowledge of similar outreach by fellow campaign staffers. Stressing the need for accountability to safeguard future elections, Franken declared that these latest findings severely undermine public and congressional trust in the Attorney General's testimony. 

This follows previous assertions by Sessions in June, where he maintained he was completely uninformed about any discussions involving potential Russian election interference by anyone associated with the campaign.

DHAKA (Reuters) — Khaleda Zia, the former prime minister and leader of the opposition in Bangladesh, flew back to the country on Wednesday following a medical trip to Britain that lasted over three quarters of a year—more than three months. Ecstatic crowds of supporters greeted her arrival. For years, the political landscape of Bangladesh has been defined by the bitter feud between Khaleda and Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, meaning her reappearance could spark a surge in political engagement ahead of the general election slated to take place before the end of next year. Both political figures share ties to past national leaders and have taken turns holding the office of prime minister over the years. 

During the time she was away, a minimum of two arrest warrants were handed down against her regarding political unrest, though she already held bail status concerning various legal matters. While her legal counsel has brushed off these charges as politically motivated harassment, Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) spokesperson Mohammad Shamsuddin indicated that she could potentially present herself in court on Thursday to address the matters. Meanwhile, the inspector general of police, Mohammad Shahidul Huq, mentioned to the press that orders for her apprehension had not been given to him. 

A massive crowd of party members carrying banners and placards assembled near the international airport located in the capital city of Dhaka to greet her return. At the same time, Bangladesh faces the monumental challenge of managing the arrival of more than half a million Rohingya Muslim refugees fleeing Myanmar starting in late August, a humanitarian crisis that threatens to turn into a contentious point of division as the election approaches.

Rather than limiting himself to his own criticisms of Hillary Clinton, Trump has chosen to lean on quotes from Putin to amplify his sharp jabs directed at the former Democratic presidential candidate. 

On a Friday evening via Twitter, the president-elect expressed agreement with Vladimir Putin’s viewpoint regarding the outcome of the 2016 presidential race for Hillary Clinton. As reported by the Washington Post, the Russian leader stated that Democrats were "losing on all fronts and looking elsewhere for things to blame," adding that such behavior "degrades their own dignity." While Trump has rejected the notion that Russia was behind the email theft and claimed the true identity of the hackers remains a mystery, he has actually been given intelligence briefings pointing to Russian responsibility, despite opting to disregard them in his public remarks. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Following a dominant string of victories on Super Tuesday that propelled her further ahead in the race for the Democratic presidential nomination, Hillary Clinton quickly turned her attention to the Republican front-runner, Donald Trump. Claiming victory in seven out of eleven contested states—most notably the populous state of Texas—the former first lady solidified her lead over challenger Bernie Sanders as both vie to head the Democratic ticket in the upcoming November 8 presidential election. These wins, which included sweeping the South, also set the stage for a prospective matchup against the billionaire real estate mogul and reality television personality, who similarly triumphed in multiple Republican contests on Tuesday. 

Amidst these electoral successes, campaign fundraisers reported that financial backers are increasingly eager to support her bid through the general election. Dane Strother, a Democratic strategist based in Washington D.C. who is unaligned with any campaign, remarked that Clinton is effectively the nominee and must now pivot toward confronting Trump. 

During a Miami rally following her multi-state wins on Tuesday evening, Clinton directly addressed Trump, criticizing his tendency to insult opponents while reiterating her opposition to his proposed 1,000-mile wall along the Mexican border. Emphasizing that the stakes in the election have never been higher, she argued that the rhetoric from the opposing side has reached unprecedented lows, adding that attempts to divide America into "us and them" are fundamentally wrong.

According to delegate tallies compiled by the New York Times early Wednesday morning, Clinton secured 527 delegates for the upcoming Democratic nominating convention compared to 325 for Sanders, out of the 2,383 required to clinch the nomination. Jim Manley, a Washington-based Democratic strategist backing Clinton, noted that shifting her focus to Trump was a necessary yet hazardous maneuver. Pointing out that Trump is likely to retaliate aggressively—noting that "he'll go right in the gutter"—Manley warned of the inherent risks. Trump has frequently targeted Clinton over her handling of crises in Iraq and Syria during her four-year tenure as secretary of state, and has hinted at reviving past controversies surrounding former President Bill Clinton.

Members of Clinton’s national finance committee indicated that the campaign is observing renewed enthusiasm from contributors looking past the primary season. Tom Sacks-Wilner, a committee member, noted a clear transition toward the general election, observing that the finance department is no longer raising objections to it. Federal rules permit donors to contribute $2,700 for the primary phase and an additional $2,700 for the general election, allowing a combined total of $5,400 per individual. Furthermore, a Los Angeles-based fundraiser reported an uptick in local inquiries regarding contributions for post-California campaigning, alongside a surge in willingness among volunteers to offer their time following the recent victories.

This optimistic outlook represents a notable contrast to conditions from three weeks prior, when the campaign was reeling from Sanders’ decisive victory in New Hampshire and a narrow second-place finish in Iowa, where the Vermont senator captured a substantial share of younger voters. That momentum began to shift following Clinton's win in South Carolina, bolstered by robust backing from African-American voters—a demographic where Sanders has faced challenges connecting through his democratic socialist platform. National figures from a Reuters/Ipsos tracking poll conducted between February 26 and March 1 showed nearly 53 percent of Democrats favoring Clinton versus 43 percent for Sanders, recovering from a dead heat earlier in the month and improving significantly since just before the South Carolina primary on February 27.

Meanwhile, Sanders has also sought to frame himself as a viable general election opponent against Trump. Jeff Weaver, Sanders’ campaign manager, released a statement on Tuesday highlighting the campaign's $42.7 million fundraising total for February. Stressing that Trump will command substantial financial resources for November, Weaver emphasized the necessity for the Democratic nominee to secure hundreds of millions of dollars to successfully challenge the Republicans.

Additionally, progressive groups connected to the party cautioned against dismissing Sanders prematurely despite the Super Tuesday outcomes, pointing out his stronger polling prospects in upcoming northern states with predominantly white electorates. Charles Chamberlain, executive director of Democracy for America, issued a statement arguing that political pundits in Washington were mistaken when they initially claimed the nomination contest was settled before Sanders entered the race, and remain wrong in declaring it over now. 

(Editing by Richard Valdmanis and Alistair Bell) This article was funded in part by SAP. It was independently created by the Reuters editorial staff. SAP had no editorial involvement in its creation or production.

text:
French leader Emmanuel Macron urged Baghdad over the weekend to dissolve all armed groups in the country, specifically pointing to the state-approved, Tehran-supported Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF). This public demand from a prominent Western figure is unusual. The statement, delivered after talks in the French capital with Kurdish officials from Iraq, highlights the delicate diplomatic tightrope Baghdad must walk between Tehran and Western nations—countries that remain at odds—following their joint efforts against Islamic State.

During a press briefing alongside Iraqi Kurdish representatives in Paris, the French president emphasized the necessity of a step-by-step demilitarization, particularly targeting the Popular Mobilisation groups that have taken root in the country recently, alongside the gradual disbanding of all other militias. 

Leadership under the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) contends that the predominantly Arab Shiite PMF has committed numerous violations against Kurdish populations residing in regions of Iraq shared by multiple ethnic groups. Meanwhile, the administration of Iraqi Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi rejects claims that these forces engage in widespread or organized abuses, promising legal consequences for any personnel found culpable of infractions. As government troops come closer to proclaiming a final defeat of Islamic State, stripping the PMF of its weapons is widely viewed as Abadi's greatest political hurdle.

A subsequent statement issued by Abadi's office in Baghdad noted a telephone conversation with Macron, reporting that the French leader reiterated support for maintaining a united Iraqi state. However, the official readout omitted any reference to Macron's push for dissolving the militias.

A sharper rebuke came from Iraqi Vice President Nuri al-Maliki. The former premier, who had previously faced pressure from both Washington and Tehran to step down due to his inability to halt Islamic State, characterized Macron's remarks as an intolerable meddling in domestic matters. In a published statement, Maliki asserted that France's stance is completely unacceptable and damages the sovereignty and official bodies of Iraq.

The gathering in Paris between Macron, KRG Prime Minister Nechirvan Barzani, and Deputy Prime Minister Qubad Talabani marked the initial high-level international engagement for Kurdish authorities following the independence vote held on September 25. While foreign ministers like U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and British Prime Minister Theresa May traveled to the country subsequent to the vote, their visits were restricted to Baghdad, omitting any stops in the Kurdish regional capital of Erbil. Prior to the vote, Western governments had urged the Kurds to abstain from the referendum and pursue talks with the central authorities instead.

Reiterating his backing for talks, Macron stressed the importance of negotiations between the central authorities in Baghdad and the semi-autonomous Kurdish administration based on the Iraqi charter. He expressed confidence that meaningful discussions could result in Baghdad lifting its measures against the Kurdish territory.

The vote for secession defied the central government and sparked concern in neighboring Turkey and Iran, both of which deal with their own Kurdish populations. In response, government forces in Iraq took control of Kirkuk and other contested zones. The fallout led to the resignation of longtime Kurdish president Masoud Barzani, prompting the regional administration—now headed by his nephew Nechirvan—to seek a negotiated resolution to the standoff.

Speaking on Saturday, the Kurdish premier expressed hope that Paris could assist in mediating the conflict with Baghdad, adding that the regional administration acknowledges the ruling by Iraq's Supreme Federal Court which declared the independence vote unconstitutional and its outcomes invalid. According to the Erbil-based media outlet Rudaw, Barzani stated that they have entered a different phase, the matter of the referendum is concluded, and the regional government's stance is well-established.

Additionally, Macron advocated for the long-overdue application of Article 140 of the Iraqi charter to resolve ownership of regions contested by Baghdad and Kurdish authorities. The provision originally mandated a vote by the conclusion of 2007 in Kirkuk and other oil-rich zones claimed by both sides to decide whether local inhabitants preferred integration into the Kurdish territory. Because that vote never materialized, the KRG frequently pointed to it as justification for proceeding with its own unilateral independence referendum.

NEW YORK/FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. — For a significant portion of Donald Trump’s base, his choice to launch missile strikes against a Syrian airfield in response to a chemical weapons attack demonstrated decisive leadership and strength, aligning with their expectations from the November election. Speaking with reporters, more than a dozen individuals who voted for Trump acknowledged that direct military engagement in Syria seemingly contradicted the isolationist, “America First” platform he championed during his run for the White House. Yet, unlike prominent far-right figures who openly condemned the military action in Syria, the majority of Trump supporters surveyed across Texas, New York, and Florida argued that the strike did not violate his pledge to prioritize American interests above all else. 

Anthony Calvanese, a 28-year-old construction foreman interviewed on a sidewalk in Staten Island, New York, expressed enthusiastic approval, stating he loved the decision and that the president had made it clear from day one that he would not tolerate nonsense and needed to project global superiority. 

This military order marked a departure from Trump's 2016 campaign promises to steer clear of Middle East entanglements, as well as his past criticism four years prior of then-President Barack Obama for not retaliating against the Syrian government after a previous chemical attack on its citizens. These apparent contradictions drew sharp criticism from his most dedicated supporters on the far right. Paul Joseph Watson, a London-based editor for the U.S. conspiracy-promoting outlet Infowars—which Trump has previously praised—posted on Twitter that he was completely off the Trump train, while prominent white nationalist leader Richard Spencer labeled the move a betrayal and the death of the “America First” agenda.

Conversely, several voters maintained their faith in the president's ability to fulfill his commitments. Todd Recknagel, managing partner at a private equity firm in Panama City Beach, Florida, explained via phone that the action deepened his backing by proving Trump is capable of adapting his perspective based on unfolding events, adding that he values a leader who stands up for principles and compares the stance to former President Ronald Reagan. 

Other supporters felt the sheer brutality of the poison gas attack left the administration with no alternative. Tom Harney, a 64-year-old yacht broker from Lauderhill, Florida, remarked outside a local diner that failing to respond would have made the nation as culpable as those who ignored Adolf Hitler's march across Europe during World War II. 

This perspective was shared by Brooklyn attorney Joseph Mure Jr., who told a reporter outside a Staten Island courthouse that innocent victims, including women and infants, were murdered, adding that he wished the military had deployed twice the volume of ordnance. The assault involved U.S. naval warships in the Mediterranean firing a barrage of Tomahawk missiles at the targeted airfield. 

Additional supporters pointed out that the move reinforced Trump’s tough persona and campaign vows to rebuild the armed forces, signaling that the United States retains its global leadership role. Art Tillberg, 67, of Coral Springs, Florida, noted that the country was no longer leading from behind, invoking a frequent Republican critique of Obama’s 2011 campaign against Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.

At the same time, dissent remained among certain Trump voters who shared the far-right's view that the operation violated campaign pledges. Anthony Sage, a 42-year-old retired Army staff sergeant with service tours in Iraq and Afghanistan, argued outside the Fort Hood Army base in Killeen, Texas, that the operation ran counter to the “America First” doctrine, dismissing the engagement as a misuse of American resources and time while domestic needs should take precedence. 

Similarly, Abdi Mohamed, a 23-year-old Somali immigrant and Trump voter residing in St. Paul, Minnesota, voiced concern during a phone interview that the president was reversing his outsider stance and yielding to the influence of the political establishment and standard system. 

Meanwhile, a small group of voters experienced internal conflict, feeling uneasy about entangling the nation in the prolonged civil war in Syria while remaining reluctant to turn away from the president. Melanie Groves, a 39-year-old small business owner from Louisville, Illinois, who had recently organized a pro-Trump rally, admitted she was undecided, hoping the action served strictly as a firm warning regarding crossed red lines while acknowledging fears from critics that it could spiral toward a major global conflict.

During the funeral service for Dick Gregory, Maxine Waters took the opportunity to launch into a harsh critique of President Trump. Knowing her audience well, she began her remarks by declaring, "I've got work to do." Waters proceeded to repeatedly label the president a "dishonorable human being" and alleged that his administration's cabinet is populated by members of the Ku Klux Klan and the Alt-right. Additionally, she speculated on how the late comedian would view current geopolitical events, wondering aloud if Gregory would confirm Russian collusion by saying, "Yeah, he did it." 

Expressing determination to make a lasting impact regardless of impeachment proceedings, Waters vowed not to allow someone she referred to as a "thing" in the White House to bring dishonor, stating, "When I get done with Donald Trump, he s gonna wish he had been impeached." Critics argue that her accusations are hypocritical given her own record and claim she does not even reside within her assigned district, instead living in a multi-million dollar mansion while being described as a "poverty pimp."

text:
While Senator Ted Cruz has been enjoying momentum in the Republican primary race, this trend likely persists only because the electorate has not yet gotten to know him well. Finding a more profoundly unlikable presidential contender would prove nearly impossible, according to practically every individual who has ever crossed paths with him personally. 

Although opposition from Democrats who view his conservative platform as morally and intellectually objectionable comes as no shock, alarms are now ringing within his own political ranks. Former presidential hopeful Bob Dole stepped forward this week to publicly challenge Cruz, delivering some blunt assessments. Voicing doubts regarding his party loyalty, Dole remarked that hearing Cruz utter the word "Republican" is a rarity. Instead, Dole noted, Cruz consistently relies on the term "conservative," before offering his own label for the senator: an "extremist." Dole also questioned how Cruz plans to manage relations in Congress, bluntly stating that nobody likes him.

Yet, Dole's critique may actually understate the reality. Cruz's ultimate loyalty belongs neither to the Republican Party nor to conservatism, but rather to himself. This is the exact politician who nearly single-handedly forced a federal government shutdown simply to make a point regarding Obamacare. The maneuver cost the nation billions of dollars, damaged the international financial credibility of the United States, and ultimately achieved nothing—though it certainly elevated Cruz's public profile. When considering whether Cruz would repeat such actions, the answer is that he has already attempted to do so.

Dislike for Cruz extends far beyond political figures across the aisle, however. His past is populated by acquaintances eager to share accounts of how socially awkward, eccentric, and misanthropic he was during earlier years. Craig Mazin, his former college roommate at Princeton and now a well-known figure, has spent recent years continuously ridiculing Cruz online while painting an unsettling portrait of their time together. 

Mazin has noted on social media that gaining thousands of followers was hardly worth the experience of rooming with Cruz for a year. He has explicitly stated that Cruz is not a friend, and that he loathes both the man and everything he stands for, even labeling him a "huge asshole" around the time of his Senate election.

Any suspicion that Mazin held a petty or isolated grudge—perhaps over messy living habits—is dispelled by other college contemporaries who echo the exact same sentiments. Another former classmate corroborated Mazin's portrayal, noting that anyone who suspects Mazin is exaggerating is mistaken, as he personally loathed Cruz within an hour of meeting him during freshman week. 

When The Daily Beast sought out additional college peers to verify these accounts, they uncovered a widespread consensus characterizing Cruz as a creepy and politically extreme jerk. Alongside Mazin and another individual named Leitch, several anonymous classmates described the young Cruz using terms like abrasive, intense, strident, crank, and arrogant. Specifically, four different people independently used the word creepy, pointing out Cruz's peculiar habit of wearing a paisley bathrobe while walking to the far end of the dorm hallway where female students resided. Mazin recalled frequently fielding complaints from the women asking him to keep his roommate out of their hallway.

The unsettling impressions left by Cruz are so pervasive that they surface even in contexts entirely unrelated to his personal popularity. A recent report in The New York Times detailing his stint as a law clerk for Chief Justice William Rehnquist quickly shifted focus toward former colleagues expressing discomfort over what they described as a morbid fascination with murder that unsettled everyone in the office. 

Interviews with roughly two dozen former Supreme Court clerks—spanning both liberal and conservative chambers—portrayed Cruz as obsessively fixated on capital punishment. Several felt that his delivery when recounting crimes resembled a dime-store novel, appearing better suited for a prosecutor addressing a jury than a clerk advising the nation's highest court.

Unpopularity is not restricted to coworkers, roommates, lawmakers, and commentators, as ordinary citizens share similar views. An ABC News analysis from 2014 evaluated political popularity by examining Facebook discourse and discovered that 61 percent of all mentions of Ted Cruz on the platform were decidedly negative.

Despite universal animosity from those who encounter him, Cruz manages to sustain his political career through backing from a compact yet influential faction of millionaires supportive of his anti-government agenda. Furthermore, his relentless, opportunistic drive for the spotlight ensures his survival; in the realm of politics, the adage that any publicity is good publicity holds true. As Cruz continually appears on Fox News, conservative audiences gradually acclimate to his inherent creepiness.

Translating this particular behavioral pattern into an effective presidency remains difficult to envision. At a critical juncture in international diplomacy, placing an overwhelmingly unlikable figure in the Oval Office could prove disastrous. Furthermore, Cruz's history demonstrates a willingness to prioritize self-aggrandizement over the national interest, as evidenced by the government shutdown. 

The widespread aversion toward Cruz—which intensifies the closer one gets to him—should serve as a major red flag regarding his character, raising serious questions about whether such an individual is fit to lead the most powerful country in the world.

By speaking with the president of Taiwan on Friday, Donald Trump appears to have triggered a diplomatic crisis with China. Observers of the political landscape were baffled by the decision, struggling to understand how anyone could view it as a wise move. The explanation boils down to a familiar motivation—Trump acts out of self-interest, seeking personal gain. On this occasion, the objective appears to be a new luxury resort. 

Ever since the United States cut formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan in 1979 and embraced a One China policy, American presidents and presidents-elect have avoided direct communications with the nation's leader. Beijing views Taiwan as a breakaway province, meaning Trump's conversation with Taiwanese President Tsai Ying-wen is bound to provoke anger from the Chinese government. The rationale behind the call becomes clearer when considering that the Trump Organization has been exploring Taiwan as a potential site for a luxury resort development.

According to a report published in November by the China-focused news outlet The Shanghaiist:

On Wednesday, the mayor of Taoyuan verified speculation that president-elect Donald Trump was weighing the possibility of building luxury hotels and a resort complex in the northwestern Taiwanese city.

Taiwan News previously reported that a Trump Organization representative traveled to Taoyuan in September to show interest in the city's Aerotropolis, an expansive urban development initiative designed to leverage Taoyuan's position as a major East Asian transportation hub. Although the Aerotropolis review remains ongoing, the mayor of Taoyuan characterized the discussions as preliminary investment speculation. Additional reports suggest that Eric Trump, the president-elect's executive vice president and second son, plans to visit Taoyuan later in the year to further explore the business prospect.

The potential fallout from this brief phone call is severe. Trump's readiness to put his own interests ahead of the country follows a pattern that has drawn intense scrutiny over his foreign financial ties and business conflicts of interest as he prepares for the presidency. Even before taking the oath of office, critics argue he is prioritizing his personal wealth over national interests, fueling arguments against his leadership. Featured image via Ty Wright/Getty Images

text:
European governments are anticipating that Prime Minister Theresa May will attempt to unfreeze stalled Brexit negotiations very soon by indicating a willingness to compensate the European Union in exchange for temporary participation in the single market following Britain's departure. Key insiders handling the separation process in Berlin, Brussels, and other European centers noted that no formal proposals had reached them prior to Friday's scheduled address in Florence, Italy, where the Prime Minister is anticipated to outline her perspective on the United Kingdom's upcoming ties with the bloc. Furthermore, these sources minimized a Financial Times story suggesting that Oliver Robbins, May's European Union adviser, had communicated to Angela Merkel and other continental leaders that a 20 billion euro proposal might be put forward by May to fund a post-departure interim phase. 

An official representing the German administration stated that no advance word regarding specific negotiating terms had been communicated by the UK administration. Nevertheless, various officials—who requested anonymity—indicated that hints had arrived from London suggesting May intends to overcome the prolonged stalemate that has sparked anxieties across the English Channel regarding a potential departure in 2019 absent any agreement on future relations. 

According to these sources, expectations are high that May will soon intimate a desire to maintain British membership in the single market for a duration of two to three years while acknowledging the financial cost required for such privileges. Uncertainty remained, however, regarding whether this gesture would materialize during the Florence address, at the upcoming negotiations in Brussels on Monday, at the Conservative Party gathering in early October, or at forthcoming European gatherings in Tallinn and Brussels. 

An insider closely tied to the discussions remarked that a three-year extension within the customs union and single market necessitates financial contributions, a fact the UK understands, adding that conceding to payments during that timeframe would represent a significant development. This individual was among more than half a dozen continental European sources who discussed the matter with Reuters on Wednesday. 

At the same time, certain representatives adopted a more guarded stance, voicing worries that the UK might be blending two distinct matters together: the expenses associated with post-Brexit market entry and the initial financial settlement London owes for past obligations. A Berlin-based source described the situation as a delicate phase, warning that progress will prove challenging unless the entirety of the monetary settlement is properly addressed. 

Three months have passed since exit discussions commenced, and both parties continue to grapple with preliminary hurdles that Brussels insists must be settled prior to initiating discussions about subsequent commercial ties. These prerequisites involve the status of expatriate citizens, the management of the Irish border, and the exit bill linked to Britain's withdrawal. European Commission estimates place the potential British liability at roughly 60 billion euros based on past pledges made while a member.

With the March 2019 departure deadline approaching, the UK is eager to commence trade discussions to dispel the lingering ambiguity troubling businesses operating between Britain and the continent. Without this clarity, British enterprises might opt to relocate functions to member states to preserve uninterrupted entry to a single market encompassing 440 million consumers, a step some corporations have already initiated. 

While trade talks were initially anticipated to commence in October, Michel Barnier, the chief negotiator for the European Union from France, has indicated that such a timeline currently appears improbable. Barnier is scheduled to reconvene with his British counterpart in Brussels on Monday. 

On Wednesday, European representatives delivered mixed messages regarding whether acknowledging monetary duties for a transition phase would suffice to overcome the impasse and initiate substantive trade discussions. A high-ranking source within an administration generally favorable to the UK suggested that any financial proposal from May could prove beneficial, noting that continental leaders recognize the Prime Minister might combine exit costs and transition fees to appease domestic Eurosceptic supporters wary of compromises. 

Conversely, a third European Union insider remarked that a full grasp of the reality has not yet taken hold, stating that if they were in the Prime Minister's position, they would present a transparent and immediate offer demonstrating readiness. A second German representative observed that while May's Florence address would likely be pleasant, the ultimate test remains whatever proposals the British delegation formally submits in Brussels on Monday.

WASHINGTON — U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson recently engaged in discussions with Saudi Foreign Minister Adel al-Jubeir regarding ongoing developments within the kingdom, according to a State Department representative who spoke on Thursday. The diplomatic contact comes in the wake of a sweeping anti-corruption sweep that has resulted in numerous arrests.

During a briefing, State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert noted that the American charge d affaires stationed in Riyadh held a meeting on Wednesday with Saad al-Hariri, who recently stepped down from his role as Lebanon's prime minister while visiting Saudi Arabia. When questioned regarding assertions that Hariri was being detained within the country, Nauert refrained from disclosing the location of the encounter or commenting further on Hariri's current circumstances, characterizing the interaction as a sensitive, private, diplomatic exchange.

Nauert also shared that during his Tuesday phone call with Jubeir, Tillerson encouraged Saudi officials to handle any upcoming corruption trials fairly and transparently. 

The kingdom's recent anti-corruption campaign, which commenced on Saturday, has targeted dozens of individuals including businessmen, government figures, and members of the royal family. Those detained face various accusations, such as extortion and money-laundering. In Saudi Arabia—an absolute monarchy governed by an Islamic system lacking a codified body of law and an elected legislature—the boundaries separating state resources and royal finances have historically remained blurred.

President Donald Trump's administration has voiced support for the purge, marking a significant intensification of bilateral ties. This strengthened partnership has been largely motivated by a shared commitment between Washington and Riyadh to counter Iran's expanding influence in the region. Numerous analysts view the crackdown as a strategy orchestrated by Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman, leader of the newly formed anti-corruption committee, to consolidate authority, advance a broader agenda of social, economic, and political overhauls, and solidify his path to succeeding King Salman.

WASHINGTON — President Barack Obama’s nominee to the U.S. Supreme Court, Merrick Garland, was unable to convince Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley during a Tuesday closed-door session to schedule confirmation hearings for his appointment. In an official release, Grassley’s office characterized the 70-minute discussion in the Senate dining room as “cordial and pleasant,” adding that the senator “explained why the Senate won’t be moving forward during this hyper-partisan election year,” mirroring remarks made the previous week. Decades earlier, the Iowa Republican had similarly attempted to obstruct Garland's appointment to the federal appeals court where he now serves as chief judge.

Following that encounter, Garland held a private discussion with Senator Lisa Murkowski, identifying as one of the shrinking faction of moderate Republican senators. A statement released by her office likewise suggested that the possibility of confirming Garland was off the table. 

Obama, a Democrat, put forward Garland's name on March 16 to take the place on the high court left vacant following the passing of conservative Justice Antonin Scalia on February 13. The Senate, currently under Republican control, has declined to move the nomination forward, leading Democrats to charge them with obstruction and a failure to fulfill constitutional duties. GOP lawmakers argue that the empty seat ought to be filled by the incoming president chosen in the November 8 election and inaugurated on January 20, maintaining hopes for a Republican victory that would lead to the selection of a conservative nominee instead of the centrist Garland.

While Democrats praised GOP members willing to sit down with Garland, they maintained that public hearings remain a necessity. New York Senator Chuck Schumer voiced his criticisms to the press, stating, “Dark-money groups (conservative contributors) are trying to do the Republicans’ dirty work and sully Judge Garland’s name while Republican senators prevent Judge Garland from explaining his views to the public. That is cowardly, it’s backward and it is wrong.”

Meanwhile, the White House shared correspondence addressed to Senate leaders from 15 former presidents of the American Bar Association, which called for a prompt confirmation vote and hearing for Garland. The letter from the former ABA heads noted that “the stated refusal to fill the ninth seat of the Supreme Court injects a degree of politics into the judicial branch that materially hampers the effective operation of our nation’s highest court and the lower courts over which it presides.”

Conversely, conservative organizations such as the Tea Party Patriots and the Judicial Crisis Network commended Grassley for standing his ground against holding hearings. 

Data from a Reuters-Ipsos poll carried out between April 5 and April 12, which surveyed 900 registered Democrats and 788 registered Republicans, indicated that 55 percent of participants believed the Senate ought to conduct confirmation hearings. Opinion on the matter broke sharply along partisan divisions, with 61 percent of Democratic respondents backing Garland's confirmation, contrasted with 22 percent of Republican respondents.

GENEVA (Reuters) - According to the medical humanitarian organization Medecins Sans Frontieres, the move by U.S. President Donald Trump to halt the resettlement of Syrian refugees will result in fatalities. In a published statement, the organization—frequently referred to as Doctors Without Borders—argued that the executive order signed by the president leaves individuals stranded within active conflict areas, placing them in immediate physical danger. 

Jason Cone, who serves as the executive director for MSF-USA, criticized the policy in the organization's announcement, noting that the U.S. has maintained a stringent vetting process for refugees over a long period. He described closing American borders as a direct blow to the fundamental principle that individuals ought to have the ability to escape perilous situations to save their lives. Cone also mentioned that personnel on the ground witness individuals daily trying desperately to find refuge at blocked borders and trapped within conflict zones where escape is impossible.

Data from the United Nations refugee agency, the UNHCR, indicates that 4.9 million Syrians have sought refuge in adjacent nations, nearly one million have made their way to Europe, and upwards of 6 million remain internally displaced inside Syria.

Throughout his campaign, Trump criticized his predecessor, Barack Obama, for raising the intake of Syrian arrivals due to concerns that individuals escaping the civil war might pose security threats. According to recent UNHCR figures shared on Friday, roughly 25,000 vulnerable refugees found new homes in the U.S. between October and the end of the year under the agency's framework.

The current administration implemented a suspension on travelers and refugees hailing from seven predominantly Muslim nations. This directive sparked widespread demonstrations involving tens of thousands of participants across major U.S. urban centers, alongside pushback from several notable figures within the Republican Party. By Sunday, the administration adjusted the directive to clarify that lawful permanent U.S. residents possessing green cards would be exempt from the entry restrictions. In addition to Syria, the targeted nations encompass Libya, Yemen, Iraq, Iran, Sudan, and Somalia.

Earlier, in a joint statement released on Saturday, the UNHCR and the International Organization for Migration emphasized the critical importance of the American resettlement initiative, though they refrained from directly condemning the new government's approach. Representatives from both the UNHCR and the IOM were not reachable for immediate comment on Monday.

Bush’s era who eventually transitioned to managing a white supremacist blog.

According to his Facebook page, Huber has frequently traveled to various properties owned by Trump as well as the White House. While it remains uncertain whether he managed any personal interactions with the president during these trips, Huber claims he received a direct phone call from him on Valentine's Day.

However, what truly distinguishes Huber is his peculiar habit involving a life-sized cardboard cutout of Donald Trump. During a post-rally interview with CNN, Huber detailed his daily routine with the inanimate replica, which involves regular conversations and what appears to be prayer directed toward the cardboard figure. He proudly shared photographic evidence on social media, referring to the cutout as the best visitor he could possibly host.

Unsurprisingly, Huber's public admissions regarding his daily salutes and chats with the cardboard likeness drew a wave of astonishment and mockery across social media. Users expressed everything from speechlessness to severe skepticism regarding the unorthodox display of loyalty, with many posting harsh punchlines and questioning the supporter's state of mind.

DAKAR/LIBORE, Niger — For Mabingue Ngom, who directs the U.N. Population Fund across West Africa, addressing the region's birth rates means dealing directly with religious leaders. Specialists are increasingly concerned that unchecked population growth—driven by the highest birth rates globally—will intensify competition for dwindling farmland and water supplies, while exacerbating malnutrition, conflict, and the flow of economic refugees. Demographic reports and family planning data underscore these challenges. Alongside international charities and regional governments, U.N. bodies also hope to lower maternal mortality rates, which currently outpace those found anywhere else in the world according to UNFPA statistics. 

However, preachers influenced by puritanical Wahhabist Islam and various traditional figures frequently speak out against birth control. They argue that Western powers promote contraception out of a fear that Africans will eventually outnumber them. Pointing to Koranal passages that urge Muslims to multiply, critics often frame family planning as a foreign conspiracy designed to diminish the influence of Islam. 

Dakar-based Wahhabist imam Hassane Seck expressed this perspective directly, stating that Western policies aim to shrink regional populations while promoting contraceptive use that has rendered European women less fertile. He asserted that African populations will continue to grow, which causes foreign nations anxiety.

To shift these perceptions, population strategists are attempting to engage moderate religious figures. During a September gathering with several prominent Senegalese clerics, Ngom deliberately steered clear of the concept of overpopulation, choosing instead to emphasize shared Koranal values such as proper maternal care and the parental duty to adequately feed and educate children. Speaking to Reuters, he noted that standard presentations and speeches often backfire by increasing hostility, stressing the necessity of direct engagement.

Bou Mouhamed Kounta, the deputy head of the Islamic Supreme Council in Senegal, acknowledged after hearing Ngom that while family planning remains a sensitive topic locally, collaboration was possible because the UNFPA demonstrated respect for religious traditions.

The most extreme demographic pressures remain concentrated in Niger, a deeply impoverished nation stretching into the Sahara. United Nations projections indicate the country's population will reach 72 million by 2050—tripling its current size—despite persistent droughts that already make food security difficult. Niger has recorded the world's highest fertility rate over the past decade, maintaining an average above seven children per mother for a quarter-century. Child marriage remains widespread, with over 20 percent of girls wed by age 19, and maternal mortality stands at 553 deaths per 100,000 live births. In neighboring Chad, that figure reaches 856 per 100,000, compared to just 12 in wealthy nations.

Efforts by Niger's government to curb birth rates have faced fierce pushback from imams and traditional leaders known as marabouts. While the precise footprint of Wahhabism across West Africa is difficult to quantify, adherents hold influence over critical houses of worship, including the main university mosques in Senegal and Niger. Religious television broadcasts in Niger frequently feature preachers warning of divine punishment for anyone utilizing contraception. Reproductive health workers in the southern city of Maradi reported that a local imam at a major mosque routinely condemns birth control as a white conspiracy to reduce the population. 

When President Mahamadou Issoufou and the UNFPA attempted to introduce school sex education in 2015, demonstrators set textbooks ablaze outside U.N. facilities. A similar backlash forced the cancellation of a bill proposed three years earlier that sought to stop the removal of young girls from school for marriage. 

Reflecting on these events, Ngom questioned whether decades of lecturing Africans about family size had proven counterproductive. He concluded that the message required a more delicate approach, leading him to hold numerous discussions with moderate imams while wearing a traditional Senegalese bubu robe. He told Reuters that in an environment marked by suspicion, delivery matters more than the underlying topic, emphasizing the need to understand one's audience.

Atamo Hassane, who heads Niger's family planning division, expressed a similar view in Niamey, noting that terms like "limit" or "reduce" provoke immediate opposition from religious leaders. While spacing births alone may not solve overall population growth, Hassane hopes that initial experiences with contraception will demonstrate its benefits, encouraging broader use and eventual declines in fertility.

Other moderate voices include Sheikh Ali Ben Salah, Niger's former minister for religious affairs. Speaking at a Dakar conference on child marriage, Salah maintained that Islamic teachings permit family planning for the sake of child and maternal welfare, provided adherents do not aim to cut off childbearing entirely.

A significant turning point occurred in July when the highest Islamic authority in Chad organized a symposium alongside regional religious leaders and the U.N. agency—an unprecedented event for the topic. Ngom highlighted that framing the discussion around reducing maternal mortality by a third resonated with participants. Cheikh Abdeldahim Abdoulaye, secretary-general of Chad's Supreme Council of Islamic Affairs, confirmed his support, noting that the Koran allows for birth spacing to protect maternal health.

Aminatou Bakah, an aid worker with Marie Stopes International—an organization providing reproductive health services across 37 countries—explained that the charity historically battled accusations of Western interference. Locals nicknamed them "Marie Stop," assuming their goal was to halt childbearing altogether, which required staff to clarify that the mission was to assist with family planning rather than dictate choices.

At a temporary clinic operated by the charity in Libore, located 20 kilometers outside Niamey, mothers gathered to seek contraceptive guidance. Among the nine women interviewed in the village, none expressed a desire for smaller families, viewing contraception strictly as a temporary method for spacing children. Rahinatou Kadri, a 24-year-old mother of four, stated she would willingly have 15 children if it were God's will. She noted that her husband, an imam with three wives, includes a senior wife who has borne 16 children. When her husband requested another child, Kadri discontinued her contraceptive implant. Another mother, 34-year-old Mariane Hamadoun with five children, affirmed that religious beliefs forbid putting an end to childbearing.

These prevailing perspectives help explain why birth rates in parts of Africa have not followed the downward trends seen in Europe, Asia, and the Americas as living standards rose. 

Even so, individual perspectives are beginning to shift. Lamodi Soulye, a 39-year-old devout Muslim working in a Niamey Chinese restaurant, grew up among 28 siblings born to one father and three mothers. Recalling periods of hunger and an incomplete primary education due to his father's financial limitations, Soulye stated his intention to avoid repeating that cycle with his own family and plans to have no more than three children.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — President Donald Trump warned on Saturday that government disbursements to insurance providers would be cut off unless lawmakers pass a replacement for the Affordable Care Act, while also challenging lawmakers not to give up on their multi-year effort to overturn the legislation. Writing on Twitter over the weekend, Trump declared that a failure to swiftly pass fresh healthcare legislation would result in the prompt termination of financial bailouts for both insurance firms and members of Congress. 

This social media post followed the inability of Senate Republicans on Friday to secure sufficient votes to dismantle components of the signature healthcare law enacted under former President Barack Obama. The initial portion of Trump's message seemingly targeted the roughly $8 billion allotted annually for cost-sharing reduction subsidies, which the federal government utilizes to help reduce healthcare costs for low-income citizens. Meanwhile, the latter part appeared to target the government contributions toward health insurance for congressional members and their staff, who were transitioned onto the legislation's exchanges as part of the 2010 enactment.

Trump has previously raised the prospect of halting these subsidies, which are managed by the Department of Health and Human Services. Back in April, a similar warning was issued directed at Democrats over negotiations regarding the healthcare legislation. 

In a written statement reacting to the weekend tweet, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer warned that implementing such a threat would drive up costs and worsen coverage affordability for millions, noting that industry experts are in unanimous agreement on the matter. Schumer urged the president to cease playing politics with citizens' health and to adopt a more presidential leadership style.

Shortly after, Trump took to Twitter again to encourage Republican senators to make another attempt at passing a healthcare measure before the chamber departs for its August recess, which is slated to begin after one more week of sessions. Asserting that the repeal-and-replace push is far from finished unless Republicans prove to be total quitters, he called for a new vote prior to considering any other legislation.

Health insurers have been seeking clarity from the administration and Capitol Hill regarding the ongoing provision of these yearly subsidies. Absent any guarantee of funding, multiple providers intend to hike rates by an additional 20 percent ahead of the August 16 deadline for finalising premiums. With the legislative push to undo the law currently in disarray, numerous counties across the nation face the prospect of being left without private health coverage options for 2018 as companies weigh exiting those regions.

Addressing the situation on Friday, Trump reiterated his stance that his administration would allow the healthcare framework to collapse. Past actions by the president include easing mandates for individuals to obtain insurance, threatening funding cuts, and altering plan structures through regulatory changes.

Despite the setback, certain Republican lawmakers continued exploring alternative pathways. Senator Lindsey Graham released a statement on late Friday revealing that he, alongside fellow senators Dean Heller and Bill Cassidy, met with Trump following the vote defeat. Their discussion centered on Graham’s plan to redirect federal tax funds collected under the statute back to individual states via healthcare block grants. Graham asserted this strategy would thwart Democratic ambitions for a national single-payer system by shifting control to local governments. He noted that the president viewed the proposal with optimism and pledged to keep collaborating with the administration on the concept.

Even so, public opinion data indicates that a substantial portion of the population is ready to move past the issue. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published Saturday revealed that 64 percent of the 1,136 individuals surveyed over Friday and Saturday favor retaining Obamacare, either unmodified or with targeted fixes. When queried about legislative priorities, the majority favored focusing on alternative areas like infrastructure, foreign relations, and tax reform. In contrast, merely 29 percent expressed a desire for congressional Republicans to press ahead with a new healthcare measure.

LAHORE/ISLAMABAD (Reuters) - Following his recent release from house arrest, a Pakistani Islamist leader accused of planning the deadly 2008 Mumbai attacks branded former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif a traitor on Friday for pursuing peace with India. 

Hafiz Saeed’s freedom has sparked uncertainty over whether he might step into the political arena to participate with a newly established political party created by his followers. Both Washington and New Delhi voiced strong disapproval over his liberation, demanding that he face prosecution for the atrocities in Mumbai that claimed 166 lives, which included American citizens. 

Carrying a $10 million American bounty on his head, Saeed addressed worshippers during Friday prayers at a Lahore mosque. A judicial panel had ordered his freedom after concluding there was insufficient evidence to keep him confined. When Sharif held the premiership in January, he ordered Saeed's detention, a decision that pleased New Delhi, which has long been outraged that Saeed remained a free man in Pakistan. Although Pakistan's high court removed Sharif from power in July amid corruption probes, his political party remains in control of the government with a loyalist serving as prime minister. 

Nevertheless, Saeed argued that Sharif's diplomatic outreach to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi justified his downfall. Addressing the crowd, Saeed remarked that Sharif questions the reasons behind his ousting, and stated that he considers it an act of treason against Pakistan due to Sharif's attempts at friendship with Modi, whom Saeed accused of being responsible for the deaths of countless Muslims.

India's foreign ministry criticized the decision to set Saeed free, asserting it demonstrates a lack of commitment by Pakistan in bringing terrorists to justice. Meanwhile, Washington expressed deep unease over the development. State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert urged Pakistani authorities to take immediate action by detaining Saeed and filing criminal charges against him.

Throughout the years, Saeed has consistently denied any connection to the 2008 siege in India's financial hub, where a team of 10 attackers targeted several locations, among them a railway station, a rabbinical center, and two high-end hotels. That crisis pushed the two rival nuclear powers dangerously close to armed conflict.

AJACCIO, France (Reuters) — Following a strong showing in a regional election where they captured nearly half of the vote, Corsican nationalists urged the French administration on Monday to begin discussions regarding increased self-governance for the Mediterranean territory.

The nationalist movement—which includes factions pushing for wider autonomy alongside those aiming ultimately for complete separation from France—became the dominant political power in Corsica during the December 2015 regional elections. In Sunday's election for a newly formed local assembly, "Pe a Corsica" (For Corsica), a coalition uniting the two primary nationalist factions, secured 45.36 percent of the vote, placing them in a strong position ahead of the Dec. 10 runoff.

In light of the recent independence vote in Catalonia, Corsican leaders have minimized any goals of breaking away entirely, pointing out that the island does not possess the economic strength or population size of the Spanish area. Corsica is home to roughly 320,000 residents and maintains a modest economy valued at 8.6 billion euros (10.2 billion dollars). Their scaled-back goals, alongside general discontent with the central authorities in Paris, likely contributed to the coalition's electoral gains on Sunday.

Pe a Corsica, bringing together the moderate autonomist group Femu a Corsica and the separatist organization Corsica Libera, has formulated a decade-long plan aimed at securing a special status that grants the island expanded autonomy and fosters improved economic growth.

Gilles Simeoni, a member of Femu a Corsica and the outgoing leader of the island's Executive Council, stated that Paris needs to finally initiate conversations with Corsica, adding that the distinct identity of the Corsican people requires formal recognition.

Officials in the French government indicated they would refrain from issuing statements regarding the election until the second round concludes. Traditionally, France operates as a centralized republic, and past administrations have frequently responded to calls for greater self-rule with annoyance and a refusal to hold talks. 

Nonetheless, backing for the nationalist political platform has grown since the National Front for the Liberation of Corsica (FLNC), the most prominent underground militant organization, abandoned its arms in 2014 following an insurgency lasting nearly forty years. Corsican nationalists reject the political and cultural hegemony exerted by France over the island—which was annexed by Paris in 1768 and is the birthplace of Napoleon—and past nationalist aspirations sparked decades of violent conflict.

Speaking to France Inter radio on Monday, Corsican Assembly president and Corsica Libera chief Jean-Guy Talamoni emphasized that the desires of the local population cannot be ignored indefinitely. At the same time, he conceded that supporters of total independence remain a minority group. He noted that if a majority of Corsicans desire independence in a decade or a decade and a half, nobody will be capable of standing in their way.

Meanwhile, the political movement led by French President Emmanuel Macron finished fourth in Sunday's ballot, capturing 11.26 percent of the vote. Representatives from his Republic On the Move party remarked that the results highlighted a waning faith in Paris among Corsicans and stated their intention to work toward restoring trust throughout the country.

BELLEVILLE, Ill. — Online activity shows that the man who opened fire on Republican lawmakers during a Wednesday baseball practice held deep animosity toward President Donald Trump and looked up to Bernie Sanders as the sole politician who understood ordinary workers. Federal authorities identified the shooter as 66-year-old home inspector James Hodgkinson, hailing from the St. Louis suburb of Belleville, Illinois. He ultimately died from wounds suffered in a gunfight with Capitol Hill police officers stationed at the Alexandria, Virginia, venue just outside Washington. 

A high-ranking U.S. official noted that investigators believe Hodgkinson was an individual characterized by intense beliefs, though no further details were provided. An image published by the Belleville News-Democrat from 2012 captured Hodgkinson wearing a goatee and sunglasses while protesting outside a local post office, gripping a handmade sign that demandeding to tax the wealthy. On March 22, Hodgkinson published a message declaring that Trump ruined democracy and acted as a traitor, adding that the time had come to dismantle Trump and his associates. His profile featured an American flag image accompanied by a description defining democratic socialism through the phrase “We the People.” His brother informed the New York Times that Hodgkinson traveled to the Washington area several weeks prior to protest the presidential outcome. Bill Euille, the former mayor of Alexandria, recounted to the Washington Post that he crossed paths with the suspect nearly every morning at the local YMCA for over a month, even attempting to assist him in securing employment after noticing he was living out of a gym bag. Local attorney Stephen Brennwald also spotted Hodgkinson at the facility wearing trousers instead of athletic gear and noted that he frequently appeared to be gazing blankly into space. State records list Hodgkinson as standing 5 feet, 6 inches tall, weighing 190 pounds, with brown eyes, and detail a criminal background that included a 2006 battery arrest that was subsequently dismissed alongside multiple traffic infractions, most of which were also dropped.
