ISTANBUL — American authorities have indicted a former Turkish economy minister alongside the former chief of a state-run bank, accusing them of plotting to break sanctions against Iran by funneling hundreds of million of dollars through the American banking network for Tehran. 

Announced by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York in a Wednesday statement, the charges represent the first time an individual with such close historical ties to President Tayyip Erdogan has been implicated in the expanding investigation. This probe has already created friction between Ankara and Washington. 

Alongside ex-minister Zafer Caglayan, prosecutors also named former Halkbank general manager Suleyman Aslan and two additional individuals in the indictment. They face allegations of conspiring to route hundreds of millions in transactions via the U.S. financial system on behalf of the Iranian government and other blacklisted entities. Furthermore, the suspects are accused of misleading American officials regarding the nature of the transfers, washing illicit funds, and deceiving various financial institutions by hiding what the money was actually used for. Caglayan specifically stands accused of accepting tens of millions of dollars in cash and jewelry as bribes.

The legal action grows out of an ongoing case concerning Reza Zarrab, a prominent Turkish-Iranian gold merchant who was taken into custody in the United States last year for dodging sanctions. President Erdogan has previously claimed that American officials acted with hidden agendas in prosecuting Zarrab, who maintains his innocence. 

Requests for comment from Caglayan and Aslan were not immediately answered by Reuters. Meanwhile, Halkbank released a statement asserting that all its operations consistently adhered to domestic and international rules, describing the U.S. legal developments as misleading to both investors and the general public.

Diplomatic ties between Washington and Turkey—a key NATO partner essential for operations addressing the Syrian conflict—were already strained following the failed coup against Erdogan in July of last year and the subsequent government crackdown on domestic opposition. Ankara continues to press, unsuccessfully so far, for the extradition of a U.S.-based Muslim cleric whom it blames for orchestrating the putsch. Fethullah Gulen, the cleric in question, has rejected the accusations.

Current Economy Minister Nihat Zeybekci came to the defense of his predecessor, noting that American prosecutors have yet to substantiate their claims. Speaking to reporters, Zeybekci maintained that Caglayan did nothing against Turkish interests, adding that it is irrelevant to Turkey if Caglayan conflicted with the interests of other nations.

According to the indictment, Caglayan and Aslan both received significant bribes. Prosecutors stated that Caglayan took tens of millions in cash and jewelry derived from the scheme aimed at serving the Iranian government while hiding those activities from U.S. officials.

U.S. authorities allege that between 2010 and 2015, Zarrab and his co-conspirators devised methods to supply gold and currency to Iran through the Turkish bank in defiance of sanctions. To pull this off, the group utilized front companies and falsified invoices to deceive American banks into processing the funds under the guise that they were food-related transactions, which were permitted under the sanctions framework.

The new American indictment mirrors details found in a leaked 2014 Turkish police file previously covered by Reuters. That report claimed a criminal syndicate helped Iran bypass Western restrictions that initially allowed Tehran to trade oil and gas revenues for gold. When Western governments outlawed the gold trade in 2013, the network allegedly fabricated records showing massive, unrealistic shipments of food to maintain Iran's access to foreign currency.

Iran eventually stepped out of its economic isolation in January 2016, when global powers rolled back crippling financial barriers after Tehran fulfilled obligations under an agreement to restrict its nuclear program. Those sanctions had previously severed the nation of 80 million people from international finance, reduced exports drastically, and brought severe economic hardship to ordinary Iranians.

According to prosecutors, Caglayan, Aslan, and the other individuals indicted on Wednesday remain at large. Conversely, Zarrab and Mehmet Hakan Atilla, a Halkbank deputy general manager, were apprehended while visiting the United States—Zarrab in March 2016 and Atilla a year later. Both men are set to stand trial in October. To aid in his defense, Zarrab has retained former New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani and former U.S. Attorney General Michael Mukasey. Giuliani has noted that both American and Turkish officials remained open to a diplomatic resolution, citing the nature of the allegations and Turkey's strategic importance as an ally. 

A presidential decree issued a fortnight ago granted Erdogan the power to approve prisoner swaps involving foreigners held or convicted in Turkey for individuals detained abroad, provided national security or national interest demands it.

On the markets, Halkbank shares dropped 3.4 percent to trade at 13.81 lira by 1337 GMT, lagging behind the broader BIST 100 index, which remained relatively unchanged.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Twenty-seven U.S. senators from both major parties addressed a letter to President-elect Donald Trump on Thursday, pressing him to adopt a firm stance against Russia regarding its actions in Ukraine, which the lawmakers described as a military land grab. This communication—signed by 15 Democrats and 12 Republicans, including prominent foreign policy figures from Trump’s own party—highlights an early indication that Congress intends to challenge the incoming administration publicly on foreign policy disagreements. The incoming president, a former New York real estate developer, is scheduled to take office on January 20. 

Throughout his presidential campaign, Trump hinted at a more conciliatory approach toward Moscow, frequently complimenting Russian leader Vladimir Putin on his governance. More recently, Putin mentioned that Trump had assured him of a desire to repair relations. 

Spearheaded by Senate Ukraine caucus co-chairmen Richard Durbin, a Democrat, and Rob Portman, a Republican, the letter states: “In light of Russia’s continued aggression and repeated refusal to respect Ukraine’s territorial integrity and sovereign right to choose its own destiny, we also renew our call for the United States to increase political, economic and military support for Ukraine.” 

According to a copy reviewed by Reuters ahead of its official publication, the lawmakers additionally asserted that the U.S. must reject Russia's annexation of Crimea and maintain the existing sanctions implemented against Moscow due to its actions in eastern Ukraine. 

Relations between President Barack Obama and Putin have proven difficult, marked by deep divisions regarding conflicts in Syria and Ukraine. Friction between Moscow and Obama's party has intensified further following cyber attacks during the American presidential election that were blamed on Russia. 

Signatories belonging to the Republican Party included John McCain, who leads the Senate Armed Services Committee, and Lindsey Graham, chairman of the appropriations subcommittee responsible for the State Department. Additional signatures came from a majority of both Democratic and Republican members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee—such as top Democrat Ben Cardin—along with Jack Reed, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Armed Services panel.

AG Loretta Lynch Just Eviscerated NC Governor Pat McCrory For ‘Right To Discriminate’ Lawsuit (VIDEO)

Following North Carolina Governor Pat McCrory’s (R) announcement that his administration would sue the federal government over efforts to block the state’s transgender bathroom restrictions, Attorney General Loretta Lynch delivered a sharp rebuttal. Lynch took to the podium during a press briefing called shortly after McCrory committed millions of state dollars to a legal fight aimed at keeping transgender individuals out of public restrooms. During her remarks, she delivered a strong defense of equal access to public facilities without harassment or exclusion.

Lynch dissected and denounced the provisions of the legislation known as HB 2, labeling it state-sponsored discrimination. She maintained that the statute is clearly unlawful and confirmed that the Department of Justice intends to persist in its opposition, regardless of the state's legal challenge. 

Addressing the transgender population in North Carolina and nationwide who have witnessed these legislative actions, Lynch offered direct reassurance. She conveyed that the Obama administration and the Department of Justice are fully committed to supporting and defending them throughout the process, stating that they are seen, supported, and protected, and assuring them that history favors their cause. Lynch referenced her personal connection to her birth state of North Carolina, recalling her upbringing during an era marked by historical segregation and drawing parallels to past practices where rest rooms bore signs barring African Americans.

In her address, Lynch cautioned North Carolina officials that financial fallout from ongoing boycotts would be just the beginning of their concerns. A determination that the state violated federal anti-discrimination statutes could jeopardize federal funds allocated for entities such as the state university system and the Department of Public Safety. 

Lynch’s stance highlights the widening ideological divide between the nation's two major political parties. While the Obama administration has signaled a firm commitment to defending the LGBT community, numerous Republican presidential contenders recently campaigned on the argument that transgender people pose a threat as potential predators seeking entry to women’s restrooms—a premise underlying the North Carolina legislation, despite a lack of recorded incidents of sexual assault committed by transgender women against women or girls in public restrooms.

ANKARA (Reuters) - According to a party representative, a Turkish judicial body has mandated the freedom of a lawmaker who previously acted as the spokesperson for the nation's main pro-Kurdish opposition faction. Speaking on Friday, the official explained that the decision regarding Ayhan Bilgen came during a routine monthly assessment of his ongoing incarceration. Bilgen had initially been taken into custody in Diyarbakir, a city in the south, on allegations linking him to an armed terrorist organization. Prior to his arrest, he held the position of parliamentary group leader and spokesman for the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP). 

This judicial development unfolds against a backdrop of mounting anxiety from human rights organizations, Western allies of Turkey, and domestic opposition groups who argue that President Tayyip Erdogan is leveraging post-coup measures to silence political opposition. Following the aborted putsch, approximately 50,000 individuals have faced arrest, while upwards of 150,000 workers and service members have experienced termination or suspension across the military, government administration, and private industries.

Within the HDP specifically, nine parliamentary deputies remain behind bars awaiting trial. Additionally, over 70 elected mayors belonging to the party's southeastern branch have been detained amid terrorism probes, leading to state-appointed trustees taking control of their local administrations. Beyond these measures, thousands of rank-and-file party members have also been detained. 

State authorities in Turkey maintain that the HDP functions as an extension of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), a militant group that has maintained a decades-long insurgency against the government and is designated as a terrorist entity by Ankara, the European Union, and the United States. The HDP, however, rejects any direct association with the group. 

Furthermore, the Turkish legislature has stripped four HDP parliamentarians—among them co-chairwoman Figen Yuksekdag—of their official status, diminishing the footprint of the country's third-largest political force within the 550-member legislature. The party originally secured 59 seats during the general election held in November 2015. Meanwhile, Selahattin Demirtas, the co-leader of the party, has likewise been detained since November of the previous year.

According to the Saturday night release of the Washington Post/ABC poll, Trump currently commands 46 percent support among registered voters, whereas Clinton trails at 44 percent. 

This reflects an eleven-point movement in Trump's direction in comparison to the previous iteration of the survey from March. Specifically, Trump gained six points among registered voters, while Clinton dropped by five points.

LONDON (Reuters) - Virgin Group founder and billionaire Richard Branson disclosed that he became the target of a con artist who pretended to be Britain's defense minister in an attempt to secure a $5 million contribution for an alleged covert ransom payment. In an appeal for public assistance to track down the imposter, Branson noted his suspicion that this same individual subsequently mimicked him to swindle $2 million from an acquaintance under the guise of collecting donations for Hurricane Irma victims. Describing the ordeal in a blog post, Branson remarked that the situation resembled a plot from a James Bond movie or a John le Carre novel, yet confirmed its authenticity. 

Widely known across Britain for his flowing blond hair and beard, Branson leads a brand whose name appears on numerous enterprises spanning telecommunications, fitness centers, railways, and airlines. Half a year ago, Branson recounted, an intricate plot began with a message on counterfeit official stationery, leading to a telephone conversation with an individual claiming to be Defence Secretary Michael Fallon. The caller explained that terrorists had abducted a British diplomat and demanded a ransom. Although the government maintained an official policy against paying ransoms, the caller stressed that exceptional circumstances required rescuing the diplomat, prompting a confidential request for a group of British entrepreneurs to finance the operation. 

According to Branson's account, the impersonator requested $5 million toward the ransom and promised the British government would arrange reimbursement. Growing wary, Branson contacted officials to verify the claim and discovered Fallon had never made the call, prompting a report to the authorities. Half a year later, Branson discovered that a successful American friend had received a call from someone mimicking his own voice and identity. 

The fraudster executed a precise vocal impersonation and fabricated an urgent need for financial assistance while claiming Branson was attempting to coordinate relief efforts in the British Virgin Islands, as detailed in his post. Branson possesses a private island in the BVI chain that suffered severe destruction during Hurricane Irma, a disaster that received widespread media coverage. The perpetrator exploited this specific situation. The scammer convinced the American businessman that UK communications blackouts prevented access to British banks and that the satellite call was established with great difficulty, Branson explained. The businessman generously provided $2 million, which vanished immediately. 

A representative for Fallon confirmed awareness of a pair of impersonation incidents targeting the minister for fraudulent purposes—with one instance excluding Branson—and stated that Fallon's office is cooperating with police investigations to apprehend the culprits.

This week, the legislative push against abortion access by Florida Republicans continues to advance. Earlier on Monday, members of the House took an initial step by voting to advance legislation designed to outlaw nearly every abortion in the state. By an 8-3 margin, the House Criminal Justice Committee approved House Bill 865, known as the Florida For Life Act. Under this legislation, life would be legally defined as beginning at the moment of conception, and two separate doctors would need to verify that an abortion is necessary to prevent the death of the pregnant woman. 

While the likelihood of the legislation reaching the House or Senate floors for a full vote remains minimal, Republican lawmakers acknowledged this expectation during the vote. The primary motivation behind introducing the measure was simply to satisfy Rep. Charles Van Zant. Currently serving his final term, the lawmaker has introduced this identical bill during every year he has held office. 

Rep. Ross Spano, who cast a vote in favor of the bill, remarked to the Associated Press that his vote was essentially a time-wasting exercise, noting that the proposal will likely never receive a hearing in the Senate. Despite the steep hurdles the bill faces before reaching a full vote, a slight possibility remains that it could advance further. Florida currently leans heavily conservative politically, and Republicans nationwide have shown a strong eagerness to roll back reproductive rights. The renewed GOP push to ban abortion was fueled by misleading videos regarding Planned Parenthood that were circulated by individuals facing felony charges.

As reported by the Associated Press, this measure is only one of multiple anti-abortion proposals currently moving forward within the Florida Legislature. Additional bills that have cleared at least one committee include initiatives to ban Medicaid funding for any clinic providing abortions, mandate that abortion providers hold local hospital admitting privileges, subject abortion facilities to the identical construction and licensing standards applied to ambulatory surgical centers, and outlaw the research use of fetal tissue obtained from abortions. 

Consequently, lawmakers are pursuing multiple avenues to restrict reproductive healthcare. Proponents of these measures proceed regardless of the time and financial resources consumed by voting on them, reflecting an ideological stance where partisan priorities supersede constitutional principles and fiscal prudence.

BAGHDAD (Reuters) - Iraqi Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi stated on Thursday that the Kurdish independence referendum must be completely annulled. This stance appeared to dismiss a recent overture from the Kurdistan region to halt its push for independence in an effort to initiate negotiations and de-escalate tensions. In an official statement, Abadi emphasized that nothing short of the vote's cancellation and adherence to the Constitution would be accepted. 

The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) had announced an immediate ceasefire the day before, alongside freezing the outcome of the vote and beginning open discussions with federal authorities grounded in the Iraqi Constitution. From the outset, Baghdad deemed the Kurdish secession vote unlawful. Following the referendum, the central government retaliated last week by reclaiming Kirkuk, its surrounding oil fields, and other regions previously wrested from the Islamic State militant group by Kurdish forces. 

Furthermore, Abadi directed military forces to retake all contested regions and insisted that Baghdad take charge of Iraq's border crossings with Turkey, specifically the Fish-Khabur crossing situated inside the Kurdish autonomous zone. This location holds critical strategic value; a pipeline carrying crude oil from both government- and Kurdish-controlled areas in northern Iraq runs through Fish-Khabur into Turkey, serving as the primary export pathway essential for any viable Kurdish independence movement. 

This military conflict between federal forces and the Kurds presents a delicate dilemma for the United States. Washington maintains close ties to both factions, having provided weaponry and training to both the Iraqi national army and Kurdish fighters to combat Islamic State.

N'DJAMENA (Reuters) - Authorities in Chad have pushed back strongly against claims originating in the U.S. that President Idriss Deby accepted a $2 million payoff to grant petroleum exploration privileges to a Chinese petroleum enterprise while bypassing standard international bidding processes. 

These accusations surfaced when American authorities unveiled criminal complaints on Monday targeting Chi Ping Patrick Ho, previously the home secretary of Hong Kong, alongside Cheikh Gadio, a former top diplomat for Senegal. The pair are accused of orchestrating bribe payments meant for prominent leaders within Chad and Uganda. 

In an official release issued late Wednesday, Chadian authorities expressed profound outrage, calling the accusations a hostile assault on the nation's leader and emphasizing that Deby has consistently championed openness in managing the country's oil and mineral wealth. 

According to the U.S. Department of Justice, financial records show Gadio accepted wire transfers totaling $400,000 originating from Ho through New York financial institutions. These funds were allegedly meant to secure Gadio's services as an intermediary to deliver the illicit payments to Deby on behalf of a Shanghai-based energy corporation. 

Both Ho and Gadio were taken into custody the previous week and have yet to issue public statements regarding the charges leveled against them. 

Chad, a landlocked African nation, currently extracts roughly 130,000 barrels of crude daily. Globally, the country sits near the very bottom of the United Nations Human Development Index and holds the 159th position out of 176 nations evaluated in Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index.

text:
Despite popularizing the catchphrase "You're fired!" during his days hosting the reality television show The Apprentice, President Donald Trump apparently prefers not to say those words in actual everyday situations. This reluctance helps explain why Trump delegated the task of dismissing freshly ousted FBI Director James Comey to his former bodyguard, Keith Schiller. 

So, who exactly is Keith Schiller? Having guarded Trump for nearly twenty years, Schiller has elevated his standing following the election victory, securing the position of Director of Oval Office Operations. Former campaign manager Corey Lewandowski noted that the president holds extraordinary trust in Schiller, confident that any task assigned to him will be successfully completed. 

Schiller's initial connection with the Trump family began in 1999 while he was serving as a New York City police detective. He crossed paths with Marla Maples, Trump's second wife, inside the Manhattan prosecutor's office where she was filing a report regarding a theft committed by an employee. Shortly after he sat down, a man approached and introduced himself as Trump's existing bodyguard. In a rare 2015 video interview, Schiller remembered thinking the man lacked impressive physical stature, which sparked the thought that he could easily do the job himself, noting he was no stranger to physical confrontations. He subsequently contacted Trump and secured a part-time bodyguard job. 

Following his retirement from the police force in 2004, Schiller transitioned to full-time employment with the Trump Organization as security director. This responsibility included traveling alongside Trump on the campaign trail, continuing to provide supplemental security even after the Secret Service assumed primary protection duties. 

While Schiller rarely speaks to the media, associates frequently do. Political adviser Michael Caputo, who collaborated with Trump from 2013 through 2016, arguably offered the most accurate assessment of Schiller's standing within the organization, describing him as much more than a simple bodyguard who understands the internal dynamics of Trump's circle better than anyone else. 

This profound trust was vividly demonstrated in April when Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, visited Iraq. Even though a designated Iraq specialist was left behind because of space limitations on the aircraft, Schiller secured a seat during discussions with Iraqi officials and was featured in official delegation photographs. 

Before integrating into Trump's inner circle, Schiller built a reputation among his NYPD peers for remarkable physical power. David Chong, who managed Schiller for eight years on a New York City drug-trafficking task force, described him as possessing the strength of an ox. Chong recalled that during police raids, Schiller frequently volunteered to carry the sixty-pound battering ram to breach doors at the end of stairwells. 

Schiller also acted as Trump's primary assistant during a WWE appearance, stepping briefly into public view after Trump physically struck World Wrestling Entertainment head Vince McMahon in the ring. During the scripted sequence, when McMahon retaliated by charging toward Trump, Schiller intercepted him, pushed him back repeatedly, and ultimately allowed Trump to force him to the ground. 

Naturally, associations with the Trump organization often attract controversy, and Schiller has encountered his share. During the 2015 presidential campaign, in September, Schiller confiscated a placard from a demonstrator. The protester, Efrain Galicia, unexpectedly lunged forward and was struck in the face by Schiller, prompting ongoing legal action from Galicia and other demonstrators. During legal testimony, Schiller admitted that he lacked an active New York state security guard license at the time of the altercation. Days prior to that event, Schiller physically ejected Univision news anchor Jorge Ramos from a campaign press conference after Ramos persistently shouted questions concerning immigration.

Given this background, it seems entirely consistent that Donald Trump avoided confronting the towering James Comey personally, choosing Schiller instead of a lower-ranking staff member to deliver the termination. After all, such a decision feels natural when an enforcer of that caliber is stationed just desks away.

Featured image by Drew Angerer/Getty Images

NEW YORK (Reuters) - Following Hillary Clinton securing the Democratic nomination for the November 8 presidential race, President Barack Obama expressed his desire on Wednesday that party fractures would begin to mend shortly. Speaking publicly for the first time following Tuesday's primary victories in California and other states—which secured Clinton's win against challenger Bernie Sanders following an intense, months-long battle—Obama stated, "My hope is that over the next couple of weeks we’re able to pull things together."

Appearing on NBC's "The Tonight Show" for an interview scheduled to air on Thursday, Obama told host Jimmy Fallon, "What happens during primaries is you get a little ouchy." Although Sanders has not yet exited the race, he is scheduled to have a meeting with the president at the White House on Thursday morning.

Addressing approximately 60 Democratic donors who contributed up to $33,400 each to attend a fundraiser at the Central Park West residence of venture capitalist and BuzzFeed chairman Kenneth Lerer, Obama mentioned he was "not too worried" regarding any "bruised feelings" remaining from the primary contests. 

"We just ended - sort of ended - our primary season," Obama remarked, correcting himself as the audience chuckled nervously. 

"I am concerned about us doing the hard nuts-and-bolts work of turning out people to vote, particularly young people, particularly low-income people," Obama added.

When questioned about whether the president believed the Vermont senator ought to conclude his campaign promptly, White House spokesman Josh Earnest noted that Sanders had "more than earned the right to make his own decision about the course of his campaign." 

The party is set to formalize Clinton's nomination during its July convention in Philadelphia. 

During his conversation with Fallon, Obama characterized the contested primary as "a healthy thing for the Democratic Party," while commending Sanders for injecting "enormous energy and new ideas" into the race. 

"He pushed the party and challenged them. I thought it made Hillary a better candidate," said Obama.

With the president maintaining high popularity among Democrats, the White House has indicated he will take on a unifying function during the campaign. 

"The main role I’m going to be playing in this process is to remind the American people that this is a serious job. This is not reality TV," Obama told Fallon, making a clear reference to presumptive Republican nominee Donald Trump, a real estate figure known for hosting a reality television program.

Paul Craig Roberts: ‘By Cooperating with Washington on Syria & Russia Walked Into a Trap’

By Paul Crag Roberts

Thirty days have passed since the publication of my previous essay, titled “He Who Hesitates Is Lost And Russia Hesitated.” The fallout from that delay has now materialized:

1. A United Nations document, engineered by Washington, places the blame for alleged war crimes in Aleppo squarely on the shoulders of Syria and Moscow. The findings claim that indiscriminate bombing campaigns in the eastern quarters by government forces and their Russian allies account for the vast majority of non-combatant deaths, categorizing these actions as war crimes and, potentially, crimes against humanity given their systematic nature. Consequently, the UN Human Rights Council has approved the launch of an independent probe aimed at prosecuting Russia and Vladimir Putin as war criminals, with recommendations that the matter be forwarded urgently to the International Criminal Court without exceptions for any faction. Considering that the United States is the primary financial contributor to the United Nations, the organization conveniently ignores the fact that Washington was responsible for dispatching ISIS into Aleppo.

While dragging Putin before the International Criminal Court remains an impossibility for both the US and the UN, slapping him with war crimes accusations serves Washington's underlying goal of restricting his international travel and diplomatic outreach. The core value of this orchestrated maneuver is propaganda. Amid American anxieties that certain Eastern European nations might threaten NATO with non-participation out of fear of a Washington-led conflict, branding Russia as a war criminal makes it significantly harder for these states to distance themselves from the alliance's trajectory.

2. Washington has facilitated the rise of the hardline Law and Justice Party in Poland. These political actors have revived investigations into the fatal plane crash involving Polish President Kaczynski, alleging that Moscow orchestrated a terrorist attack to decapitate the nation's leadership. Despite overwhelming evidence debunking this theory, the party's assertions gain ground thanks to the ongoing demonization of Russia by Washington, ultimately serving to further isolate and tarnish the Russian government.

3. Acting as the standard-bearer for neoconservative warmongers, Hillary advocates for the implementation of a no-fly zone in Syria. Such a measure would compel Washington to block Syrian and Russian aerial operations targeting ISIS elements. Naturally, neither Damascus nor Moscow would acquiesce to losing control of their sovereign airspace while fighting insurgents backed by the US for regime change, mirroring the events that preceded the fall of Gaddafi in Libya. Short of total capitulation by Syria and Russia, establishing this no-fly zone would inevitably trigger a direct military clash between Washington and Moscow.

To build momentum for the no-fly zone, the narrative regarding chemical weapons has been revived through dubious claims that the Syrian military has targeted its own citizens with toxic agents. Reports surfaced indicating that the UN-Led Joint Investigative Mechanism briefed the Security Council regarding a chemical incident in Qmenas, alleging it stemmed from a Syrian military helicopter dropping a cylinder containing toxic substances. The findings claimed three such attacks were executed by Syria and one by the Islamic State. 

Given that Moscow successfully dismantled and removed Syria's chemical arsenal back in 2014—prior to the alleged Qmenas incident—the report lacks any real credibility. Nevertheless, facts have consistently been absent from Washington's fifteen-year campaign across the Muslim world, just as they are absent from its current efforts to vilify Russia.

4. Analyst Diana Johnstone has pointed out that Hillary's ultimate objective is regime change in Moscow, a goal she intends to pursue from the presidency.

It is difficult to conceive of a more hazardous and reckless agenda. Numerous figures within the Russian administration have noted that constant provocations and smear campaigns have reduced trust between the nuclear-armed states to practically nothing, leaving Moscow resolved never again to fight a war on its domestic soil.

text:
During the upcoming regional visit by United States Vice President Mike Pence, Palestinian President Mahmoud Altman will refuse to hold discussions with him, according to a statement made on Saturday by the Palestinian foreign minister. This decision serves as a direct rebuff to the recent declaration by President Donald Trump acknowledging Jerusalem as the capital of Israel, a policy shift that reverses decades of established American foreign relations. 

Following the announcement made on Wednesday, protests in Gaza turned violent for the third consecutive day. The unrest was fueled further after Palestinian factions designated Friday as a "day of rage," leading militants to launch rockets into Israel. In response, Israeli air strikes on Saturday resulted in the deaths of two Palestinian gunmen.

The Trump administration's decision regarding Jerusalem has sparked widespread anger throughout the Arab world and caused concern among Western partners, who view the step as a setback for peace efforts that could potentially ignite additional regional conflict. Following an emergency gathering in Cairo late Saturday, Arab foreign ministers formally requested that Washington reverse its choice, characterizing the action as a catalyst for widespread regional hostility. The Arab League issued a declaration labeling the announcement a severe breach of international law that carries no legal weight and is considered null.

Ahead of discussions in Paris on Sunday with French President Emmanuel Macron—followed by meetings with European foreign ministers in Brussels—Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed his critics publicly. He noted that while he has encountered European disapproval over the U.S. decision, he has not heard any corresponding condemnation regarding the subsequent rocket attacks directed at Israel or the harsh incitement faced by the country. 

While Israel views the entirety of Jerusalem as its capital, Palestinians claim East Jerusalem as the seat of government for an independent nation they hope to establish in the future. The majority of the international community regards East Jerusalem—annexed by Israel following its capture during the 1967 conflict—as occupied territory, maintaining that the ultimate status of the municipality ought to be determined through upcoming bilateral negotiations. Meanwhile, the current U.S. administration asserts its ongoing dedication to the peace process, arguing that any credible peace framework would place Israel's capital in Jerusalem while declining to specify the city's boundaries. Furthermore, American officials contend that previous approaches are obsolete and must be discarded to restart stalled talks.

Speaking to reporters in Cairo prior to the Arab League assembly, Palestinian Foreign Minister Riyad al-Maliki announced that the Palestinian leadership will seek a replacement for the United States as a mediator in peace negotiations and intends to pursue a resolution through the United Nations Security Council. He stated that they will look to Arab allies and the broader international community for a new facilitator. Additionally, a Turkish presidential source revealed that leaders Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Emmanuel Macron will collaborate in an attempt to convince Washington to alter its stance. 

State news agency MENA also reported that Egypt’s Coptic Church has declined a potential meeting with Pence. Representatives for the White House and the State Department did not provide comments when asked. Palestinian officials confirmed that Pence had originally scheduled a meeting with Abbas for December 19. Efforts to revive the stalled peace talks are currently being spearheaded by Trump's advisor and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, though these initiatives have yielded limited visible progress so far.

In the aftermath of Friday night's rocket fire from Gaza toward Israeli communities, Israel reported that its retaliatory air strikes successfully hit two weapons manufacturing sites, a military compound, and a weapons depot. Hamas, the group governing Gaza, verified that the two individuals killed in the early morning strikes were its members, and the organization has continued to encourage Palestinians to maintain their confrontation against Israeli forces.

The proposed accord was detailed in an official decree bearing the signature of Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev, dated Nov. 28. Within the document, the Russian Defence Ministry is instructed to engage in discussions with Egyptian counterparts and to execute the agreement upon reaching a mutual consensus. 

Prior to the decree's release, Russian Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu traveled to Cairo for discussions with the nation's political and military leaders on Wednesday. Since initiating a military campaign in September 2015 to back Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, Russia has shown indications of a desire to broaden its footprint in the area. American officials asserted in March that Moscow had stationed special operations forces in Egypt close to the Libyan frontier, though the Kremlin disputed the claim. 

Furthermore, Moscow has built strong relations with prominent Libyan commander Khalifa Haftar. Haftar spoke with Shoigu through a video link originating from a Russian aircraft carrier in the Mediterranean earlier in the year and has also traveled to Moscow. 

Under the terms of the draft text, Russian and Egyptian military jets would gain mutual access to airbases and airspace by providing a five-day notification in advance. The agreement is anticipated to remain in force for a duration of five years, with the possibility of a renewal.

While most avoided issuing outright condemnations of Trump, some did voice anxieties that the leaked footage—which captured the former reality television personality bragging on an open mic about attempting to seduce a married woman and grabbing women—might dampen voter turnout among evangelicals on November 8. Rather than breaking with the candidate, these leaders emphasized the critical necessity of blocking Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton from capturing the White House, influencing the composition of the Supreme Court, and advancing progressive policies.

While acknowledging Trump's remarks were deeply improper, Bauer argued that the core dilemma of the election remained unchanged, warning that Clinton would champion measures that undermine religious freedom, foster abortion, compromise national security, and leave borders vulnerable.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - According to a high-ranking member of the transition team on Wednesday, President-elect Donald Trump plans to select former Georgia Governor Sonny Perdue for the position of agriculture secretary on Thursday. At 70 years of age, Perdue previously worked on the agricultural advisory panel for Trump's campaign. The Senate, which is controlled by Republicans, will need to confirm the choice, which finalizes the proposed cabinet selections for Trump right before his inauguration ceremony on Friday. 

By selecting a past governor originating from the South, Trump bypassed potential candidates originating from core Midwestern Farm Belt regions, which account for the majority of the nation's wheat, corn, and soybean production—staples of agricultural exports. In contrast, Georgia stands out as a major producer of peanuts and cotton. During his tenure leading Georgia, Perdue faced a major drought in 2007, implementing water conservation measures and even organizing a prayer gathering for rain outside the statehouse. 

A Republican, Perdue won two gubernatorial terms and held office from 2003 through 2011. Prior to that role, he served as a state senator for a rural district situated approximately 100 miles, or 160 kilometers, south of Atlanta. In 1998, he changed his political affiliation from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party amidst changing demographics and local redistricting efforts. 

Amidst a declining farm economy marked by dropping commodity prices, the agricultural sector backed Trump strongly. American Soybean Association (ASA) President Ron Moore expressed his belief that Perdue would advocate for agricultural exports during a phone interview, stating that he expects the nominee to heavily support trade. Earlier this month, the ASA joined forces with 16 other agricultural organizations to call upon the incoming administration to safeguard and improve trade in agriculture and its benefits for rural communities. 

Because Trump frequently targeted China during his campaign for unfair trade practices, trade remained a central theme, which is vital to the farming sector. In 2015, American food and agricultural exports shipped to China exceeded $20.2 billion. Driven by robust demand from China—which purchases nearly 30% of the domestic harvest—soybean prices climbed 16.2 percent throughout 2016. Furthermore, these soybean shipments contributed to an increase in the U.S. gross domestic product during the third quarter. 

Nevertheless, certain agricultural producers worry that Trump’s rhetoric regarding China might sour trade dynamics and jeopardize exports. Earlier in the week, a prominent state-operated newspaper in China cautioned that American plane manufacturer Boeing Co and U.S. agricultural goods could become targets of retaliation should a trade war begin under Trump. 

American Farm Bureau President Zippy Duvall voiced support for Perdue, describing him as a powerful advocate. Conversely, environmental organizations criticized the selection. Kari Hamerschlag, who serves as the deputy director of food and technology at Friends of the Earth, argued in an official statement that farmers require a leader within the USDA dedicated to defending conservation initiatives that build resilience against severe weather, rather than someone who relies on praying for rain. 

Following the conclusion of his tenure as governor, Perdue established a global trading company named Perdue Partners, which offers consulting and services to businesses seeking international export opportunities. His cousin, David Perdue, holds a seat in the U.S. Senate representing Georgia. The nominee does not share any family relation with the poultry executive Frank Perdue.

PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron laid out a grand blueprint for European renewal on Tuesday, advocating for tighter integration on defense and immigration alongside a dedicated budget for the euro zone—though translating these proposals into reality could prove difficult. 

Taking the stage at the Sorbonne just two days after Germany's federal election, where Chancellor Angela Merkel's CDU/CSU conservative alliance suffered its worst showing since 1949 and saw its room to maneuver on European policy constrained, the 39-year-old French leader delivered a nearly two-hour address marked by immense self-assurance and ambition. Yet, with the European Union currently strained by east-west tensions and struggling to move past nearly a decade of debilitating economic turbulence, Macron's earnest and occasionally lofty discourse ran the distinct risk of being ignored.

Framing Europe as an institution in urgent need of a relaunch, the former philosophy student and investment banker, framed by French and European Union flags, argued that deep cooperation is vital across a wide array of areas, including asylum policy, border security, corporate taxation, intelligence sharing, defense, and financial stability. 

"The only path that assures our future is the rebuilding of a Europe that is sovereign, united and democratic," he stated, adding that by the start of the next decade, the continent ought to establish a joint intervention force, a common defense budget, and a unified action doctrine.

Overhaul of the European Union was a cornerstone of Macron's centrist presidential campaign. Both he and Merkel have frequently emphasized their desire for France and Germany—the two largest economies in the bloc and its traditional engines of change—to spearhead integration. However, only five months into his five-year term, Macron confronts the reality that the 63-year-old Merkel, who is seeking a fourth term, has less political capital to expend than either leader might have wished. While her conservative alliance remains the largest force in the Bundestag, forming a workable majority will likely require a coalition with the Greens and the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP), both of which are hostile to many of Macron's core proposals.

German Foreign Minister Sigmar Gabriel, a high-ranking member of the Social Democrats (SPD)—whose party has ruled out joining another grand coalition—praised the address as "a passionate plea against nationalism and for Europe." 

"He can count on us," Gabriel affirmed.

Rather than moderating his message to align with the preferences of Merkel, the Greens, or the FDP, Macron kept his vision sweeping and expansive, while also putting forward concrete suggestions for bolstering the euro zone. Highlighting the necessity of democratic accountability, he argued that a budget must be paired with robust political leadership headed by a shared finance minister, alongside rigorous parliamentary oversight at the European level.

The fiscally conservative FDP strongly opposes the creation of a euro zone budget or any mechanism that could facilitate financial transfers from wealthier member states to poorer ones, as well as the potential pooling of national debt. Furthermore, the party has advocated for phasing out Europe's ESM bailout fund—which Macron wants to transform into a European Monetary Fund—and supports amending EU treaties to permit member countries to exit the euro zone.

"You don't strengthen Europe with new pots of money," Alexander Lambsdorff, an FDP member of the European Parliament, posted on Twitter following the address. In an official statement released by the FDP in Berlin, Lambsdorff added, "The problem in Europe is not a lack of public funds, but the lack of reform. A euro zone budget would set exactly the wrong incentives."

Without shying away from addressing Germany directly, even as Berlin navigates the political fallout from Sunday's vote, Macron challenged the two nations to completely integrate their markets and corporate regulations by the year 2024. 

"We share the same European ambitions and I know her commitment to Europe," Macron said of Merkel. "I'm proposing to Germany a new partnership. We will not agree on everything, not immediately, but we will discuss everything."

Speaking in Berlin on Monday, Merkel stressed the importance of moving beyond empty catchphrases and offering specific details on how to improve Europe. It remained uncertain whether Macron's speech satisfied that criterion from her perspective. 

Nonetheless, Martin Selmayr, chief of staff to European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker, noted that the French proposals for strengthening the euro zone would be evaluated alongside Juncker's own ideas during a euro zone summit scheduled for December. Meanwhile, Italian EU Affairs Minister Sandro Gozi predicted the address would spur European leaders into action.

"An excellent speech by Emmanuel Macron on reviving the European Union. Let's work on this together, starting tomorrow at the Lyon Summit," Gozi remarked, referencing an upcoming meeting between French and Italian leaders focused on industrial policy.

Macron noted that he hoped his recommendations would influence Germany's coalition negotiations, which are not anticipated to kick off until mid-October and could drag on for months. 

"Some had said I should wait for the coalition talks to be concluded," Macron observed, noting that had he waited, the reaction in Berlin likely would have been: "Your proposals are great but it's too late, the coalition deal already lays out what will we do on Europe for the next four years."

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - According to a Reuters/Ipsos survey published on Monday, fifty percent of America’s likely voters are counting on the presidential debates to assist them in choosing between Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton and Republican contender Donald Trump for the November 8 election. 

This data highlights the immense pressure facing the two White House contenders as they get ready for their initial face-to-face encounter at Hofstra University in Long Island, New York. This upcoming prime-time television event is projected to attract a massive viewership of 100 million citizens, comparable to the Super Bowl. 

The survey indicates that roughly half of likely voters believe the showdowns will assist in clarifying their vote, a figure that includes 10 percent who are currently undecided. Conversely, 39 percent stated the debates would offer no assistance, while 11 percent remained uncertain about the impact. 

Demonstrating a strong desire for clarity from the broadcasts, 72 percent of those surveyed indicated they expect moderators to fact-check the candidates and correct false statements. The poll showed this sentiment was shared by 73 percent of Trump backers and 82 percent of individuals supporting Clinton. 

“It helps the audience, particularly me, to recognize what’s bull crap and what’s real,” remarked 63-year-old teacher Harvey Leven from Farmington Hills, Michigan, adding, “It’s easy for the candidates to quote a statistic and people accept it.”

At present, Clinton maintains a narrow national lead in the majority of national polls and holds vital edges in essential battleground states such as North Carolina and Ohio. The most recent Reuters/Ipsos data puts her 4 percentage points ahead of Trump nationwide. Her support had experienced a decline over the preceding weeks following renewed scrutiny regarding her private email server usage as secretary of state, alongside questions concerning her family's foundation.

NO TO NAME-CALLING

Following several months of aggressive campaigning and reciprocal insults, numerous voters anticipate a more restrained and civil encounter. Trump has previously suggested that Clinton belongs in prison over her email practices during her tenure as America's chief diplomat, whereas Clinton has characterized Trump as racially biased and temperamentally unsuited for the presidency. 

The survey revealed that 61 percent of participants have no desire to witness such mudslinging. 

“Quit picking on each other,” expressed 48-year-old Lisa Miller from St. Louis, Missouri. “This isn’t a playground. Grow up and talk about your plan.”

The survey additionally indicated that the largest share of likely voters hopes the contenders will focus their discussions on employment and economic matters. 

“I’ll tell you with Donald Trump I want to see that he has rational answers to questions without name calling,” Leven stated. “I want to try to get beyond the political hocus pocus that both of them are doing and try to see who they really are.”

Carried out in English across all 50 states via the internet, the Reuters/Ipsos poll gathered responses from 2,124 American adults. This group included 1,337 individuals classified as likely voters based on their registration status, voting background, and declared commitment to participate on Election Day. The survey's measure of accuracy, known as a credibility interval, stands at 2 percentage points for the entire pool of respondents and 3 percentage points for the likely voters.

The U.S. Department of Justice advised Judicial Watch that the FBI has found 30 pages of records concerning the June 27, 2016, airport tarmac encounter involving former President Bill Clinton and former Attorney General Loretta Lynch. The Justice Department suggested that any non-exempt portions should be turned over by November 30, 2017, according to the lawsuit Judicial Watch v. U.S. Department of Justice, docketed as No. 1:16-cv-02046. 

These upcoming records are being provided due to a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit. The legal action was initiated after the Justice Department failed to answer a July 7, 2016, FOIA submission that asked for multiple items: all FD-302 forms from the FBI's probe into former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's private email server use while in office; all communication records among FBI personnel concerning that same investigation, which covers exchanges with the Department of Justice, the White House, the Democratic National Committee, and the Hillary Clinton presidential campaign; and all documents tied to the June 27, 2016, interaction between Bill Clinton and Loretta Lynch.

Initially, the FBI told Judicial Watch that no records existed regarding the tarmac gathering. Yet, through a separate legal matter, the Justice Department uncovered emails showing Justice Department personnel corresponding with the bureau about the meeting. Consequently, an August 10, 2017, letter from the FBI explained that a deeper review suggested relevant records might exist, prompting the reopening of the FOIA request. Meanwhile, the Trump Justice Department has declined to release the talking points formulated by the Obama Justice Department to handle media questions regarding the disputed June 27 encounter at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport between Bill Clinton and Loretta Lynch.

The private meeting took place on a parked private aircraft at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport in Arizona on June 27, 2016, unfolding while the investigation into Mrs. Clinton's email server was active and shortly before the public release of the Benghazi report involving the Obama administration and Mrs. Clinton. On June 30, Judicial Watch petitioned the U.S. Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General to launch an inquiry into the rendezvous. 

Tom Fitton of Judicial Watch expressed sharp criticism, stating that the FBI is out of control and that it is remarkable these records were only discovered after the agency was caught concealing them in a separate legal proceeding. He added that Judicial Watch will keep fighting in court for clarity regarding the FBI's document handling, and demanded that the bureau end its obstruction and immediately make the new files public. This litigation has already compelled the FBI to make part of its Clinton investigative file public, though over half of those files remain withheld, and the bureau indicated it expects to finish processing those materials by July 2018.

Questions have long persisted over whether the Obama Justice Department and the FBI afforded special treatment to Clinton and other potential targets or witnesses. The Obama administration granted several immunity deals, encompassing Cheryl Mills, former Chief of Staff to Clinton; John Bentel, former head of the State Department’s Office of Information Resources Management; Heather Samuelson, executive assistant to Clinton; Brian Pagliano, a State Department IT worker who managed Clinton's private server; and a staff member at Platt River Networks, the firm that serviced the server. It remains uncertain if Hillary Clinton herself was granted any form of immunity.

Additionally, a political action committee directed by McAulilffe—a longtime ally and political backer of Bill and Hillary Clinton—contributed nearly $500,000 in 2015 to Jill McCabe during her run for the Virginia State Senate. The Virginia Democratic Party, heavily influenced by McAuliffe, provided an extra $207,788 to Jill McCabe's campaign. At that time, in July 2015, Andrew McCabe led the FBI’s Washington, D.C., field office, which supplied personnel to the Clinton email investigation, prompting multiple lawsuits from Judicial Watch concerning the McCabe, FBI, and Clinton controversy.

During a recent broadcast of The View, panelist and self-described conservative Jedediah Bila surprised viewers by departing from her usual pattern of rarely opposing her progressive co-hosts. While the panel discussed the ongoing Senate Intelligence Committee hearings concerning the firing of FBI Director James Comey, Bila labeled Comey a "coward" and ridiculed his testimony. 

Her remarks prompted co-host Joy Behar to interject, telling Bila that her perspective on Comey was "irrelevant." The conversation intensified when Bila criticized Comey for acquiescing to former Attorney General Loretta Lynch's request to label the Hillary Clinton email inquiry a "matter" rather than an "investigation." 

This critique immediately drew pushback from the rest of the panel. Whoopi Goldberg stepped in to caution Bila against attempting to "muddy the waters" in the manner "they" try to do. Throughout the exchange, the program's co-hosts pushed back against Bila's rare departure from the prevailing viewpoints on the table.

A federal appeals court decided on Friday to freeze a controversial Arizona voting statute backed by Republicans, blocking its implementation until the conclusion of Tuesday's election. This ruling provides a win for Democrats amid a broader, nationwide web of lawsuits concerning voter access. Earlier in the legislative session, Arizona lawmakers approved the measure to ban advocacy organizations from gathering completed early ballots from citizens and dropping them off at election centers as part of voter mobilization campaigns. 

The legal challengers, which featured the Democratic National Committee, contended that the legislation was unconstitutional due to its disproportionate negative effect on minority voting access. Within the state's presidential contest, recent polling has indicated a narrow advantage for Republican Donald Trump over his Democratic rival, Hillary Clinton. 

Earlier in the week, the San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals agreed to reconsider a prior decision that had declined to halt the statute, opting for a hearing before an expanded panel of 11 judges. According to court documentation, that panel delivered a 6-5 vote on Friday to bar the state of Arizona from implementing the rule immediately. Subsequently, Arizona submitted an emergency request to the U.S. Supreme Court on Friday afternoon, seeking an overturn of the 9th Circuit decision. 

Democrats have maintained that Republican-led states pursue such regulations to suppress turnout among minorities and other demographic groups that typically support Democratic contenders. Conversely, Republicans argue that these rules are essential safeguards against electoral fraud. 

In his opinion, 9th Circuit Chief Judge Sidney Thomas noted that the ruling would not interfere with the administration of the presidential election in Arizona. He stated that the order merely blocks the enforcement of legislation that would otherwise turn the collection of validly cast ballots by third parties into a criminal offense. Thomas and five other judges, all of whom were appointed by Democratic presidents, formed the majority. Meanwhile, five dissenting judges—every one of whom was appointed by a Republican president—maintained that the judiciary ought not to intervene in state statutes so close to Election Day while early voting is actively taking place. The jurisdiction of the 9th Circuit encompasses nine Western states, which includes Arizona. 

Arizona Secretary of State Michele Reagan expressed dissatisfaction with the outcome in a public statement, warning that the ruling would create voter confusion and lower participation rates. Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the Democratic National Committee was not immediately available for remarks. 

In a separate legal development on Friday involving a key battleground state, a federal judge in Ohio issued an order prohibiting Donald Trump’s campaign from verbally harassing voters or taking photographs of them near polling locations.

At a Monday presidential campaign event, an audience member whose son is in the U.S. Air Force faced jeers from the crowd after trying to question Vice Presidential nominee Governor Mike Pence, continuing a pattern of hostility toward military families associated with Donald Trump's campaign. The incident unfolded in a Carson City, Nevada, casino venue where Pence was fielding questions from attendees following a typical campaign address.

The mother stepped up to ask the second question, bringing up Trump's public dispute with Khizr and Ghazala Khan, Muslim parents whose decorated Army veteran son lost his life in Iraq back in 2004. Directing her inquiry to Pence, she asked if there would ever come a moment when he could look Trump in the eye and declare that "enough is enough," which immediately drew a chorus of boos from the surrounding supporters. 

While the woman's microphone was being removed, Pence quieted the room by remarking that the reaction represented what freedom looks and sounds like. He then stated that Captain Khan is an American hero whose family and memory deserve honor. However, neither Pence nor Trump condemned the candidate's prior criticisms of the Khans, who had previously criticized Trump's proposed Muslim travel ban during the Democratic Convention.

Trump maintained that the Khans had launched a vicious attack against him and suggested that Ghazala Khan remained silent at the convention because of her Islamic religion. In response, Khan explained through an MSNBC interview and a Washington Post op-ed that her silence stemmed from ongoing grief over her son's passing. 

The backlash against Trump's remarks included condemnation from the Veterans of Foreign Wars and various other Gold Star families demanding an apology. Although several Republican senators and governors criticized the comments publicly, they stopped short of withdrawing their endorsements for the presidential ticket.

BROWNSVILLE, Texas — Rising from a dusty patch of land on the Loop family farm in South Texas, roughly 15 miles inland from the Gulf of Mexico and a mile north of the international boundary, sits a rust-colored security barrier. Winding about 60 miles westward from the Brownsville area, the structure is punctuated by numerous large gaps that allow vehicles and pedestrians to pass freely. Even where the barrier is standing, it frequently fails to deter unauthorized crossings. Farmer Ray Loop pointed out muddy footprints scaling multiple sections on his land, remarking that climbers can clear the height in about a minute and a half.

Authorized back in 2006, this imperfect South Texas barrier highlights the myriad obstacles—including difficult terrain, international treaties, expensive legal battles, and massive costs—that could hinder President-elect Donald Trump’s signature campaign promise of erecting an unbreakable wall across the entire 2,000-mile frontier. Denise Gilman, a law professor and director of the Immigration Clinic at the University of Texas at Austin, described the barrier as consisting of “more holes than it is fence.” Internal government emails secured by Gilman via a court order and reviewed by Reuters indicate that these gaps were the result of local political pushback, property rights litigation, and cost-efficiency calculations.

Jason Miller, a spokesperson for the Trump transition team, declined to address these potential hurdles, stating that the incoming president will have ample opportunity to delve into policy specifics following his January inauguration. However, during an interview on CBS’ “60 minutes” the previous month, Trump acknowledged for the first time that fencing could be utilized in certain sections. “There could be some fencing,” he remarked, adding, “I’m very good at this. It’s called construction. There could be some fencing, but some areas, a wall is more appropriate.”

Fifty-one-year-old Ray Loop backs tougher immigration measures and voted for Trump, yet he remains skeptical about physical barriers. Speaking from his pickup truck while driving past border patrol vehicles on his property, Loop dismissed the concept: “That is not going to work. There are places where it makes sense logistically, but all the way from Texas to California? No.”

Acting as a primary artery for unauthorized crossings, the Rio Grande Valley has emerged as a central hub for immigration enforcement. U.S. Customs and Border Protection defended the infrastructure in a statement, emphasizing that fencing forms part of a broader strategy that incorporates ground agents, cameras, motion sensors, and aerial surveillance. Meanwhile, Jon Feere, a legal policy analyst at the Washington-based Center for Immigration Studies, which advocates for robust border security, suggested that a comprehensive approach must extend beyond a single wall. He noted that while fencing can significantly complicate clandestine crossings, it cannot serve as a standalone solution.

The Secure Fence Act, enacted in 2006 under Republican President George W. Bush, severely miscalculated the expenses required to build roughly 670 miles of planned barriers spanning from California to Texas. By the time Democratic President Barack Obama declared the project largely finished in 2011, the allocated $2.4 billion had only funded about half of that intended distance, figures from a U.S. Government Accounting Office report show. Both Obama and Democratic presidential contender Hillary Clinton had voted in favor of the legislation during their time as U.S. senators.

In the South Texas region, original blueprints calling for a double layer of reinforced fencing spanning roughly 200 miles between Brownsville and Laredo were eventually reduced to a single-layered, interrupted barrier covering only about a third of that span. Challenging border geography sparked numerous land rights disputes that drove up expenses and prolonged construction timelines. With roughly 1,200 miles of the frontier situated along the winding Rio Grande in Texas, constructing a barrier directly on the actual border is physically impossible. 

Furthermore, the International Boundary and Water Commission, established jointly by the two nations in 1889, prohibits any obstruction to the river’s natural flow, meaning any wall must be positioned on flood plain levees. In South Texas, this requirement pushed the fence as far as two miles north into U.S. territory. As a result, properties ended up stranded on the Mexico-facing side in a sort of no man’s land, forcing the government to reimburse owners for diminished land value. 

Loop’s residence and the vast majority of his farmland sit on the southern, Mexico-facing side of the barrier inside U.S. territory, though he resolved his eminent domain litigation with the government under confidential terms. Another prolonged legal battle dragged on for seven years across 140 court filings as Eloisa Tamez challenged government efforts to strand a portion of her family's historic acreage—originally granted by the King of Spain in 1767—behind the wall. The federal government ultimately settled for an undisclosed amount and agreed to install several access gates through the fence on her property. 

Economic fallout is also evident elsewhere; the Fort Brown Memorial Golf Course in Brownsville was trapped behind the barrier and ultimately shut down in 2015 after suffering steep losses from patrons who mistakenly believed entering the facility meant leaving the United States. 

Legal authorities note that while Trump would likely face little difficulty acquiring land via eminent domain for national security projects, property owners may now demand higher payouts since earlier construction phases established clear precedents of falling property values. Legal experts indicate that several compensation and property disputes initiated during the Bush administration could bleed into the Trump era, potentially triggering a fresh wave of litigation. Efren Olivares, regional legal director for the Texas Civil Rights Project’s South Texas office—which has represented landowners in barrier disputes—warned that court battles will inevitably stall any construction efforts for months or even years.

Economic and local political factors also present significant hurdles. A major gap persists just west of Brownsville, where residents in an affluent community successfully fended off construction. Internal correspondence from U.S. Customs and Border Protection reveals that authorities deliberately steered clear of high-value real estate. In a March 2007 operational report, divisional bureau chief Jeffrey Self wrote that the agency would avoid building fences in urban zones where real estate prices proved too prohibitive.

Apprehensions along the southwestern border have surged recently as border security took center stage during the political campaign. According to data from Customs and Border Protection, U.S. authorities detained 408,870 individuals attempting to cross over the twelve-month period ending in September, marking a 23 percent increase compared to the previous year. 

In McAllen, situated about 55 miles west of Brownsville, Mayor Jim Darling reported that human smugglers are actively boosting their trade by urging migrants to cross before a Trump wall materializes. Darling, who holds a nonpartisan seat but backed Republican Texas Governor Greg Abbott during his 2014 bid, stated that the community now faces an escalated immigration challenge. Should the existing South Texas fencing be extended westward, it is expected to terminate near Rio Grande City. There, independent Mayor Joel Villarreal views the project as a misallocation of taxpayer funds that could inadvertently enrich Mexican criminal cartels controlling the smuggling routes. He warned that traffickers will retain the means to guide people across, forcing migrants to pay the cartels their cut.

Comedian and "A Child's First Book Of Trump" writer Michael Ian Black, known for his opposition to President Trump and firearms, recently utilized Twitter to address an inquiry concerning the impact of parenthood on his comedic style. His response shocked many Americans, as the entertainer stated that his children were the source of all his "baby rape jokes." 

The specific social media post from October 7, 2011, read: "Question I keep getting in interviews is whether having kids changed my comedy. Yes. They inspired all my baby rape jokes." 

This is not the initial instance of Black joking about child molestation. Following the conviction of Subway spokesperson Jared Fogel for child pornography possession and interstate travel for illicit sexual contact with minors, Black replied to a related post with what appeared to be a joke, stating: "We used to molest kids together." Furthermore, Black has expressed the view that the NRA functions as a "terrorist group," writing on December 6, 2017—coinciding with a House gun bill vote—that a friendly reminder was in order regarding the organization's alleged terrorist status.

Black penned the anti-Trump publication titled "A Child's First Book Of Trump," available for purchase via Amazon and Barnes and Noble. The Barnes and Noble overview of the work, co-authored by Marc Rosenthal, describes it as a New York Times bestseller offering advice from the comedian regarding encounters with a "wild Trump" during election season. It is characterized as a satirical picture book intended for adults, depicting the creature known as an "American Trump" with bright orange skin, a plump figure, complex hair, and small hands. 

The description details the confusion surrounding the business mogul, reality television host, and political candidate who dominates news coverage, leaving children and adults wondering about his authenticity and actions. Black utilizes a traditional picture book format to present the "Americus Trumpus" and his campaign for the presidency.

Additionally, Black is slated for performances in Boston at the Laugh House from November 9 through 11, with the venue reachable at (617) 725-2844 for those wishing to voice opinions on their support for the comedian. His acting credits also include appearances alongside liberal performers in the Netflix project "Wet Hot American Summer: Ten Years Later" and the earlier "Wet Hot American Summer."

During Wednesday night’s broadcast, *The Daily Show* correspondent Jessica Williams targeted the absurd restroom legislation pushed by Republican politicians aimed at targeting and marginalizing the LGBT population. As transgender visibility increases, conservative lawmakers have ramped up efforts to introduce restrictive measures dictating restroom usage. 

In an attempt to decode this political fixation, Williams interviewed multiple transgender individuals alongside one of their primary critics, Colorado Republican State Representative and Chaplain Gordon Klingenschmitt. Williams challenged the lawmaker regarding his assertion that transgender individuals are merely "confused," effectively dismantling his argument. Expounding on his religious views, Klingenschmitt explained to Williams why he views transgender people as a danger to the nation, stating that they desire to confuse not only their own identities but everyone else's as well, and questioning why the government should participate in this pretense and force others to be dishonest. 

Conversely, when Williams asked transgender people about their actual desires, their sole request was for respect. They expressed no intention to deceive anyone regarding who they are, maintaining that gender identity is not a choice, a point supported by research.

Klingenschmitt attempted to pivot the conversation toward religion, though he insisted on a wardrobe change beforehand, stating he would discuss religious freedom once he changed into his "alter ego." Williams waited for him to complete his transition so he would feel at ease during the discussion, while Klingenschmitt remained oblivious to the irony of the moment.

When pressed by Williams on his intense dedication to advancing anti-transgender measures, Klingenschmitt characterized the situation as perversion, claiming individuals adopt transgender identities simply to gain access to violate others' rights. Addressing his background as a chaplain, Williams then posed the question of whether it would be fair to assume all priests are pedophiles. Klingenschmitt answered in the negative, and when asked why, he responded that some individuals engage in criminal behavior while others do not. However, Klingenschmitt claimed he could not apply that identical reasoning to transgender people, dismissing the comparison as "apples and oranges." Williams ultimately gathered that Klingenschmitt’s core worry was that permitting transgender women to use restrooms corresponding to their gender identity would lead to sexual assault, despite the total absence of any documented instances of sexual assault occurring as a result of such policies.

text: Court filings released on Wednesday show that a federal judge in Alabama has finalized a permanent injunction that prohibits state authorities from refusing marriage rights to same-sex couples. U.S. District Judge Callie Granade submitted the order on Tuesday, resolving a legal challenge against Alabama's prohibition on gay marriage that began in 2014 and reaffirming her early 2015 ruling that found the state statute unconstitutional. The question of gay marriage stood at the forefront of a nationwide controversy until the Supreme Court of the United States determined in June 2015 that the U.S. Constitution guarantees marriage rights to same-sex couples. Even after that nationwide ruling, authorities in Alabama persisted in fighting the legal shift. Roy Moore, the chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court, faced suspension last month after directing state probate judges through an administrative directive to withhold marriage licenses from gay couples. Meanwhile, in March, the state's highest court threw out requests from opponents of same-sex marriage aimed at reviving the state-level ban, though it declined to rescind or nullify its own March 2015 decision supporting the restriction, which had been issued shortly before the high court's nationwide ruling. Susan Watson, who serves as the executive director for the American Civil Liberties Union of Alabama, remarked that the measure establishes closure by permanently barring the state from applying marriage regulations that discriminate against gay relationships, adding that this permanent protection was essential given the intense opposition from the state. Representatives representing Alabama Attorney General Luther Strange, who is listed as a defendant in the case, were unavailable for statements on Wednesday. Legal counsel for Strange had previously requested the dismissal of the lawsuit on the grounds that the state was already adhering to federal regulations. Nonetheless, Judge Granade argued in her decision that a commitment to stop the behavior does not make a permanent injunction obsolete. She pointed out that the behavior of the suspended chief justice and other authorities implied that further efforts might arise to challenge the constitutional marriage rights of gay couples, noting in the text that there is no absolute certainty that the unconstitutional marriage statutes of Alabama will not be implemented again in the future.
