Two Dozen Cops Across Five California Precincts Had Sex With Teenager (VIDEO)

A troubling scandal initially shaking the Oakland, California police department has now widened to encompass multiple other East Bay Area districts. Nearly twenty-four law enforcement officers in California are currently facing accusations of engaging in sexual relations with a minor whom they referred to as "Juve," which was short for Juvenile. The controversy came to light after a federal monitor, appointed to supervise the police department, uncovered text messages exchanged between the young girl and Oakland county law enforcement personnel. 

Speaking with KPIX during an interview, the individual, who has since reached adulthood, stated that a minimum of two dozen officers had engaged in sexual activity with her. According to her statements, the police provided her with confidential information—such as warnings regarding upcoming anti-prostitution operations—in exchange for sex. Additionally, she claimed that officers offered her enhanced police protection while she engaged in street prostitution. Reports also indicate that an unnamed officer in his eighties paid $250 to have sex with her.

Because of his personal connection to the misconduct, Oakland Police Chief Sean Whent was removed from his post on June 9. Although investigating these claims fell under Whent's responsibilities, the young woman at the focal point of the inquiry stated that he was among the officers who partook in the actions. A CBS affiliate in San Francisco reported that Whent's departure from leadership coincides with both criminal and internal affairs investigations targeting multiple Oakland police officers suspected of having sexual contact with an underage girl.

This situation is deeply alarming on multiple fronts. Given their roles as law enforcement agents, these officers had a duty to shield the teenager from sex traffickers, yet they chose to partake in the offense instead. MADRID/BARCELONA (Reuters) - Amid an escalating political standoff that has already impacted the economy and sparked concerns about ongoing instability, regional officials in Catalonia stated on Saturday that they refuse to submit to direct governance from Madrid. Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy had announced earlier in the day that he would utilize special constitutional authorities to dismiss the local administration and trigger fresh elections, responding to the region's push for a break from Spain.

Catalan President Carles Puigdemont characterized Rajoy's actions as the most severe assault on the Catalan populace since the era of Spain's military dictatorship. Puigdemont made this assertion following his October 10 symbolic independence declaration, which came in the wake of a secession referendum. This marks the initial instance of the central administration seizing control of a regional body since the country transitioned back to democracy. 

Justifying the measures, Rajoy argued they are vital for resolving a division within the nation that has already forced a downward revision of economic growth projections for the euro zone's fourth-largest economy. Following participation in a peaceful protest, Puigdemont rejected the central government's intervention, though he held back from confirming whether he would actualize threats to press forward with independence before the intervention is officially enforced. 

In a televised broadcast, Puigdemont stated he is asking the Catalan parliament to convene a plenary session so that citizen representatives can evaluate this attempt to dismantle their government and democracy, allowing them to determine an appropriate response. 

To enact direct rule, Rajoy requires the approval of the Spanish upper house, having secured support from King Felipe and the primary opposition faction in Madrid. The objective, according to Rajoy, is to reinstate legal order and societal harmony—both of which have suffered significantly—safeguard the economic recovery currently facing risks in Catalonia, and hold elections under normal conditions.

The Senate vote, slated for next Friday, would grant Madrid complete authority over Catalan public media, police, and finances, while limiting regional parliamentary powers for a duration of up to half a year. This timeline could potentially provide the secessionist camp with strategic flexibility. 

Carme Forcadell, the speaker of the regional parliament, rejected Madrid's actions and labeled Rajoy's move a coup. During a televised address, Forcadell asserted that Prime Minister Rajoy aims to strip the Catalan parliament of its democratic status, a development she vowed would be resisted. 

The regional assembly is anticipated to convene on Monday to consider scheduling a session that could formally declare a Catalan republic. Furthermore, local media outlets have suggested Puigdemont might opt to dissolve the assembly and schedule his own elections prior to next Friday, which, under regional regulations, would occur within a two-month span. Such a step would allow Puigdemont to bypass the six-month schedule outlined by Rajoy and capitalize on strong anti-Madrid sentiments currently prevalent in the area.

Pro-independence organizations have historically mobilized crowds exceeding one million individuals to protest Madrid's reluctance to negotiate an arrangement. Alongside his cabinet, Puigdemont participated in a Barcelona rally, displaying yellow ribbons to back two prominent pro-independence figures currently imprisoned on sedition allegations. Tens of thousands chanted for freedom while waving secession flags and holding placards with slogans such as "Defending our land is not a crime" and "Let's proclaim the republic."

Abel Fernandez, a 38-year-old builder wearing an independence flag at the protest, expressed his view that Rajoy's activation of the constitutional article would accomplish nothing, adding that authorities cannot silence the portion of Catalonia supporting independence or the right to self-determination.

According to Catalan officials, roughly 90 percent of participants in the October 1 referendum voted in favor of breaking away. However, turnout stood at 43 percent of the electorate, with most unionist voters boycotting the ballot. The secession drive has encountered fierce resistance throughout the rest of Spain, caused deep internal divisions within Catalonia, and resulted in hundreds of businesses relocating their legal headquarters outside the region, though Rajoy appealed to them on Saturday to remain.

Rajoy’s center-right People's Party administration maintains that Puigdemont repeatedly violated the law while advancing the independence agenda, and the government has secured solid backing from the opposition Socialist Party. Pedro Sanchez, the Socialist leader, emphasized that there are no differences between his party and the PP regarding territorial unity. 

The secessionist movement has decried the detention of leaders as political prisoners, while human rights organizations have criticized the aggressive police methods deployed to block the referendum.

BRUSSELS (Reuters) - Amid rising euroscepticism and with the UK's 2019 departure on the horizon, the European Commission put forward a series of concepts on Wednesday to strengthen euro zone integration as a way to help unify the wider European Union. The executive branch of the EU unveiled these measures to offer the 19 nations using the single currency stronger safeguards against future economic downturns. Nevertheless, initiatives to reinforce solidarity among these 19 countries have triggered anxiety among the eight member states outside the currency union, who fear marginalization as second-tier members with diminished influence and reduced funding going forward. In an effort to calm these anxieties, the Commission emphasized that every initiative remains accessible to all EU participants, despite this approach contradicting the vision of certain currency bloc leaders like French President Emmanuel Macron. Macron has advocated for establishing a separate euro zone parliament, a dedicated finance minister, and a currency bloc budget totaling hundreds of billions of euros. The Commission's blueprint includes financial incentives rewarding nations for structural overhauls, alongside dedicated funds to help non-euro states prepare for eventual currency adoption, a requirement for all members except Denmark. However, Germany, a dominant political force, promptly dampened expectations regarding a central element of the strategy, casting uncertainty over its prospects. 

The Commission expressed support for establishing a designated "stabilisation function" for the currency bloc, arguing that the European Central Bank's monetary policy cannot adequately address downturns affecting only isolated members of the euro area. According to the Commission, this mechanism would function as a financial pool utilizing loans and a comparatively "limited grant component" to safeguard investments. To remain credible and impactful, officials stated it should possess the capacity to disburse a minimum of 1 percent of GDP while retaining borrowing privileges. Oversight of this "stabilisation function" would rest with the Commission, and participation would be restricted to countries that comply with EU regulations. Financing would be generated through EU budget loans, voluntary state contributions, and borrowings from the currency bloc's rescue fund backed by guarantees from the broader EU budget. The Commission noted that achieving this requires establishing "a limited borrowing capacity" within the upcoming EU financial framework. 

Germany voiced skepticism, however. Acting German Finance Minister Peter Altmaier remarked that it is unhelpful to anticipate outcomes, noting that the departing administration remained unconvinced regarding the necessity of establishing additional safety nets at the European level. Rather than creating a euro zone finance minister, the Commission suggested appointing a pan-European Minister of Economy and Finance. This individual would simultaneously serve as a senior official within the European Commission and lead the gatherings of currency area finance ministers. Additionally, this official would direct the operations of the bailout fund as head of its governing board, a role presently filled by the president of the Eurogroup representing euro zone finance ministers. The Commission indicated that this position could be established upon the inauguration of the subsequent European Commission in November 2019, with the appointee answering directly to the European Parliament. Presently, the leader of the euro zone finance ministers—the closest equivalent to a unified financial chief—frequently appears before the parliamentary economic committee, though that body holds no authority to hold them accountable. Furthermore, currency bloc finance ministers show little eagerness to permit the Commission, which currently holds merely observer status at their regular sessions, to direct their deliberations.

Additional proposals for currency bloc integration, originally advanced by Berlin, involve converting the government-controlled bailout mechanism into a European Monetary Fund. The Commission endorsed this concept while insisting that the EMF operate as an official EU entity subject to oversight by the European Parliament—a condition officials suggest national governments will reject. The Commission aims to secure consensus on the EMF from national governments and the European Parliament by the middle of 2019, intending for the fund to supply a 60 billion-euro backstop to support the bank-financed Single Resolution Fund. At the same time, the Commission omitted any mention of the initiative—championed by Germany, Slovakia, and the Netherlands—to institute a sovereign insolvency framework designed to compel governments into maintaining disciplined fiscal habits. Market analysts remained underwhelmed by the Commission's announcements. ING economist Carsten Brzeski remarked in a client briefing that an initial review of the paperwork suggests virtually nothing will transform, describing the day's initiatives as positive in intent yet derivative and far from revolutionary.

ANKARA (Reuters) - Legal authorities in Turkey announced on Thursday that they have opened a probe into accusations that relatives of President Tayyip Erdogan transferred millions of dollars overseas for tax evasion purposes, though they noted questions remain regarding the validity of the paperwork supporting the assertions. 

The leader of the primary opposition faction, the Republican People's Party (CHP) headed by Kemal Kilicdaroglu, stated earlier in the week that Erdogan's relatives funneled $14 million to an enterprise located in the Isle of Man, displaying paperwork he claimed substantiated the financial movements. 

Erdogan rejected the claims as fabrications, asserting on Thursday that Kilicdaroglu would face consequences. Having led the nation's political landscape for roughly a decade and a half, Erdogan continues to stand as Turkey's most widely supported political figure by a large margin. Critics contend that his governance has grown progressively authoritarian, particularly following an unsuccessful coup attempt in the previous year; nonetheless, the CHP faces difficulties in mobilizing backing to contest the President. 

The opposition party has stopped short of alleging that Erdogan, his kin, or any of the firms reportedly tied to the financial transfers engaged in illegal behavior. 

The chief prosecutor's office in Ankara stated it was initiating an inquiry into the claims and mentioned that a representative for Bellway LTD—the entity identified by Kilicdaroglu as the recipient of the Erdogan family's capital—had labeled the records as fraudulent. Furthermore, authorities requested that the CHP surrender all related files. 

Ozgur Ozel, who serves as the deputy chairman of the CHP, indicated that the political organization would cooperate with the prosecutor's directive. 

In addition to these developments, the CHP submitted a formal parliamentary request calling for a probe into the accusations, though the legislative body, where Erdogan's governing AK party holds a majority, voted down the motion on Thursday.

Following the sudden dismissal of the official heading the probe into the administration's connections to Russia, White House press secretary Sean Spicer reacted in a peculiar fashion. Late Tuesday evening, following a short interview with Fox Business on the White House grounds, Spicer sought shelter in the bushes to dodge inquiries, as reported by The Washington Post. Along with his staff, Spicer crouched behind a high hedge. Returning to his office required navigating a crowd of journalists eager for answers regarding Donald Trump's abrupt termination of FBI Director James Comey.

To make it back inside, the press secretary had to get past that horde of reporters. For hours, Spicer and his team twisted themselves into knots trying to justify the unexpected firing. According to The Washington Post, Spicer initially intended to release the major news via an email statement, but the transmission was too slow, leading him to stand in the press office doorway around 5:40 p.m. and yell the statement to nearby reporters. He promptly disappeared while his staff locked the office door. Although the press team initially hinted at a possible briefing, they soon announced there would be no further comments that evening.

However, as both Democratic and Republican lawmakers raised alarms and voiced heavy criticism over the firing, Spicer and two top spokeswomen were soon briskly walking up the White House drive to defend the president across CNN, Fox News, and Fox Business. In the intervals between these television appearances, Spicer spent several minutes concealed within the foliage. Janet Montesi, a press office executive assistant, eventually stepped out from the bushes to inform journalists that Spicer would address questions on the condition that they did not film him. 

That was when Spicer emerged from his hiding spot to engage with the press corps. "Just turn the lights off. Turn the lights off," Spicer insisted. "We'll take care of this. Can you just turn that light off?" His request was accommodated, leaving him positioned in near total darkness between a pair of tall hedges, surrounded by more than a dozen journalists. For the next ten minutes, he addressed a barrage of inquiries, often hemming, hawing, and stammering. When asked when Trump and Comey last spoke, Spicer responded, "Uh, I don't know. I don't know. There's some—I don't know. I don't know."

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — The White House pushed back on Friday against a media report suggesting the Trump administration weighed a plan to deploy the National Guard for gathering up undocumented immigrants, insisting no such strategy exists. While addressing the press, White House spokesman Sean Spicer stopped short of completely ruling out that the concept might have been brought up informally within some corner of the administration. 

The initial story came from the Associated Press, which detailed a draft memo from the Department of Homeland Security outlining a potential mobilization of as many as 100,000 National Guard members. Spicer strongly condemned the reporting during his briefing, calling the claim entirely false and emphasizing that there is zero initiative underway to employ the National Guard for rounding up undocumented individuals. 

Echoing those denials, Department of Homeland Security spokesperson David Lapan stated clearly that the agency is not looking into calling up the National Guard to enforce immigration laws. 

According to the Associated Press, the Jan. 25 draft document had reportedly circulated among DHS personnel for roughly a fortnight, directed at the acting leaders of both U.S. Customs and Border Protection and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The 11-page paper allegedly proposed a historic level of military involvement in immigration control spanning the four states sharing a border with Mexico—Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California—along with seven neighboring states: Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Colorado, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Louisiana. Furthermore, the news outlet noted the text was intended to guide the execution of President Donald Trump's sweeping Jan. 25 executive orders concerning border security and immigration.

A Homeland Security official, who spoke anonymously, characterized the paperwork secured by the news organization as a very preliminary draft assembled by staffers for Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly. The anonymous source explained that any mention of the National Guard was removed prior to reaching Kelly's attention. Although the final memo intended for Kelly remains incomplete, the official indicated it is anticipated to wrap up shortly.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Donald Trump, a leader typically recognized for a stern and abrasive public persona, faces a chance this Saturday in Houston to display a softer, more compassionate demeanor, potentially reaching citizens who have voiced opposition to his administration. Previous president Barack Obama earned the title of "comforter-in-chief" for his frequent participation in comforting those affected by mass violence and terrorism. However, the severe flooding resulting from Hurricane Harvey represents the initial major national crisis during Trump's tenure. According to White House announcements, Trump's itinerary includes meetings with flood victims and rescue volunteers in Houston, followed by a trip to Lake Charles, Louisiana, another location severely impacted by the weather event.

During his initial journey to the region on Tuesday, Trump deliberately avoided the actual disaster area to prevent interfering with ongoing rescue operations. Instead, his schedule consisted of briefings with cabinet officials, local and state authorities, and emergency responders. Nevertheless, he faced backlash for failing to interact with those suffering from the most destructive storm to strike Texas in half a century, with critics arguing his focus was placed too heavily on governmental logistics rather than human hardship.

Matt Mackowiak, the Travis County Republican Party chairman in Texas, acknowledged that the criticism was fair, despite commending the administration's overall management of the crisis. 

With more than one million individuals forced from their homes by Harvey and an estimated death toll reaching up to 50 amid record-breaking river levels and gridlock in Houston, Saturday's excursion presents Trump with an opportunity that Mackowiak urges him to maximize. Establishing an emotional bond with the nation remains beneficial for a U.S. president, Mackowiak noted, suggesting it could prove particularly advantageous regarding the portion of the population currently critical of his administration. Data from the Reuters/Ipsos tracking poll indicates that roughly 59 percent of Americans express disapproval of Trump's presidential job performance.

While Obama became well-known for crying following the 2012 elementary school shooting in Newtown, Connecticut, that claimed the lives of 20 children, Trump's public expressions of emotion have historically been limited mostly to frustration directed at journalists and detractors. A notable departure occurred following the April chemical weapons assault by the Syrian government that resulted in the deaths of over 70 people, a significant portion of whom were children. During a press conference after the event, Trump remarked on the lethal nature of the chemical gas used against innocent babies and children, stating that such actions cross numerous boundaries. 

Earlier, during his presidential campaign, families who lost relatives to undocumented immigrants praised him for personally conveying condolences regarding their tragedies. 

Conversely, he drew heavy criticism for his handling of the civil unrest in Charlottesville, Virginia, the previous month, where critics felt he prioritized assigning blame and arguing with opponents over calming a shaken country. 

Trump initially built his public reputation as a Manhattan real estate developer known for aggressive negotiation tactics, an image he further reinforced through a hit reality television program where he routinely dismissed underperforming participants without sentiment. Throughout his campaign for the presidency, he frequently emphasized the importance of being "tough" and lauded business leaders described as "killers." Mackowiak observed that, judging by his background and professional history, public displays of sympathy or empathy do not appear to come naturally to him.

On the other hand, Family Research Council president and pastor Tony Perkins argues that a warmer disposition exists beneath the surface. Perkins accompanied Trump during a campaign stop to visit flood victims in rural Louisiana the previous year, where Trump and current Vice President Mike Pence traveled through the disaster zone distributing diapers and bottled water. 

According to Perkins, Trump instructed his motorcade to pull over repeatedly so he could converse directly with affected residents, revealing a compassionate demeanor and a visible emotional reaction to the devastation. 

Gerard Landry, mayor of Denham Springs—a Louisiana municipality of 10,000 residents where nearly 80 percent of structures suffered flood damage—spoke with Trump at a local high school. Landry recalled that the president shook his hand, placed a hand on his shoulder, and expressed confidence in the city's recovery and the mayor's leadership. Anticipating the loud persona seen at campaign rallies, Landry instead encountered someone entirely unexpected, describing him as grounded and very different in person. 

Perkins believes the Saturday journey gives Trump an opportunity to demonstrate that specific aspect of his character to the broader public, describing it as entirely genuine and authentic.

WASHINGTON, 2016 — A leading adviser to Donald Trump pushed back Sunday against an audio recording from the 1991 archives, expressing doubt that the Republican presidential front-runner ever pretended to be his own publicist to boast about his dating life. This media storm unfolded right as the Democratic camp intensified its scrutiny of the billionaire businessman's personal integrity. 

The Washington Post published the audio file on Friday, featuring an individual calling himself "John Miller," a representative for Trump, discussing the real estate mogul's relationships with a journalist from People magazine. During an appearance on CNN's "State of the Union," top campaign aide Paul Manafort stated that the voice on the tape did not sound like Trump, despite the candidate's history of acknowledging the past use of fake names. 

Manafort remarked that the audio was barely intelligible, adding that he could not identify the speaker and ultimately chose to believe Trump's denial. Trump himself asserted on NBC’s “Today” program on Friday that the voice did not belong to him, even though he previously admitted to adopting at least one pseudonym when talking to the press years ago.

The original 1991 feature in People playfully referred to Miller as an enigmatic public relations agent who bore a striking vocal resemblance to Trump. Just days after publication, the reporter behind the tape, Sue Carswell, stated that Trump had confessed to pulling a prank by acting as Miller and offered an apology. 

Having essentially secured the GOP nomination earlier in the month for the upcoming November 8 election, Trump has focused on bridging divisions within the party following resistance from several prominent figures. Meanwhile, supporters of front-runner Hillary Clinton have characterized Trump as untrustworthy, placing particular emphasis on his past remarks about women. 

Since locking down the nomination, Clinton has stepped up her attacks on Trump's character, recently pointing to his withheld tax returns as a sign that he is concealing information. In response to accusations that he frequently judges women based on physical appearance, Trump reacted with frustration and retaliated by questioning how Clinton and her spouse, former President Bill Clinton, handled women who came forward with allegations of sexual misconduct against the former president. Bill Clinton previously acknowledged engaging in extramarital relationships with White House intern Monica Lewinsky and Arkansas performer Gennifer Flowers.

On Sunday, Trump took to Twitter to mock a New York Times piece featuring accounts from multiple women who claimed his remarks regarding their physical appearance and unwanted advances made them uncomfortable over the years. The same article also noted his history of elevating women to high-ranking roles, an uncommon practice within the real estate sector at the time. In a Sunday post, Trump wrote that everyone was mocking the newspaper over what he termed a weak hit piece concerning him and women.

Also on Sunday, Democratic President Barack Obama used a university commencement address to take aim at Trump's platform, specifically targeting his call for a temporary prohibition on foreign Muslims entering the United States. Speaking to graduates at Rutgers University in New Jersey, Obama argued that isolating or looking down upon Muslims and proposing differential treatment at the border violates American values and goes against national identity.

While news reports from the early 1990s frequently mentioned that Trump occasionally adopted fake PR personas to influence press coverage, the actual recording of such an instance only surfaced recently and rapidly gained traction across the American media landscape. The NBC sketch comedy series "Saturday Night Live" even featured a parody involving an actor playing Trump who phoned journalists under the alias "John Pepperoni." 

Trump's history of using fictitious representatives first came to light in 1990 during a legal deposition, where he testified to communicating with reporters via telephone under the alias John Baron, which appeared in some media accounts as John Barron. Newsday quoted him following the testimony as saying that numerous individuals employ pen names, citing Ernest Hemingway as an example.

STRASBOURG, France — According to the president of the European Commission, the bloc ought to establish a unified economy and finance ministerial post, though he argued against setting up an independent budget or legislative assembly exclusively for the currency union. During his address on the state of the union delivered Wednesday to the European Parliament, Jean-Claude Juncker proposed that this official should oversee economic matters across the entire bloc rather than just the countries sharing the single currency, while also presiding over the group of currency-zone financial chiefs and answering directly to European lawmakers. 

Officials within the bloc explained that opting for a single finance chief spanning all member states instead of strictly the currency block is a deliberate strategy to ward off a split among the 27 nations remaining after the UK departs in 2019. The concept of a dedicated financial lead for the euro area has previously been championed by Emmanuel Macron, the French leader. A French diplomatic insider disclosed on Wednesday that Macron plans to present comprehensive reform plans regarding the currency area on the 26th of September, arriving just days after the German federal elections. Additionally, during discussions last month, German Chancellor Angela Merkel informed Macron that she could envision a merged European economic and financial portfolio.

Stressing the need for reform, Juncker told the parliament that the bloc requires a dedicated economy and finance leader who can encourage and back structural changes throughout member nations. He added that this official ought to synchronize all available financial tools designed to assist any member country suffering through an economic downturn or severe crisis. 

Rather than establishing a completely brand-new office, Juncker suggested that the responsibilities should be assigned to an existing vice president of the European Commission—a proposition certain to draw fierce opposition from currency-zone administrations, particularly in Berlin. 

His remarks form part of a broader conversation concerning the long-term structure of the 19-member currency area. Juncker asserted that this group should eventually grow to encompass all remaining member states that currently operate outside the single currency and lack a formal exemption from adopting it. 

To facilitate this, Juncker announced plans for a new accession mechanism to provide technical and monetary support for countries seeking to transition to the euro, though he omitted specific details. He maintained that by the time of Britain's exit in March 2019, participation in both the single currency and the bloc’s banking union—featuring unified supervision, a resolution authority, and a joint deposit guarantee framework—ought to be standard for every member. 

Despite this vision, while nearly all EU nations outside the currency union are legally bound to adopt the euro once specific conditions are satisfied, certain major economies like Poland and Sweden currently have zero intentions of doing so anytime soon, arguing that maintaining their national currencies provides greater economic adaptability.

Regarding proposals from Paris and Berlin to institute an independent currency-zone budget alongside the broader long-term EU spending plan, as well as a distinct parliament for the single-currency nations, Juncker dismissed both concepts outright. He argued that instead of a standalone budget, the currency area requires a robust budgetary line embedded directly within the overarching EU budget, and he expressed opposition to a separate legislative body, emphasizing that the European Parliament already serves as the parliament for the currency zone.

Furthermore, Juncker proposed converting the currency-zone's rescue mechanism, known as the European Stability Mechanism (ESM), into a fully integrated European Monetary Fund operating as an official institution of the bloc, transitioning away from its current intergovernmental structure. He indicated that the anticipated European finance minister would likewise oversee this new fund. While withholding specifics regarding potential new responsibilities for the proposed fund, he noted that the Commission intends to unveil formal proposals outlining both the fund's new duties and the powers of the European finance minister in December. 

Meanwhile, financial ministers from the single-currency area are scheduled to kick off discussions regarding the future of the monetary union on Friday during an informal gathering situated in Tallinn, the capital of Estonia.

President Trump Fires Acting Attorney General, Sally Yates

21st Century Wire reports that an official statement released today by the Office of the Press Secretary announced the dismissal of acting Attorney General Sally Yates. This decision came after Yates directed attorneys within the Department of Justice to avoid defending the administration's executive order concerning travel restrictions. According to the Press Secretary's announcement, Yates let down the Department of Justice by declining to uphold a lawful directive intended to safeguard American citizens. Meanwhile, President Trump utilized Twitter to voice his frustration, posting a critical message stating that Democrats were intentionally stalling his cabinet nominees solely for political motives, noting they are focusing entirely on obstruction. 

To fill the vacancy, Dana Boente, serving as the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, was appointed as the new acting attorney general. Within the official release, Boente provided a statement expressing his privilege to assist President Trump in this capacity while awaiting the confirmation of Senator Sessions, adding that he intends to uphold and apply national laws to safeguard the public and the country. Coverage from RT further elaborates on the unfolding situation, noting that Yates was removed from her position on a Monday, shortly after reports emerged regarding her instructions to Justice Department lawyers. 

In a social media post, Press Secretary Sean Spicer confirmed that President Trump designated Dana Boente from the Eastern District of Virginia to step in as Acting Attorney General, following the dismissal of Sally Yates. The official statement from the Office of the Press Secretary reiterated that Yates had turned her back on the Department of Justice by failing to execute a legal order crafted to defend the population of the United States. 

Boente, originally appointed during the Obama administration, had previously won confirmation through the Senate for his former role as U.S. Attorney. Representatives from the Trump administration informed journalists on Monday evening that this prior confirmation sufficed to permit him to sign Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act warrants, which authorize surveillance targeting perceived foreign dangers inside the United States. Observers noted this situation is highly unusual, given that Boente's previous Senate approval did not explicitly include authorization for FISA approvals—a power traditionally limited to the attorney general and deputy attorney general, both of whom have historically received direct Senate confirmation for those specific offices. Questions remain regarding whether this administrative step will encounter legal challenges. 

Addressing his new assignment, the newly appointed Acting Attorney General stated in the press release that he felt deeply privileged to aid President Trump until Senator Sessions receives confirmation, emphasizing a commitment to defending and enforcing domestic laws to guarantee the protection of the nation and its people. 

Before her dismissal, Yates authored a letter—highlighted by the New York Times—explaining her stance, in which she stated her responsibility to ensure that legal positions maintained in court align with the institution's fundamental duty to pursue justice and uphold righteousness. She added that she was currently unpersuaded that defending the executive order aligned with those duties, nor was she convinced of the order's legality. 

In reaction to Yates's actions, the President turned to Twitter to denounce the move, attributing it to broader Democratic obstructionism driven by political agendas, and remarked on the involvement of an Obama-appointed attorney general. Following her firing, former Attorney General Eric Holder, who held office under President Obama, took to social media to back Yates, praising her as a skilled attorney and individual of integrity who has devotedly served the country with distinction and whose judgment deserves trust.

BRASILIA (Reuters) - Brazilian President Michel Temer acknowledged on Friday that the overhaul of the nation's expensive pension system could miss its target of passing through Congress within the current year. This marks the initial admission by the president that such a setback is possible. Speaking to the Poder360 news portal, Temer explained that the administration must re-engage with members of the ruling political coalition, several of whom have already expressed skepticism regarding the timeline for 2017 approval. 

While the pension overhaul is central to Temer's strategy for closing the national budget gap and reining in excessive pension expenditures, the proposed changes—specifically raising the retirement age—have proven deeply unpopular among the public. Temer attributed the postponement to a series of corruption accusations that paralyzed his legislative initiatives for half a year. 

According to the president, the administration is weighing a scaled-back iteration of the legislation, validating earlier reports from authorities indicating willingness to accept a compromise centered around establishing a baseline retirement age of 65 for males, a significant jump from the existing average retirement age of 55. This modified package would additionally require a phased rollout of the updated regulations alongside equal treatment for both public and private sector pensions, Temer noted. 

Eliseu Padilha, the president's chief of staff who participated in the same discussion, stated that the administration anticipates a reduced scope reform can still deliver three-quarters of the targeted financial savings, provided it encompasses reductions to benefits enjoyed by government workers. 

Additionally, Temer mentioned that the administration might utilize a temporary decree to prolong the Refis initiative—which grants citizens and businesses the opportunity to restructure overdue tax obligations—by a matter of weeks.

text:
Democratic state attorneys general are preparing for a legal battle following Donald Trump's executive order instructing the Army Corps of Engineers and the Environmental Protection Agency to look into rescinding regulations designed to safeguard the nation's waterways from pollution. This move comes alongside the appointment of the EPA leader, who previously criticized the agency at the Conservative Political Action summit. 

According to Talking Points Memo, a coalition of attorneys general representing New York, Hawaii, Massachusetts, Oregon, Vermont, and the District of Columbia issued a joint statement strongly condemning the administration's decision to weaken Clean Water Act safeguards, arguing it threatens both public health and the environment.

Spearheaded by New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman, the group explicitly raised the prospect of litigation against the administration. The statement emphasized that they are fully prepared to defend their populations and natural resources by vigorously challenging in court any presidential actions that disregard the law and the public's essential need for unpolluted water. Furthermore, the officials warned that scrapping the Clean Water Rule could result in unchecked contamination of vital water supplies and negatively impact state economies by increasing the financial burden of treating pollution originating from upstream states that fail to regulate it.

Meanwhile, Scott Pruitt, chosen by Trump to lead the EPA, recently faced revelations that he utilized a private email account for official state matters during his tenure as Oklahoma's attorney general and provided false testimony under oath. Notably, Trump selected a nominee who had previously filed 13 lawsuits against the very agency he was nominated to direct.

text:
PARIS (Reuters) - Following the recent breakdown of United Nations-brokered peace negotiations regarding Syria in Geneva, the French government reiterated its strong support for the process on Friday, asserting that blame for the stalled dialogue rests squarely on the shoulders of the Syrian administration. 

Staffan de Mistura, the United Nations mediator, noted on Thursday that the conclusion of the latest diplomatic round represented a significant missed opportunity, though he suggested that discussions could potentially resume in January if viable methods emerge to persuade President Bashar al-Assad's administration to participate meaningfully. 

During a regular press briefing, Alexandre Georgini, the deputy spokesman for the French foreign ministry, reaffirmed Paris's backing of the U.N. envoy, emphasizing that a political settlement negotiated between the two sides under United Nations supervision remains the sole viable path forward. 

Georgini expressed regret over the stance taken by the Syrian authorities, accusing them of declining to take part in the dialogue and holding them accountable for the absence of any headway during the talks.

text:
During an interview with Reuters on Monday, the chief executive of France's state-backed utility EDF stated that the company is eager to get involved in Saudi Arabia's upcoming nuclear reactor projects. The kingdom aims to cut down on domestic oil usage by targeting the development of 17.6 gigawatts of nuclear power generation by the year 2032. As part of this initiative, Riyadh has already issued a request for information to global vendors regarding the construction of a pair of reactors. 

According to insiders speaking last month, EDF has previously engaged in discussions with Saudi officials concerning the potential sale of European Pressurized Reactors, engineered by Areva, and is keen to bid if a formal tender is launched. Chief Executive Levy emphasized the utility's desire to support the nation's transition away from fossil-fuel dependence. EDF intends to pursue this prospect across every energy sector where it holds expertise, encompassing solar, wind, and nuclear power, according to Levy.

Competition for the Saudi nuclear contract is already shaping up, with South Korean and Russian firms announcing their intentions to submit bids. Additionally, insiders report that Westinghouse, the U.S. company owned by Toshiba, is holding discussions with domestic partners to assemble a consortium for the tender. 

This follows a previous regional bid in 2009, when EDF and Areva were unsuccessful against South Korea's KEPCO for the construction of the United Arab Emirates' nuclear reactors, which marked the inaugural nuclear project in the Middle East. Meanwhile, EDF remains on schedule to complete its acquisition of Areva NP, the reactor engineering branch of the French nuclear group. Levy confirmed that the transaction is proceeding as planned and is expected to conclude before the current month ends.

text:
Lawmakers in Alabama passed comprehensive legislation on Friday to safeguard Confederate monuments, historical titles, and various other memorials, arriving at a time when several Southern municipalities are reconsidering whether such symbols belong in public spaces. 

Under the newly approved legislation, any monument, memorial building, memorial street, or architecturally significant structure located on public property for four decades or longer would be shielded from relocation, removal, modification, renaming, or any other form of interference. For memorials and names that have been in place for a duration between twenty and forty years, any proposed alterations would require authorization from a newly established state commission.

Throughout the legislative proceedings, Black lawmakers consistently resisted the measure, arguing that it permanently embeds an embarrassing history of chattel slavery. Senator Hank Sanders, a Democratic lawmaker from Selma who is African-American, voiced his opposition by stating that the legislation does not truly preserve history, but rather upholds structures symbolizing subjugation for a significant portion of Alabama's population.

Conversely, proponents of the bill maintained that the legislation is designed to preserve a broad spectrum of history rather than exclusively focusing on Confederate iconography. The Republican author of the measure, Senator Gerald Allen, pushed back against what he described as an ongoing trend of political correctness that seeks to erase tributes dedicated to historically important figures, regardless of any personal shortcomings those individuals may have possessed.

text:
Donald Trump is known for offering sharp remarks that strike a chord with the public due to their candid nature. This appeal is why supporters believe he is headed for a landslide victory, as voters grow weary of politicians who avoid straight talk. Amid the announcement that the PGA is relocating an event away from Trump Doral, Trump offered a memorable quip: "I hope they have kidnapping insurance." 

The presumptive Republican nominee made this statement in reaction to the PGA shifting the 2017 World Golf Championship from Miami to Mexico. Pointing out the anger in Miami over the relocation of the World Golf Championships to Mexico City, Trump stated that such occurrences would cease if he were elected president. Furthermore, he criticized the state of the American economy, arguing that the nation is being exploited by Mexico. 

While the BBC reported that the PGA Tour attributed the shift to an inability to secure sponsors, Trump contended that the organization prioritized profits over numerous American jobs. PGA Tour Commissioner Timothy Finchem indicated that Trump's personal brand created sponsorship challenges, noting that asking corporations to invest millions into branding a tournament while sharing space with the host's brand complicates decisions. Finchem maintained that politics played no role in the relocation.

Describing the move as a disappointing moment for Miami, the United States, and golf as a whole, Trump argued that the choice exemplifies the exact motivations behind his presidential campaign. During an appearance on Fox News, he reiterated his sharp take on the situation by remarking on the need for kidnapping insurance.

Republicans who hoped Donald Trump would adopt a more conventional presidential demeanor following his nomination have certainly been disappointed. text:
Right as the Department of Justice got ready to launch an investigation into the toxic water crisis in Flint, Michigan, an unoccupied office holding the municipality's water documentation was reportedly broken into. For upwards of a year and a half, local citizens had been raising alarms regarding the smell, appearance, and taste of their tap water. Back in January 2014, reports noted that the water tasted foul, smelled bad, and resembled "chocolate milk on tap." Nonetheless, representatives within the administration of Republican Governor Rick Snyder insisted to the citizens for months that the water posed no danger. These claims persisted despite independent analyses revealing elevated lead concentrations within the municipal water supply.

Public anger and intense media scrutiny grew as subsequent testing verified a steep rise in lead levels found in the blood of Flint children. Investigative journalist Curt Guyette, working with the ACLU, subsequently brought to light significant compromising evidence demonstrating that Snyder's staff was aware the municipal water was unsafe for consumption. This ACLU inquiry revealed that officials manipulated tests and fabricated paperwork, violating the law repeatedly to conceal the reality that the water was essentially toxic. 

On January 6, the U.S. Department of Justice formally declared it was getting ready to initiate an official probe into the lead-poisoning crisis in Flint. Amidst these developments, an alleged break-in occurred at Flint City Hall. City representatives verified on January 11 that the incident specifically targeted the empty room housing the local water documents. 

Police Chief James Tolbert and Mayor Kevin Weaver have declined to clarify whether any documents were taken from the space. Regarding security footage of the incident, Chief Tolbert stated that the video fails to display anything. It appears remarkably convenient that an intruder targeted the precise empty room containing the municipal water files right as those documents were about to face heavy legal and public examination. The circumstance that the intruders entered and exited a municipal facility completely unseen by witnesses and undetected by security cameras also appears extremely convenient. 

Throughout Michigan, residents have demanded the apprehension of Governor Snyder as mounting evidence indicates he and his staff knowingly permitted the population of Flint to consume lead-poisoned water for upwards of twelve months while maintaining that it was secure. Considering current knowledge regarding Snyder, the probability that this break-in was unconnected to the contaminated water crisis remains virtually nonexistent. This water crisis tied to Rick Snyder increasingly resembles the Watergate scandal associated with Richard Nixon.

text:
An episode of the Disney-owned ABC program "Scandal" featured a character undergoing an abortion accompanied by the holiday song "Silent Night," while a narrator stated that family destroys rather than completes a person. This broadcast drew immediate criticism for functioning as an extended promotional segment for Planned Parenthood, courtesy of a media conglomerate that largely built its success on content for children. Critics questioned how supporters of the company could market theme parks as destinations for families while simultaneously broadcasting the termination of pregnancies. 

The connection between the program and the organization became clearer upon examining the background of the show's creator. Following the broadcast, the abortion provider publicly commended the episode, and cast members defended the decision to portray the procedure against the backdrop of a Christmas hymn. This alignment was unsurprising, given that "Scandal" creator and producer Shonda Rhimes serves on the board of directors for Planned Parenthood Los Angeles. 

Commentators noted that the theme was not new for Rhimes, who had previously incorporated abortion storylines into her earlier series, "Grey's Anatomy." Observers suggested her history with Catholic schooling contributed to a rebellious approach, and pointed to past personal interviews where Rhimes discussed raising children without being married and expressing no desire to have a husband in her home. Beyond "Grey's Anatomy" and its spin-off "Private Practice," ABC picked up her pilot script for "Scandal" in 2011. In a previous interview with Time magazine, Rhimes defended the inclusion of the topic on television, arguing that polarizing and debated issues ought to be discussed on screen.

The fifth-season episode, titled "Baby, It's Cold Outside," featured the lead character, presidential partner Olivia Pope—played by Kerry Washington—obtaining an abortion during the broadcast. At the same time, a fictional Republican senator, Mellie Grant, portrayed by Bellamy Young, sustained a successful Senate filibuster to prevent the defunding of Planned Parenthood. 

Immediately following the broadcast, Planned Parenthood released a statement praising the production and the creator for demonstrating that audiences will watch when women share their stories. The organization emphasized that the storyline highlighted threats to reproductive health care and the consequences of defunding services such as contraception counseling, STI testing, cancer screenings, and abortions. The statement also referenced statistics regarding the prevalence of the procedure among women and commended the network and creator, while expressing hope that members of Congress would take notice.

After the procedure, the main character is shown back at the White House drinking red wine while classical music plays. Meanwhile, the Media Research Center issued a sharp critique, condemning the broadcast as a prolonged commercial for the organization and labeling the scene featuring the Christmas hymn alongside an abortion as an exhibition of moral decay. Cast member Kerry Washington voiced her backing for the organization on social media by utilizing specific hashtags associated with the episode's plotlines.

text:
Countless surveys concerning the presidential race are currently circulating, with the vast majority pointing to either a tight tie or a lead for Hillary nationwide and in battleground states. According to the logic that this implies manipulation or bias, Breitbart opted to hire Gravis to run its very own survey. The outcome placed Hillary ahead of Trump with 42 percent to 37 percent in a four-way contest. The survey contacted 2,832 individuals on August 9 and features a 1.8 percent margin of error, meaning Hillary's advantage extends past that threshold.

Alex Marlow, the editor-in-chief at Breitbart, commented on the survey by stating that it is an open secret that surveys are routinely spun and manipulated to manufacture momentum for specific candidates or issues. He added that the initial national survey from the Breitbart News Network launches a significant effort to provide readers with an accurate evaluation of where Americans stand on important subjects and figures, free from the filter of the mainstream media. 

It is quite revealing when a survey executed with the goal of neutrality yields identical outcomes to those deemed biased. This particular effort shows Hillary ahead of Trump by five percentage points. In a four-way matchup, the latest Reuters/Ipsos survey also shows a five-point advantage for Hillary, while Economist/YouGov places her up by six points, and Rasmussen Reports has her leading by three points.

Despite large crowds for Trump and smaller ones for Hillary leading critics to call the surveys flawed, Breitbart and Gravis attempted a positive spin, arguing the data highlights opportunities for Trump to expand his voter reach. Doug Kaplan, the managing partner at Gravis, suggested that an 11 percent backing for Trump among the Black community poses an issue for Hillary, apparently basing this on the premise that her support from this demographic falls short of Obama's 2012 numbers.

Additionally, Hillary secured strong results on a question asking whether respondents agreed or disagreed that Donald Trump or Hillary Clinton would fight for people like them. In total, 39 percent believed Hillary would fight for them, compared to 38 percent for Trump. Among Muslim respondents, an impressive 84 percent expressed confidence that she would fight for them. Naturally, Trump lacks that level of backing from the Muslim community, largely due to his Islamophobic statements directed at them.

Ultimately, Breitbart ended up embarrassed, having tried to demonstrate one reality and failing completely. Their findings merely suggested that either Gravis shares the same bias or that surveys happen to be far more accurate than conservatives care to admit.

Photo of Hillary by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images. Photo of Donald Trump by Alex Wong/Getty Images. Images merged by Rika Christensen

text:
Four additional women have stepped forward to level sexual assault accusations against former President Bill Clinton. These developments unfold just as Hillary Clinton recently delivered a public address about defending women, raising questions about whether she will continue to support her husband. 

Information regarding these claims comes via Edward Klein—former editor-in-chief of the New York Times Magazine and author of multiple books concerning the Clintons, including *Guilty as Sin* from 2016 and his more recent release, *All Out War: The Plot to Destroy Trump*, which came out on October 30, 2017. According to well-positioned Democratic Party sources alongside an official who worked in both the Clinton and Obama administrations, the 71-year-old former president is facing these serious new allegations.

The sources indicate that the current claims pertain to incidents occurring after Clinton's departure from the White House in 2001, adding to a history previously marked by other allegations of sexual misconduct. Lawyers acting on behalf of these women are working in coordination and have alerted Clinton of their intent to initiate four distinct lawsuits against him.

During ongoing discussions, legal counsel for the claimants is seeking significant financial settlements in exchange for keeping the matter quiet. A representative from Clinton's legal defense has acknowledged that these new allegations exist. 

Historically, Clinton provided an $850,000 settlement in the late 1990s to resolve a sexual harassment claim brought by Paula Jones, a former Arkansas state employee—a legal battle that ultimately triggered Clinton's impeachment by the House of Representatives and subsequent acquittal by the Senate in 1999. 

Sources close to Clinton's inner circle report that current settlement talks have reached a pivotal phase. Should these negotiations break down, the four anonymous women reportedly plan to publicize their sexual assault claims through a press conference. This would place Clinton among the most prominent names on a growing roster of public figures, ranging from Harvey Weinstein to Kevin Spacey, facing recent accusations of sexual assault.

The fresh claims involve events that occurred over a decade ago during the early 2000s. At that time, billionaire investor Ron Burkle employed Clinton to work within his Yucaipa companies. Clinton aided Burkle in drumming up business, traveling globally aboard Burkle's private aircraft—a plane informally dubbed "Air F**k One"—accompanied by numerous attractive young women. The four accusers, whose identities remain undisclosed, worked in junior roles at Burkle's organization during their late teenage years and allege they were sexually assaulted by the former president.

text:
Following a series of tweets last week in which the sitting president claimed his predecessor had monitored his phones prior to the election—an assertion made entirely without supporting documentation—his administration has begun attempting to backtrack. Following the social media posts, administration officials scrambled to support the unprecedented claims directed at the former president. Concurrently, former President Barack Obama reportedly reacted to the unsupported allegations with visible disbelief.

The unfounded conspiracy theory also prompted a response from House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes (R-CA) and Ranking Member Adam Schiff (D-CA), who established a Monday deadline for the administration to supply evidence supporting the assertion. Observers noted that Nunes, typically a firm supporter of the president who had previously attempted to downplay the administration's controversy regarding Russia, apparently found the situation unsustainable.

During Monday's press briefing, White House press secretary Sean Spicer attempted to soften the impact of the unsubstantiated allegations—specifically the claim that the predecessor had ordered an unauthorized wiretap on Trump Tower—by stating that the president "doesn't really think" Barack Obama "tapped his phone personally," as noted by Politico. Spicer told the press corps that the president did not believe the former leader physically performed the wiretapping himself.

In an effort to defend his superior, Spicer argued that the tweets referred broadly to "surveillance" rather than a literal wiretap, despite the fact that the president used the specific phrase "wire tapping" in one of his March 4 posts without providing evidence. Spicer suggested that the presence of quotation marks around the term in a single tweet indicated the statement was not meant literally. Spicer remarked to reporters that numerous media outlets had previously covered surveillance and related activities during the 2016 election, pointing to the quotation marks as evidence of a broader meaning. He further questioned the whereabouts of proof while referencing reporting from outlets present in the room.

The basis for Spicer's references remained ambiguous. While news organizations have covered investigations by intelligence officials into potential connections between the campaign and the Russian government—including intercepted communications involving campaign aides and Russian officials as part of probes into election interference and monitoring of the Russian ambassador—no credible source or evidence has emerged indicating that Obama wiretapped or surveilled Donald Trump during the campaign.

The president's original March 4 statements included quotation marks in only one of three relevant posts. One tweet asked if it was legal for a sitting president to engage in wiretapping during a presidential race before mentioning a court rejection. A second tweet expressed confidence that an attorney could build a case regarding phones being tapped in October ahead of the election. A third post criticized the process as reminiscent of Nixon and Watergate, using an alternative spelling for the word "tap" and labeling the individual a "bad (or sick) guy."

Consequently, the Department of Justice has requested additional time from the leaders of the House Intelligence Committee to gather documentation substantiating the claims, indicating an ongoing lack of verified evidence.

text:
During a midnight vote, a trio of Republican senators brought down the party's healthcare legislation, revealing that certain members of the GOP were never truly invested in dismantling Obamacare. Susan Collins representing Maine, Lisa Murkowski hailing from Alaska, and John McCain of Arizona struck down the "skinny" Republican bill resulting in a final tally of 49 to 51. Observers watched as McCain entered the chamber and delivered a thumbs-down gesture to register his vote, which was met with audible astonishment from those in the room.

Explaining his decision to reject the skinny repeal measure in the early hours of Friday morning, John McCain stated through a formal release that the proposal failed to achieve the necessary objective of properly replacing Obamacare, and he felt it wrong to push through such modifications without bipartisan backing.

The complete text of John McCain's explanation regarding his vote against Donald Trump's skinny healthcare repeal reads as follows:

Ever since the start, it has been my conviction that Obamacare needed to be done away with and substituted with an alternative that boosts market competition, reduces expenses, and enhances treatment quality for citizens. The skinny repeal measure considered by the Senate today fell short of those objectives. Although the proposal would have eliminated several of the heaviest regulations imposed by Obamacare, it provided no substitute to genuinely overhaul our medical system and provide reasonably priced, high-grade healthcare to the population. The assertion by the Speaker that the House might agree to a conference committee fails to alleviate my worry that this empty legislative shell could be revived and enacted at any moment.

I have repeatedly pointed out that a primary flaw of Obamacare was its enactment by Democrats through strict party-line votes without drawing a single Republican vote. Repeating past errors that caused the breakdown of Obamacare—which has manifested in my home state of Arizona through soaring insurance premiums and insurers abandoning the market—is something we must avoid. 

We are obligated to go back to proper legislative procedures by returning the measure to committee, conducting public hearings, gathering contributions from both political parties, listening to the advice of governors across the country, and drafting legislation that ultimately brings affordable medical care to the public. The difficult labor expected and deserved by our citizens must be carried out by us.

The failure of these medical reforms delivered a major setback to the legislative agenda of Donald Trump. The inability of Senate Republicans to clear even the minimal version of the repeal measure demonstrated that broader healthcare changes might be unachievable. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky expressed his disappointment, calling it a letdown and stating his regret that their endeavors fell short on this occasion, before declaring that it was time to move forward and placing the healthcare measure on hold while the Senate pivots to different bills in the upcoming week.

On Twitter, Mr. Trump shared his reaction by stating that three Republicans along with 48 Democrats failed the citizens of the nation, reiterating his initial stance to let Obamacare collapse on its own and address it subsequently.

text:
SEOUL (Reuters) - North Korean cyber actors likely managed to infiltrate the database of Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering Co Ltd in April of last year, making off with designs for South Korean naval vessels, according to a South Korean opposition politician. 

While Pyongyang routinely faces accusations from South Korea and other nations regarding digital assaults, it typically responds by either ignoring the claims or issuing outright denials. 

Speaking with Reuters via phone, Kyung Dae-soo, a member of the primary opposition Liberty Korea Party, stated there is near-total certainty that hackers from the North executed the breach and accessed confidential files belonging to the firm. 

Because Daewoo Shipbuilding has constructed various naval craft for South Korea—including submarines and Aegis-equipped ships—there is a strong probability those specific blueprints were compromised, according to the lawmaker. 

Kyung, who was briefed on the matter, explained that the cyber intrusion was uncovered by a specialized cybercrime investigation unit operating under the South Korean Ministry of Defence. 

He noted that the probe's investigators did not reveal the exact level of sensitivity or classification attached to the stolen files. 

Meanwhile, a representative for Daewoo Shipbuilding stated that officials at the company were unaware of the situation prior to Tuesday morning and were currently verifying the information shared by Kyung. 

The determination that North Korea was responsible stems from similarities between this breach and past digital incursions attributed to Pyongyang, Kyung mentioned. 

Intelligence points to North Korean hackers as the culprits behind a recent digital bank robbery in Taiwan, which adds to a growing pattern of attacks aimed at the global SWIFT financial messaging network. 

Just earlier this month, a different South Korean parliamentarian reported that North Korean actors had pilfered a vast quantity of classified defense records, featuring joint wartime strategies formulated by South Korea and the United States. 

Furthermore, officials in Britain announced last week their assessment that North Korea orchestrated the WannaCry ransomware incident in May, an episode that paralyzed corporate operations and public sector functions globally, such as the public healthcare system in England.

text:
WASHINGTON (Reuters) — While much of the political world has fixated on whether he might launch a presidential bid, Republican Paul Ryan has effectively quieted questions regarding his fundraising prowess for fellow members of Congress. Federal Election Commission records examined by Reuters reveal that Ryan pulled in in excess of $9 million via his "Team Ryan" apparatus, spanning his inauguration as U.S. House Speaker on October 30, 2015, up through January’s close in 2016. This financial collection aids House Republicans along with party organizations, outpacing the roughly $6 million that former Speaker John Boehner brought in during the identical three-month span for the 2014 cycle, as well as the approximately $7 million he gathered during the 2012 presidential race. 

Based on FEC records submitted through February 29, Ryan has channeled a minimum of $8 million directly to the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC), an organization supporting GOP congressional bids, once again surpassing Boehner's totals from both 2012 and 2014. Consequently, the NRCC heads into an election year boasting its largest cash reserves to date, holding a $2 million advantage over its Democratic counterpart, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. 

Representative Ann Wagner, who serves as the NRCC finance chairman, described Ryan's appeal, stating that he represents an ideal asset for any finance chair when it comes to collecting donations. She added that the unpredictability surrounding the presidential nominees for both political parties this cycle has likewise boosted contributions for congressional contenders. 

These figures show Ryan overcoming critics who questioned last year whether he could keep pace with Boehner's fundraising totals while simultaneously maintaining his promise to spend weekends at home with his relatives. Within the American political landscape, fundraising capability serves as a major indicator for higher political ambitions; however, Ryan—who was the party's vice presidential nominee in 2012—has repeatedly rejected notions that he seeks a 2016 White House campaign. 

During an interview with talk radio host Hugh Hewitt while on a congressional trip to Israel, Ryan reiterated his stance, asking to be left out of the discussion and stating he is not that individual. Even so, Ryan remains the focus of rumors suggesting he could surface as a compromise choice if the party convention ends in disarray this coming July. He firmly dismissed the idea, stating he is not running for president and that the matter is settled. 

Even with his strong financial track record, Ryan faces potential hurdles on the horizon. At a recent event within Ryan's home district, backers of Republican front-runner Donald Trump responded with boos simply at the sound of his name. Furthermore, a conservative from Wisconsin has formally declared a primary challenge against Ryan for the upcoming August Republican congressional primary. Back in Washington, Ryan is also tasked with sustaining a fragile truce established among competing factions of congressional Republicans. Passing a federal budget serves as his initial hurdle, and he runs the risk of angering conservatives should compromises with Democrats become necessary to avert a government shutdown—a criticism previously leveled against Boehner. 

Kyle Kondik, a political analyst at the University of Virginia Center for Politics, noted that Ryan faces difficulties comparable to those encountered by Boehner, explaining that the current Republican base harbors strong skepticism toward its own leadership. Kondik observed that merely holding the speakership position could eventually diminish Ryan's standing among the Republican faithful.

text: Legal scholar Jonathan Turley thoroughly dismantled the argument for obstruction brought forward by Joe Scarborough against President Trump, offering a sharp and well-reasoned breakdown explaining why such charges would be unwarranted. Though identified as a Democrat, Turley is widely viewed as a balanced legal analyst who strictly follows the letter of the law. Instead of uncovering the truth behind potential treason, Nunes managed to highlight how the GOP prioritizes party defense over genuine investigation. The turning point came with a specific inquiry: whether the FBI would incorporate information regarding the Hillary Clinton campaign, its associates, or the Clinton Foundation into their probe if brought forward by the committee or the public.

text:
Republicans reportedly advised Donald Trump to stay off Twitter while former FBI Director James Comey appeared before Congress, leaving his eldest son to handle the social media outburst instead. 

During the hearing on Thursday, Comey's released Wednesday opening statement detailed a January dinner where Donald Trump requested his allegiance, quoting the president as saying, "I need loyalty, I expect loyalty." Comey also recounted a February meeting following the dismissal of Mike Flynn over discussions with Russian officials. 

According to Comey, the president brought up Flynn again, stating, "He is a good guy and has been through a lot." While maintaining that Flynn did nothing wrong in his communications with Russia aside from misleading the vice president, Trump added, "I hope you can see your way clear to letting this go, to letting Flynn go. He is a good guy. I hope you can let this go." These statements strongly suggest that Trump attempted to obstruct justice and dismissed Comey to derail the Russia probe.

As the Senate proceedings unfolded, Donald Trump Jr. launched into a series of posts on Twitter. "1/3 Flynn stuff is BS in context 2 guys talking about a guy they both know well. I hear 'I hope nothing happens but you have to do your job,'" he wrote. He followed up with, "2/3 very far from any kind of coercion or influence and certainly not obstruction!" and concluded with, "3/3 Knowing my father for 39 years when he 'orders or tells' you to do something there is no ambiguity, you will know exactly what he means." He added the hashtag #givemeabreak, remarking that hoping and telling are entirely different concepts that someone like Comey should understand.

Social media users immediately pushed back against his commentary. 

Ciaran Jenkins responded on Twitter, writing, "So that's how it works. Donald Trump's son hears different words to the ones actually coming out of his mouth." 

Another user, Crenshaw, posted, "Your dad has conditioned you to hear what you want to hear." 

David J. Maloney chimed in with, "Uday chimes in."
