text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump formally rescinded a temporary freeze on most refugee arrivals late last October, a step anticipated to clear a path for individuals escaping violence and persecution to reach America. Instead, refugee admissions have experienced a dramatic decline. State Department figures examined by Reuters reveal that during the five-week window following the termination of the ban, entries dropped by 40 percent compared to the final five weeks the restriction remained active, a decrease that has largely flown under the radar.

Alongside the lifting of the ban, the Trump administration introduced stricter screening protocols and effectively paused entries from 11 nations classified as high-risk. This second measure played a major role in driving down the overall admission figures. In fact, the newly implemented restrictions have emerged as a significantly higher hurdle for refugees than the prior temporary suspension, which had seen its reach narrowed by the Supreme Court.

Shifts are also evident in the demographics of individuals being permitted entry, according to the State Department records. While Muslim refugees accounted for a quarter of the total during the ban, that share fell to just under 10 percent once the restrictions were lifted. 

Although a five-week timeframe represents a brief window for drawing broad inferences—and resettlement numbers typically accelerate later in the fiscal year, which commenced in October—the steep decline has sparked concern among advocates. Eric Schwartz, president of Refugees International, remarked that the administration is effectively winding down the refugee program without explicitly stating that intention, utilizing bureaucratic mechanisms and national security arguments to advance unjustifiable and nefarious goals.

Conversely, officials within the administration maintained that the initial temporary ban and subsequent security measures were designed to protect the American public from potential terrorist threats. Proponents of the policy also contended that the refugee system required an overhaul and that increased stringency would ultimately reinforce its integrity. Joshua Meservey, a senior policy analyst at the Heritage Foundation—a conservative research organization—and a former African refugee resettlement worker, voiced support for the changes, stating that the program needed tightening and that enhanced vetting and fraud reduction help protect the system in the long run.

A representative for the State Department attributed the downturn to intensified background checks, evaluations intended to flag potential security risks, and a reduced annual quota of 45,000 for the current year, marking the lowest ceiling in decades. Speaking anonymously, the official noted that refugee arrivals rarely follow a steady trajectory, often starting slowly at the beginning of the year before scaling up, and argued that evaluating the pace of the 2018 fiscal year at this stage is premature.

Immigration control has remained a cornerstone of Trump’s presidency, driven by stated commitments to national security and American employment. On the 2016 campaign trail, he asserted that Syrian refugees could potentially harbor ties to Islamist militants and pledged extreme vetting for all candidates. The White House declined to provide a comment when approached.

Following the expiration of the ban, the newly instated mandates included a 10-year biographical history requirement—up from five years—a suspension of the family reunification pathway, and an in-depth threat assessment for individuals originating from the 11 designated nations. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security confirmed that this 90-day review commenced on October 25, the day after the previous ban was lifted. While officials indicated that refugees from Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Mali, North Korea, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen would be evaluated individually on a case-by-case basis throughout the review, priority would be directed toward other applicants.

Historically, over the preceding three years, individuals from these 11 countries accounted for more than 40 percent of total U.S. refugee admissions. Although nine of these nations feature Muslim majorities, the individuals seeking asylum in the United States are frequently members of religious minorities, such as Christians and Jews. In practical terms, however, only Iran, Iraq, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, and Syria consistently produce significant numbers of refugees who ultimately resettle in the U.S.

Administration representatives asserted that the 90-day review does not equate to a blanket prohibition on travelers from the 11 targeted nations. Yet, concurrent with the launch of the review, arrivals from those specific countries nearly halted altogether. State Department records indicate that in the five weeks prior to the ban's removal, 587 refugees from those 11 countries gained entry despite strict eligibility criteria, whereas only 15 were admitted during the subsequent five-week period.

Across all nations, the State Department logged 1,469 refugee admissions between October 25 and November 28, representing a 41 percent reduction from the nearly 2,500 individuals who entered during the final five weeks of the formal ban. Demographically, Muslims comprised 9 percent and Christians 63 percent of those admitted between October 25 and November 28, compared to 26 percent Muslim and 55 percent Christian during the preceding five-week span. 

Higher admission numbers during the temporary ban occurred because the Supreme Court, when greenlighting the restriction in June, mandated exemptions for individuals possessing bona fide connections to the United States. Although legal challenges have been filed against the new directives, courts have yet to issue rulings.

Each shift in American refugee policy has left 34-year-old Alireza—a gay Iranian refugee residing in Turkey—struggling with confusion, a lack of information, and dwindling confidence that he will ever reach the United States. Alireza had already completed interviews with U.S. authorities and was progressing toward resettlement when the initial ban took effect in January. He withheld his family name because his relatives remain unaware of his sexual orientation, but he provided Reuters with documentation verifying his identity and refugee status. 

When federal courts initially blocked the Trump administration's ban, Alireza resumed the vetting process and neared final resettlement, only for the Supreme Court to reinstate the ban, which was subsequently succeeded by the current restrictions. Categorized as a refugee from one of the 11 nations subjected to enhanced scrutiny, he finds himself once again trapped in uncertainty. 

Alireza questions the security rationale behind the new assessments. Following harassment, physical assaults, and extortion in Iran, he and his partner of 13 years fled to Turkey in 2014. Human rights organizations note that Iranian laws targeting sexual minorities expose them to severe violence and discrimination. In Turkey, he explained, they survive on precarious part-time labor while growing increasingly uneasy over what they perceive as rising anti-gay sentiment in the local population. Speaking by phone from the northwestern Turkish city of Eskisehir, he asked why individuals who suffered under Iran’s Islamist system would spend three years enduring hardship in Turkey simply to travel to America and engage in terrorism.

Plans are reportedly under consideration by the Trump administration to skip submitting a presidential budget to Congress next year, marking a departure from tradition. The rationale behind this potential decision is to sidestep potential criticism. Legal experts point out that while the Congressional Budget Act mandates that the president deliver the fiscal 2018 budget between January 2 and February 6, bypassing this rule is technically possible without breaking the law. According to Forbes, citing an insider within the GOP congressional leadership, Trump could argue that the legal obligation to fulfill this requirement fell to the outgoing Obama administration prior to the January 20 inauguration. 

While never done before, this possibility sparked the trending hashtag #TrumpFirsts on Twitter, drawing commentary on presidential norms. Although these initial submissions or updates to late outgoing budgets frequently arrived past the early February deadline in a shortened format rather than the standard multi-volume set, a financial blueprint outlining the new administration's agenda has always emerged over the past four decades.

Usually, a newly inaugurated president looks forward to presenting a budget as a primary vehicle to showcase upcoming plans and outline specific priorities. However, releasing such a proposal inevitably opens the administration up to scrutiny from critics. Avoiding the formal proposal entirely effectively removes that specific avenue for pushback. 

Opting out of this process would also allow the administration to bypass the release of data tables reflecting the ambitious GDP growth targets touted during the campaign, anticipated high interest rates predicted by numerous economists, and forecasts regarding employment and job creation that critics view as unrealistic.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — An appeal brought by Texas to reinstate its stringent voter-identification rules was turned away by the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday. A lower court had previously determined that these Republican-supported regulations disproportionately impacted Hispanic and Black voters. By leaving in place the July 2016 lower court ruling, the justices allowed to stand the conclusion that the 2011 statute violated federal legislation prohibiting racial discrimination during elections, while also instructing a lower tribunal to develop a remedy for the measure's discriminatory impact on minority populations.

None of the eight justices recorded a dissent regarding the decision to pass on the case. However, Chief Justice John Roberts offered a rare explanatory statement on the refusal, pointing out that proceedings regarding the issue remain active in the lower courts. Roberts mentioned that while no obstacles prevented the high court from reviewing the matter, every legal question could still be brought up on appeal later on.

The legislation—which originated in a Republican-controlled legislature and received the signature of a Republican governor—stood as one of the nation's most rigorous measures of its kind. Legal challenges against it came from individual voters, civil rights organizations, and the U.S. Justice Department during the presidency of Barack Obama. Opponents, including the Obama administration, argued that this statute and comparable measures in other Republican-led states were intentionally crafted to create voting barriers for minority groups, such as Hispanic and Black citizens, who typically lean toward the Democratic Party. Conversely, proponents defended the rules as essential safeguards against voter fraud, notwithstanding a scarcity of proof regarding such offenses.

Under the statute, exactly seven forms of official identification were deemed acceptable for proving identity, encompassing items like a driver’s license, a U.S. passport, a military identification card, and a concealed handgun license, while excluding state university identification cards and credentials given out for welfare assistance. 

A larger, 15-judge configuration of the New Orleans-based 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals determined by a 9-6 vote that the Texas statute breached the U.S. Voting Rights Act due to its discriminatory impact, though the bench split along different lines on other aspects of the verdict. The appellate court instructed a federal district judge to review arguments from plaintiffs asserting that the measure was designed with discriminatory intent rather than merely resulting in a discriminatory outcome. A district court hearing concerning that specific issue had been slated for Tuesday, though it was postponed following a motion by the administration of President Donald Trump. While the preceding Obama administration supported the lawsuit against the Texas mandates, a shift in position by the Trump administration remained a possibility.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican whose office spearheaded the appeal, expressed frustration over the court's outcome via a statement. Paxton asserted that Texas implemented a sensible voter ID measure to protect election integrity and pledged to continue defending the statute before the district court, the Fifth Circuit, and potentially the Supreme Court once more.

Opponents of the measure estimated that as many as 600,000 individuals could be disenfranchised if the rules were fully enforced, given the substantial population of voters lacking the narrow selection of accepted identification documents. Following the circuit court's decision, the state and the plaintiffs negotiated an agreement for a temporary fix implemented during the November 2016 election. 

The Texas statute represents just one of several enacted by Republican-led statehouses following the year 2010. A comparable measure in North Carolina was invalidated by a federal appellate court in July 2016.

GENEVA (Reuters) — According to a United Nations human rights committee statement issued on Monday, women in North Korea face widespread sexual assault in workplaces, domestic abuse, and systemic barriers to employment and education. Following a routine examination of Pyongyang's human rights practices, the U.N. Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women highlighted worries regarding the abuse and rape of female detainees, particularly those who are sent back to the country after escaping across borders. 

The independent expert group noted that females in North Korea experience disadvantages and low representation in higher education, law enforcement, the judicial system, security agencies, and managerial roles across all unconventional employment sectors. Nicole Ameline, a member of the committee, explained to Reuters that gathering accurate data remains a primary obstacle, noting a general absence of details regarding national policies, legal frameworks, and information systems despite numerous inquiries.

During a session on November 8, North Korean representatives informed the panel that the state actively promotes gender equality and women's rights. However, Pyongyang argued that international sanctions related to its missile and nuclear activities are placing a heavy burden on vulnerable children and mothers. 

The committee pointed out that domestic abuse is widespread, accompanied by minimal societal awareness, insufficient legal assistance, and a scarcity of shelters and psychological support services for survivors. Furthermore, the panel indicated that economic penalties heavily affect women disproportionately. 

Malnutrition rates among North Korean women are notably severe, impacting 28 percent of nursing and pregnant mothers, the report stated. Ameline emphasized that the committee urged the administration to prioritize food security and nutritional needs, viewing them as fundamental requirements that demand government investment and accountability, though she expressed pessimism regarding how fast conditions might get better.

The assessment also revealed that punishments for rape are frequently inadequate for the gravity of the offenses and that perpetrators often evade justice entirely. Amendments made to the legal code in 2012 actually decreased sentences for specific categories of sexual assault, such as crimes involving children, repeat offenses, and assaults committed by employment supervisors. Consequently, the mandated prison term for coercing a female subordinate into sexual relations dropped from four years down to three, based on the findings.

Additionally, the document indicated that women who are trafficked to other countries and subsequently repatriated frequently face imprisonment or assignment to labor training facilities on charges of unauthorized border crossing. Once detained, these individuals frequently encounter additional human rights abuses, which include forced abortions and sexual violence perpetrated by security personnel.

On Tuesday, a federal judge signed off on a settlement negotiated by the U.S. Justice Department and the municipality of Ferguson, Missouri, aimed at overhauling the local police force. This arrangement stems from the 2014 fatal shooting of an unarmed Black teenager, an incident that ignited days of intense demonstrations. 

The 129-page document, endorsed by U.S. District Judge Catherine Perry of the Eastern District of Missouri, also calls for a complete overhaul of the municipal legal codes in this St. Louis suburb. The text of the consent decree emphasizes a shared understanding between federal authorities and the city that effective public safety relies entirely on the trust and bond between law enforcement and the residents they protect.

Under the newly approved terms, personnel within the Ferguson Police Department are mandated to complete training focused on bias awareness, alongside the establishment of a robust oversight framework. Furthermore, the municipality committed to ensuring that all enforcement actions—including stops, searches, and detentions—are free from discrimination regarding race or other legally protected characteristics. 

Civil unrest had gripped the predominantly Black community following a grand jury's decision not to bring charges against Darren Wilson, a white officer involved in the death of 18-year-old Michael Brown. Prior to the judicial sign-off, the Ferguson City Council voted in favor of the package back in March, following federal guarantees that the financial burden of compliance would not devastate the municipal budget. 

Ferguson joins a growing roster of American municipalities that have adopted similar federally monitored reform pacts, a group that includes Albuquerque, New Mexico, and Seattle, Washington. 

The court's decision coincided with a separate incident roughly 10 miles southeast of Ferguson, where a white officer from the St. Louis police department shot and killed a Black suspect tied to a carjacking. According to statements provided to the press by St. Louis Metropolitan Police Chief Sam Dotson, the individual aimed a firearm at law enforcement before an officer discharged his weapon. Authorities confirmed that none of the officers sustained injuries and that the patrol vehicle was not equipped with a dashboard camera.

AUSTIN, Texas — Texas Governor Greg Abbott approved legislation on Tuesday curbing insurance coverage for abortions, mandating that women purchase an additional, separate policy if they wish to have the procedure covered. The GOP governor argued that House Bill 214 shields those morally opposed to abortion from having to financially support it. Meanwhile, Democratic opponents condemned the legislation, labeling it a mandate for "rape insurance."

As the largest state governed by Republicans, Texas consistently leads the nation in implementing limitations on abortion, often setting a trend that other socially conservative states subsequently adopt. Upon taking effect on December 1, HB 214 will make Texas the eleventh state to limit abortion coverage within privately issued state insurance policies. 

In an official statement, Abbott remarked that as a dedicated supporter of Texas values, he felt honored to enact a law guaranteeing that no resident is forced to fund a procedure terminating a fetus. State Senator Brandon Creighton, the Republican author behind the companion legislation regarding abortion insurance, previously informed regional journalists that the extra policies would run between $12 and $80 annually. 

Having cleared both legislative chambers this month largely along party lines, House Bill 214 contains no exemptions for situations involving incest or rape. Reproductive rights organizations have indicated intentions to challenge the measure in court to block its implementation. 

State Representative Chris Turner, a Democrat who voted against the measure, argued on Tuesday that by approving HB 214, the governor essentially informed women and families that they must shell out extra funds for what amounts to "rape insurance." 

Data from the Guttmacher Institute, an organization monitoring reproductive legislation, indicates that 25 states already limit abortion coverage within health plans established via state exchanges under the Affordable Care Act, which was enacted by former President Barack Obama, a Democrat. 

Furthermore, Abbott approved a separate bill on Tuesday that broadens the mandates for reporting medical complications stemming from abortions.

Monday evening brought the resignation of Michael Flynn from his role as President Donald Trump's national security adviser, following mounting controversy surrounding his communications with Russian authorities. The White House made the departure public following a period of ambiguity regarding Flynn's future, which stemmed from reports that he had provided unclear accounts of his Russian contacts to Vice President Mike Pence and other administration personnel. 

Last month, key figures within the Trump administration, such as White House counsel Don McGahn, received briefings regarding Flynn's apparent discrepancies concerning his talks with Russian representatives. Although Yates was removed from her position a few days subsequent to declining to implement the executive order on the travel ban, an insider indicated that the briefing on Flynn was seemingly unrelated to her termination. The initial disclosure of this briefing came from The Washington Post on Monday, with the White House confirming Flynn's exit soon after.

In his letter of resignation, Flynn stated that during his capacity as the incoming National Security Advisor, he participated in numerous telephone conversations with international counterparts, ministers, and ambassadors aimed at ensuring a seamless transition and establishing foundational connections between the incoming president, his advisors, and foreign leaders, noting that such discussions represent standard procedure during transitions of this scale. He acknowledged that he unintentionally provided the Vice President Elect and others with partial details regarding his interactions with the Russian Ambassador, adding that he offered a sincere apology to both the President and the Vice President, which they accepted.

Stepping in as the interim national security adviser and leader of the National Security Council is Keith Kellogg, who currently serves as the chief of staff for the National Security Council. Retired Army Gen. Barry McCaffrey, a decades-long acquaintance of Kellogg, described him on Tuesday as a capable individual who stood out as an early supporter of Trump.

Flynn had long remained a contentious figure within national security circles and faced strong disapproval from mainstream aides under Trump, who argued that he promoted the president's conspiracy theories and skepticism toward intelligence agencies. Nonetheless, he retained the backing of the president, who valued his perceived loyalty and perspective on military matters. Additionally, Flynn shared a close bond with Stephen Bannon, the chief strategist to the president, who held significant influence over the administration both philosophically and strategically.

According to a White House insider, Bannon pulled Flynn aside for a discussion over the weekend. This official noted that Gannon, who had previously backed Flynn through various difficulties, advised him to take the honorable path and step down.

Search efforts for a permanent successor have already commenced within the White House. Sources with knowledge of the schedule indicated that retired Gen. David Petraeus is set to hold a meeting with Trump at the White House on Tuesday. During the transition period, Petraeus was briefly evaluated for the position of secretary of state, though he was ultimately bypassed, partially due to his 2015 conviction related to the mishandling of classified information. 

Trump has historically held Petraeus in high regard and sought his advice. An individual close to the president remarked that Trump appreciates and holds respect for him. Requests for comment sent via email to Petraeus went unanswered.

MANILA (Reuters) — Monday saw the Philippine government voice apprehension regarding Beijing's trials of a giant dredging vessel, emphasizing that authorities intend to monitor its movements carefully, notwithstanding Chinese guarantees that the vessel will stay away from disputed territories. Beijing has invested massive sums into constructing artificial landmasses to reinforce its territorial assertions throughout the majority of the South China Sea, and it has now commenced trials for a vessel engineered to enhance its capacity for land creation. 

Delfin Lorenzana, the country's defense chief, remarked to journalists that the vessel's mere existence causes a degree of worry, adding that its destination remains uncertain. According to defense personnel, the craft—named Tian Kun—features a surface area comparable to nine basketball courts and stands to become the biggest vessel of its kind in Asia. 

Beijing asserts sovereignty over virtually the entire South China Sea, an essential waterway carrying upwards of $3 trillion in annual maritime commerce. Competing territorial claims in these waters are also maintained by Brunei, Malaysia, Taiwan, Vietnam, and the Philippines. 

Lorenzana mentioned that personnel stationed across nine Philippine-held outposts within the South China Sea have received directives to keep a close watch on Chinese naval vessels, maritime law enforcement ships, and fishing vessels operating within the Spratly archipelago. Regular air patrols, alongside ongoing tracking efforts, ensure that the movements of the exceptionally large dredging ship will be kept under observation, he noted. 

Trials for the dredger coincide with the approach of two significant regional summits taking place in Vietnam and the Philippines over the current and following weeks, which are expected to draw leaders from both Beijing and Washington. 

During August, Chinese authorities and the foreign ministers of Southeast Asian nations endorsed a preliminary framework intended to guide negotiations for a South China Sea code of conduct. While participants celebrated this development as a positive step, skeptics viewed it as a maneuver allowing Beijing additional time to solidify its maritime dominance. Although all involved governments describe the framework merely as an initial guide for drafting the code, detractors point out that the document omits any primary goal for a legally binding and enforceable agreement, nor does it include a mechanism for resolving disputes, thereby casting doubt on its ultimate efficacy. 

In the Chinese capital, Assistant Foreign Minister Chen Xiaodong told the press that discussions concerning the framework had made substantial headway and anticipated tangible outcomes during the upcoming Southeast Asian leaders' summit in Manila, which is set to feature Chinese Premier Li Keqiang. 

Chen explained that the final characteristics of the code, including whether and how it might carry legal weight, will emerge from the ongoing negotiations between Beijing and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, noting that such matters cannot be determined unilaterally by any single participant. Meanwhile, Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to participate in the separate gathering of Asia-Pacific leaders hosted in Vietnam.

During a recent CNN broadcast, Donald Trump surrogate Scottie Nell Hughes anticipated an opportunity to pitch the Republican nominee to African-American voters—despite his current lack of polling support among that demographic—only to face swift pushback from political strategist Angela Rye regarding her defense of the candidate.

The discussion opened with host Anderson Cooper airing emotional footage of three Black mothers speaking about losing their children to gun violence. Attempting to make her argument, Hughes claimed to Anderson Cooper that Trump could deliver jobs and hope to Black neighborhoods, stating that crime and gang violence are rising in 44 urban areas, which requires targeted support for those communities through education and law enforcement.

Rye immediately challenged these assertions, calling out the underlying implications of Hughes's remarks. "A couple of things. One is—gun violence specifically—the overall crime rate has been on a steady decline since the 1980s," Rye stated. "But I think that it’s really important to watch the words that we use. When we say, 'Those communities, those people,' who are we talking about?"

Referencing the pre-segment interviews, Rye highlighted one mother's skepticism regarding Trump's assertion that he could resolve Chicago's crime issues within a week. Furthermore, Rye argued that Trump has consistently shown a lack of empathy toward the Black community concerning gun violence, racial profiling, and police brutality. 

"Donald Trump was busy calling people who look like me thugs, blaming the victim in these instances of gun violence and police brutality," Rye added. "That is deeply troubling to me and not only to me, but I'm sure to several other—I can't speak for all African-Americans—but to other African-Americans."

BRUSSELS (Reuters) — According to Amnesty International, European nations share responsibility for severe human rights abuses in Libya, pointing to European backing for local forces that frequently collaborate with traffickers and subject refugees and migrants to torture. 

In a statement released on Tuesday, Amnesty reported that an estimated 20,000 individuals are currently confined within Libyan migrant detention facilities, facing systematic torture, extortion, forced labor, and extrajudicial killings—findings that echo concerns raised by other human rights groups over the past several months.

This European backing for the Libyan administration forms a core component of a broader strategy designed to stem the flow of African migration through the Mediterranean. The initiative is intended to reduce migrant drownings at sea and alleviate the political pressures that high arrival rates create for EU leadership. Italy has taken the lead in executing this strategy, notably by providing equipment and training to the Libyan coastguard and allocating millions of euros to support relief operations managed by United Nations agencies inside Libya.

John Dalhuisen, who directs Amnesty’s European program, asserted that EU capitals are fully cognizant of these violations, arguing that their active assistance in blocking maritime departures and trapping people inside Libya makes them complicit in the resulting crimes.

During an address to parliament on Tuesday ahead of an upcoming summit of the bloc's leaders in Brussels, Italian Prime Minister Paolo Gentiloni defended the current European approach, noting that maritime arrivals have fallen by two-thirds since the previous July. Pointing to the millions contributed by Italy and the EU to upgrade conditions for those stranded in the country, Gentiloni maintained that Italy's efforts have brought much-needed visibility to human rights issues in Libya.

Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the European Commission acknowledged the severe and inhumane circumstances confronting many individuals, emphasizing that the EU's primary goal aligns with Amnesty's: saving lives. The spokesperson added that European funding has enabled the International Organization for Migration (IOM) to facilitate the repatriation of more than 15,000 people from Libya back to their countries of origin in Africa, while the bloc continues the gradual process of accepting individuals identified as genuine refugees.

Serving as the primary transit point for migrants attempting maritime journeys to Europe, Libya has seen a sharp decline in departures since July, as local factions and authorities began halting boats under pressure from Italy, the principal destination for arrivals. Over the preceding four years, more than 600,000 people have crossed via this route.

Amnesty contends that while the EU assists the Libyan coastguard in intercepting travelers bound for Europe, these same local forces maintain close ties with traffickers who extort money through torture. Dalhuisen argued that by enabling the containment of people within Libya, European leaders have demonstrated that their primary objective is sealing off the central Mediterranean corridor, regardless of the human suffering involved.

Although certain diplomats and EU officials remain uneasy about the bloc's dependence on armed militias that rose to power following the 2011 overthrow of Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, the bloc's leaders are set to reaffirm their commitment to the strategy during their Brussels meeting on Dec. 14-15, citing the tangible reduction in sea crossings as proof of the policy's success. 

Previously, the leadership of Libya's U.N.-supported administration asserted last month that the nation suffers as a victim of unauthorized migration rather than acting as its source, calling on international partners to assist in halting migration flows directly at the countries of origin.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Democratic vice-presidential hopeful Tim Kaine stepped up to defend Hillary Clinton on Sunday regarding the controversy surrounding her management of sensitive government secrets while leading the State Department. According to Kaine, Clinton failed to recognize the confidential nature of certain email communications because the messages lacked proper markers. 

Back in July, the FBI criticized the Democratic presidential contender for relying on a home-brew email server during her 2009-to-2013 tenure as America's top diplomat, characterizing her actions regarding classified data as "extremely careless." Furthermore, documentation published by the bureau on a recent Friday revealed that during a July conversation with investigators, Clinton stated she had no recollection of receiving instructions regarding classified protocols or federal record-keeping regulations. 

Appearing on ABC’s "This Week," Kaine—a Virginia senator who serves on both the Senate Foreign Relations and Armed Services panels—explained that public servants process such massive quantities of data that identifying designated secrets is frequently challenging. 

“There were emails that contained classified information that had been improperly marked. So when she received the email, the material that was classified - which is supposed to be flagged and identified as classified - in many instances was improperly labeled,” Kaine stated during the broadcast. He further noted, “We look at so much material, unless it is specifically pulled out and identified, it is difficult to know sometimes whether a statement or a paragraph is classified or not.”

During the same television appearance, Kaine drew a parallel between Republican opponent Donald Trump’s recent appeal for Russia to locate 30,000 deleted messages from Clinton's server and the infamous 1972 Watergate break-in at the Democratic headquarters in Washington, an event that ultimately brought down Richard Nixon's administration. 

“He has openly encouraged Russia to engage in cyber hacking to try to find more e-mails or materials, and we know that this cyber attack on the DNC was likely done by Russia,” Kaine remarked to the Sunday audience, adding, “This is serious business.”

Trump’s remarks were directed at roughly 30,000 messages that Clinton’s legal team classified as personal and opted "not to keep," whereas thousands of other work-related messages were handed back to federal authorities in 2014. While this move is broadly understood to mean the personal records were erased, aides have consistently avoided verifying whether that actually occurred. 

Vying against Trump for the presidency in the upcoming November 8 election, Clinton has spent over a year dealing with the negative consequences of setting up an unapproved private server based in her Chappaqua, New York residence. She has maintained adamantly that she never transmitted or received secret intelligence through that channel, despite federal regulations strictly prohibiting the management of such material outside of secure networks. 

Contradicting Clinton's assertions that no sensitive information crossed her private server, the FBI reported that a minimum of 81 email threads held data that was classified at the moment of transmission, with the agency suggesting the ultimate tally could surpass 2,000. Even though the bureau reprimanded Clinton over her security practices, officials ultimately advised against pursuing criminal charges against her. Clinton has since acknowledged that looking back, utilizing a personal network as secretary of state was a mistake. 

Public opinion surveys indicate that doubts regarding Clinton's integrity and reliability remain her primary political liabilities. Recent polling data indicates a narrowing contest over the preceding several weeks. Specifically, a Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted between August 26 and September 1 showed Trump drawing 40 percent among likely voters compared to Clinton's 39 percent. Clinton's numbers in that weekly tracking poll have experienced a continuous decline since August 25, completely erasing a prior eight-point advantage.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — A fresh legal battle over immigration policy began Thursday as advocates launched an uphill campaign to salvage a portion of President Barack Obama’s directive designed to protect millions of undocumented immigrants from removal. The strategy involves a newly filed lawsuit aimed at contesting the nationwide reach of the judicial injunction that previously stalled the initiative. According to the attorneys behind the complaint, successful outcomes could eventually help dismantle the rulings that halted the November 2014 presidential program across the country. 

Had the administration's initiative gone into effect fully, it might have granted work permits to as many as four million individuals lacking legal status. The legal action was lodged in a federal tribunal in New York, naming 25-year-old Mexican immigrant Martin Batalla Vidal as a plaintiff. Vidal, who arrived in the U.S. at age seven, had previously gained advantages from the policy before a Texas judge's February 2015 decision to block the program led to the revocation of his initial three-year work permit. That earlier injunction stemmed from a challenge brought by Texas alongside 25 additional states. Despite this setback, Vidal remains qualified for a two-year employment authorization through a separate, unchallenged previous program that remained untouched by the court order. 

Representatives from the National Immigration Law Center, who are representing Vidal, argue that a victory could carry significant weight by potentially reviving the Obama initiative for roughly 60 percent of prospective applicants located in regions outside the scope of the Texas decision. The initial ruling by the Texas jurist survived an appellate review, and the Supreme Court subsequently split 4-4 on June 23, maintaining the lower court's outcome. Because Justice Antonin Scalia passed away in February, the high court currently operates with a vacancy while it weighs whether to take up the matter again once all nine seats are filled.

BOGOTA (Reuters) - Public officials in Colombia expressed outrage on Thursday over an inventory of property submitted by the FARC rebel movement for victim compensation, which featured items like shoes and citrus squeezers, prompting the administration to form a dedicated verification body. 

Under the terms of the 2016 peace accord with the state, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia committed to surrendering all financial resources and real estate to compensate those impacted by land mines, forced displacement, kidnapping, rape, and forced disappearances. For generations, the organization generated income through extortion of business owners and landowners, ransom payments from kidnapping victims, and the sale of coca—the primary component of cocaine—to narcotics traffickers.

According to officials, the inventory—initially submitted to the United Nations and kept out of the public eye—contained numerous goods lacking any meaningful financial worth, which critics argued insulted the victims. 

"Pots, orange juicers, lemon juicers, plates, boots, which will be depreciated and don't have a commercial value and which above all will not be a source of reparation for victims," Attorney General Nestor Humberto Martinez stated to reporters, while also calling for the complete inventory to be made public.

Later on Thursday, the administration announced that a specialized commission would examine the catalog to track down unlisted assets, confirm their sources, and determine how to handle them.

Justice Minister Enrique Gil warned that any property left off the inventory that is uncovered later will mandate penalties and standard judicial proceedings for FARC members. Interior Minister Guillermo Rivera added that every asset will go exclusively toward repairing victims rather than funding reintegration initiatives for former combatants.

Colombian authorities have previously alleged that the FARC holds substantial amounts of liquid cash, alongside commercial properties, cattle ranches, and high-end residences, some situated outside the country. 

Meanwhile, Enrique Santiago, an attorney acting for the FARC, informed a domestic radio station that the insurgents had stopped generating revenue years prior and were forced to spend heavily on sustaining a force of over 7,000 combatants after abandoning extortion and hostage-taking during negotiations. 

Earlier this month, the guerrillas concluded the surrender of upwards of 8,000 firearms to the U.N., which managed their disarmament process. The movement is scheduled to begin a gathering on Sunday anticipated to formalize its shift into a political entity.

LONDON (Reuters) - Turkish EU Minister Omer Celik stated in a Thursday interview that Ankara experiences a sense of betrayal due to certain European Union figures advocating for the termination of membership negotiations, though the country maintains its long-term aspiration of entering the union. Criticism of Turkey's bid has intensified across the bloc following President Tayyip Erdogan's widespread crackdown against academics, journalists, and other critics in the wake of the unsuccessful 2016 military coup attempt. Back in March, Erdogan compared German actions to "Nazi-like" methods after authorities in Germany blocked Turkish government ministers from addressing rallies of expatriates. Furthermore, German Chancellor Angela Merkel stated during a televised election debate that it had become evident Turkey ought not to become a member and that negotiations should be halted, notwithstanding Ankara's status as a vital ally within NATO.

During his interview with Reuters, Celik criticized the rhetoric employed by various EU leaders regarding Turkey's candidacy, arguing that figures like Merkel leverage anti-Turkey sentiment to distract voters from the bloc's internal crises, including migration challenges, Brexit, and institutional reforms. Through a translator, Celik asserted that these leaders sideline critical matters and cultivate hostility toward Turkey to mask their own pressing domestic difficulties, expressing explicit disappointment in Merkel and other European partners who left Turkey isolated during one of the most perilous moments in its modern history. When specifically queried on whether this amounted to a feeling of betrayal, he answered affirmatively.

The failed putsch, which resulted in over 260 fatalities as rebellious troops utilized tanks, attack helicopters, and fighter jets in an effort to overthrow the government, has widened the divide separating Ankara from Western governments. Officials in Turkey argued that numerous Western partners displayed a sluggish response in expressing solidarity with the administration following the uprising, which the government viewed as a calculated assault on Turkish democracy. In the aftermath, approximately 50,000 individuals—encompassing civil servants, dissidents, journalists, and others—have been arrested, sparking deep concern among international human rights organizations and Western capitals.

Celik noted that European leaders, including Merkel, have fallen short of honoring commitments made regarding Turkey's candidacy, which officially commenced with an application to the European Economic Community in 1987, followed by the formal opening of accession talks in 2005. Contending that the EU has failed to fulfill its pledges while Turkey has upheld its end, Celik also addressed remarks made by European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker, who stated on Wednesday that he anticipates no possibility of Turkish membership in the near future. Challenging Juncker's approach, Celik questioned what significant actions the Commission president has undertaken to bridge the gap between Europe and Ankara. 

He further warned that if Berlin continues dictating directives to European institutions, such as pushing for the severance of talks with Turkey, such a dynamic would ultimately empower racist factions throughout Europe. While formally concluding the negotiation process demands unanimous agreement among all member states—a consensus that currently does not exist—a majority vote would suffice to suspend the talks. As a potential path forward, Celik proposed convening a joint summit between European Union and Turkish leaders to repair bilateral ties, emphasizing that Ankara remains fully committed to achieving full membership and eager to negotiate constructive solutions for progress. 

European leaders are scheduled to deliberate on the status of Turkey during an upcoming summit in Brussels, though any definitive resolution regarding the relationship's future may be delayed until the following spring. Addressing separate concerns, Celik dismissed notions that Turkey's acquisition of the S-400 missile defense system from Russia signals a geopolitical shift away from Western alliances. Asserting that Turkey's geopolitical alignment is clear and that the nation has significantly bolstered European security and economic well-being, he maintained that maintaining a firm role within NATO and cultivating friendly ties with Moscow are mutually compatible rather than mutually exclusive objectives.

MADRID (Reuters) — According to official survey data released on Tuesday, the secessionist movement in Catalonia has rapidly climbed to become the second most significant anxiety for people across Spain, trailing only joblessness and jumping significantly from its position as the ninth major worry back in September. The severe political standoff involving the northeastern territory and the central administration peaked on the first of October. This occurred after regional president Carles Puigdemont proceeded with an independence referendum that Madrid deemed unlawful, subsequently making a declaration of separation prior to his dismissal and replacement by authorities. 

Based on the research conducted between October 2 and October 11, roughly 29 percent of participants pointed to the Catalan separation effort as the nation's primary issue. This represented a sharp rise from only 7.8 percent recorded in the prior survey conducted at the start of September. Meanwhile, joblessness—representing the second highest rate across the European continent—remained the top issue for 66.2 percent of the populace. 

The same study indicated that if a general election were to take place immediately, the governing People's Party would maintain its minority administration by capturing 28 percent of ballots, marking a slight decline from the 28.8 percent recorded during the previous survey in July. Conversely, the pro-market Ciudadanos party, which originated in Catalonia, experienced an increase in backing, moving from 14.5 percent in July to 17.5 percent in October. Meanwhile, the Socialists would keep their standing as the second-biggest faction within parliament, though their numbers shifted slightly to 24.2 percent from the prior 24.9 percent. The polling sample comprised a total of 2,487 respondents.

SHANGHAI (Reuters) — The ruling Communist Party in China formally integrated President Xi Jinping’s massive "Belt and Road" trade and infrastructure initiative into its constitution on Tuesday, a surprising move that elevates the policy's importance and raises the stakes for its implementation. 

The update to the party charter, which was formally adopted as the twice-a-decade congress drew to a close, includes a commitment to "pursue the Belt and Road initiative." Observers noted that this development highlights Xi's growing authority and suggests the grand, Silk Road-inspired project will outlast his time in office. Analysts also pointed out that the decision demonstrates a heightened focus on foreign affairs by the Communist Party and points to Xi's ambition for China to step into a prominent global leadership position.

"Everyone knows that the Belt and Road is very important to Xi, it has his personal stamp and authority," remarked Peter Cai, a non-resident fellow at the Lowy Institute, a think tank based in Sydney. "But to have major policy, especially an external engagement policy, to be written into a party constitution, at least in recent memory, it is something quite significant," he added.

Originally introduced by Xi during a 2013 address to students at a university in Kazakhstan, the strategy serves as a mechanism for Beijing to expand its international influence by financing and constructing trade and transport networks across more than 60 nations. Xi has been a tireless advocate for the scheme, hosting global leaders in Beijing for a landmark summit in May where he committed $124 billion (94 billion) toward the project. In response, private corporations, state-owned enterprises, and regional Chinese administrations have scrambled to back the effort through overseas loans and investments.

Detractors have suggested that the campaign is merely a way for Beijing to offload surplus industrial capacity while extending its geopolitical reach. They argue that the project—which has saddled several emerging nations with substantial debt burdens—demands better governance and greater openness.

"China has made commitments and pledges to many developing countries and it will take that length of time, 10 years or more, to complete the initiative," observed Rajiv Biswas, the chief economist for the Asia Pacific region at IHS Markit. "This has also strengthened China s soft power globally, so it wouldn t make sense for China s point of view to suddenly pull away from all of this," he noted.

Conversely, some experts cautioned that elevating the initiative could prove to be a double-edged sword, increasing the pressure to deliver results for a program that remains loosely defined and subject to wide interpretation.

"The danger of having given it greater visibility is that actually there are going to be more of those efforts to play to the policy in a political way rather than considering carefully the costs and benefits of each portion of what one is doing," explained Dali Yang, a political science professor at the University of Chicago.

Already, numerous regional governments have unveiled customized Belt and Road strategies, while commercial investors have rushed to rebrand their ventures under the initiative's umbrella. Throughout the week-long political gathering, executives from major Chinese corporations—including China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation [SASAAI.UL] and China Communications Construction Co—told Reuters that they intend to prioritize the expansion of their international operations to back the Belt and Road project. 

The party congress concluded with Xi solidifying his political dominance ahead of his upcoming second five-year term. By having his personal political philosophy written directly into the nation's charter, Xi was elevated to a status alongside Mao Zedong, the founder of modern China.

In her defense, Clinton pointed to President Barack Obama, noting that his decision to appoint her secretary of state served as a testament to her sound judgment. Emphasizing the need for a battle-tested contender, Clinton told the audience that a proven fighter is essential.

Seeking to fend off the challenge from the democratic socialist, Clinton aimed to persuade Democratic voters to look past Sanders' populist appeal and maintain their support despite widespread enthusiasm for anti-establishment figures. Unlike a traditional debate, the Drake University gathering featured individual segments where Sanders, former Maryland Governor Martin O’Malley, and Clinton each answered questions from the crowd. 

While the atmosphere remained courteous—a departure from the contentious fourth debate the previous week—Clinton appeared more energetic than usual as she raised her voice to emphasize her points, and Sanders amused the crowd with humor. Sanders pointed to Clinton's 2002 vote in the Senate approving the Iraq war, alongside her past backing of the Keystone Pipeline stretching from Canada to Texas, as proof that her longevity in politics was accompanied by flawed choices. Pointing out that Sanders had opposed both measures from the beginning, he acknowledged that experience matters, but stressed that judgment is equally critical, noting that Clinton has since changed her stance on those matters.

The Vermont senator also stood by his proposals to increase taxes in order to finance universal healthcare, infrastructure projects, and free college tuition. Admitting candidly that taxes would indeed go up, Sanders argued that families would ultimately come out ahead financially because they would no longer have to shoulder private health insurance costs.

Throughout her campaign, Clinton has highlighted her years as a New York senator and secretary of state as proof of her readiness. On the town hall stage, she deflected Sanders' jabs about her judgment by invoking President Obama, who continues to enjoy high favorability among Democrats despite having used her Iraq war vote against her during their 2008 primary battle. Recalling that Obama ultimately tapped her to lead the State Department, Clinton stated that the appointment stemmed from his trust in her judgment through their four years of working closely together.

Although Clinton held a commanding lead for months following her 2008 primary defeat, recent polling has revealed a notable rise in momentum for Sanders. Clinton has argued that while Sanders' aspirations regarding social inequality are admirable, some are unrealistic and he lacks the breadth of experience needed to handle an array of unpredictable challenges. Speaking earlier on Monday at the Jewish Federation of Greater Des Moines, Clinton remarked that life in the White House requires readiness for every unforeseen issue rather than picking and choosing topics.

Additionally, Clinton used the town hall platform to take aim at Republican front-runner Donald Trump, specifically condemning his rhetoric targeting minority groups. Pointing out his trajectory, she noted that he began by attacking Mexicans and later turned his focus to Muslims.

Meanwhile, on the same day exactly one week prior to the state's inaugural nominating contest leading up to the November 8 election, Clinton received a timely boost from President Obama in a Politico interview. Without directly taking aim at Sanders—whose platform centers on tackling income inequality and reining in Wall Street—Obama lauded Clinton's vast experience and described her approach as rooted in pragmatism. Characterizing her as exceptionally knowledgeable and wicked smart on policy, Obama observed that her extensive background can sometimes make her cautious, leading to a campaign defined more by prose than poetry.

WASHINGTON — Following the collapse of their healthcare initiative, White House officials sent a clear message to rebellious conservatives: fall in line with President Donald Trump’s legislative priorities, or face the possibility of being sidelined during upcoming battles, particularly over tax reform. 

Reince Priebus, the White House chief of staff, raised the prospect of forging a broad bipartisan alliance—potentially incorporating moderate Democrats—for the tax overhaul. This warning coincided with an announcement from the Republican leader of the House tax-writing committee, who stated his intention to advance a tax measure through his panel this spring. 

Kevin Brady, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, mentioned during an appearance on Fox News that his team continued drafting tax legislation concurrently with the unsuccessful healthcare push. According to Brady, the committee never halted its efforts and will keep making refinements, aiming to bring the bill forward in the spring. He emphasized his preference for the House framework to serve as the foundation for the president's tax plan, rather than seeing competing proposals emerge from the Treasury Department and the White House.

Wall Street investors have expressed concern that the defeat of the healthcare bill signals trouble for tax reform. Equity markets had surged following the election largely due to anticipation of tax reductions. Without the boost from fiscal stimulus, economic growth is expected to slow, and U.S. equity index futures dropped to a six-week low.

Both the president and his chief of staff took aim at hardline conservatives who voted down the administration's replacement for the Affordable Care Act. During an interview on "Fox News Sunday," Priebus left the door open to collaborating with moderate Democrats and Republicans alike on other major components of the presidential agenda, such as the upcoming budget, the restructuring of the tax code, and a renewed push for healthcare reform.

While Priebus noted that passing a bill with Republican votes alone remains the preferred path if the president's objectives can be met, he described the overture to other lawmakers as a warning shot demonstrating a willingness to negotiate more broadly than ever before.

Friday’s withdrawal of the healthcare bill from the House floor marked a significant setback for a president who campaigned heavily on his reputation as a master negotiator. The measure had to be pulled after failing to secure sufficient backing within the Republican caucus, while Democrats remained entirely opposed. Despite intensive lobbying efforts by the administration, members of the conservative House Freedom Caucus and several moderate Republicans withheld their votes, leaving leadership short of the threshold needed for passage. 

External conservative organizations—such as Heritage Action for America and the Club for Growth, both closely tied to the Freedom Caucus—lobbied aggressively against the Republican healthcare proposal and urged lawmakers to vote against it. On Sunday morning, Trump took to Twitter to criticize both the caucus and these allied groups, writing that their actions left Democrats smiling in Washington.

Priebus lamented the decision by conservative lawmakers to withhold their support, adding that the president felt let down by individuals he previously believed were loyal to him.

Following the healthcare defeat, tax reform has jumped to the forefront of the administration's legislative schedule. Priebus confirmed that the president remains committed to including a border tax in the legislation, alongside a middle-class tax cut that could potentially draw support from moderate Democrats.

Demonstrating that the Freedom Caucus is not entirely monolithic, U.S. Representative Ted Poe of Texas announced his resignation from the group, offering a glimmer of encouragement for the administration's tax efforts. In a short statement, Poe stressed the need for unity to fulfill the conservative promises made to voters over the past eight years, noting that leadership requires solutions rather than mere obstruction.

Meanwhile, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer criticized the administration's handling of the healthcare debate and predicted that Republicans would continue to encounter resistance from their own conservative flank on subsequent issues. Suggesting that the party risks repeating its healthcare missteps during the tax debate, Schumer encouraged the president to distance himself from the Freedom Caucus and engage with Democrats instead. He indicated that while Democrats would review the president's proposals, any cooperation would be shaped by their own core principles.

Rep. Mark Meadows, a Republican from North Carolina who chairs the Freedom Caucus, expressed optimism on Sunday regarding tax reform, suggesting his faction could back a proposal that lacks complete revenue neutrality. Arguing that lower taxes generate increased economic activity, Meadows stated that his personal view is that full offsets are not strictly necessary.

Another member of the caucus, Representative Jim Jordan, urged a move away from mutual recriminations in the wake of the healthcare defeat, calling instead for a renewed focus on the work ahead.

FORMER NPR CEO DITCHES AND SWITCHES: How A Liberal Learned to Love the ‘Right’ [Video]

Ken Stern, the former chief executive officer of NPR, has made a notable shift after breaking out of his previous liberal environment. In a recent discussion with Tucker Carlson, he talked about leaving behind the liberal bubble. Observers are praising his move away from the left and toward the conservative side. 

STERN RECENTLY SPOKE WITH BREITBART’S ALEX MARLOW:

Describing his background, Stern noted that he was a lifelong Democrat who previously worked in Democratic politics, led NPR, and lived within a heavily Democratic household inside an overwhelmingly Democratic ward. Driven by worries regarding the nation's growing political divide, he decided to travel into red-state America to gain a firsthand perspective of the political opposition. 

His defining "a-ha!" moment stemmed from a local neighborhood tradition in Washington, D.C., where children annually recited a pledge at a block party. The pledge welcomed everyone on Hobart Street—regardless of gender, sexual orientation, or race—with the sole exception of Republicans. Although framed as a joke, it carried a serious undertone, signaling how people were beginning to treat the opposing side. For Stern, it served as a catalyst, making him realize he needed to escape his Democratic bubble, interact with the rest of the country, and discover whether the other half of America consisted of "deplorables" or everyday citizens just like him. That realization shaped his year of exploration.

Discussing media structures, Stern pointed out that NPR differs from other organizations because its staff is spread nationwide rather than being centralized solely in political and media hubs. Pointing to outlets like The New York Times, where the vast majority of personnel are based in New York, he noted that NPR functions as a membership organization with local stations across the country, giving it unusual geographic representation. However, as he recently pointed out in the New York Post, the challenge remains that despite being geographically dispersed, mainstream journalistic entities largely draw from a liberal talent pool. This dynamic fosters groupthink and increases the likelihood that chosen stories fail to represent the broader country.

Stern argued that ideological bubbling affects both sides of the political spectrum. Because the nation has become politically fragmented, with Democrats and Republicans primarily associating only with their own, it is simple to embrace cartoonish and harsh caricatures of the opposition. He referenced a Washington Post poll from the previous year asking voters from both parties to summarize the other side in a single word, yielding extreme terms like "bigot" for Republicans and "traitor" for Democrats—exaggerated stereotypes of political opponents. 

According to Stern, Hillary Clinton’s remarks—and subsequent apology—referring to a segment of Trump supporters as a "basket of deplorables" accurately mirrors how many individuals view conservatives, though he emphasized that this tendency exists on both sides of the aisle, hindering true understanding.

His journey across the political divide involved various unconventional experiences, such as participating in a pig hunt in Texas and visiting small Assembly of God churches to engage with individuals holding different viewpoints. His travels also took him to declining coal mining communities in Pikeville, Kentucky, and to Youngstown, Ohio, among other places. The subtitle of his book, "How I Left the Liberal Bubble and Learned to Love the Right," reflects these encounters. While he did not agree with everyone he met, he encountered hundreds of individuals who were admirable, contributed positively to their communities, and completely defied stereotypical depictions of Middle America.

To test convictions he once viewed as absolute—such as guns, poverty programs, and climate change—Stern engaged directly with opposing perspectives, consulting gun-control skeptic John Lott Jr., attending gun shows, conducting his own research, and even going hunting. By intentionally viewing issues through the eyes of others, his own perspective naturally shifted.

Recounting a particularly striking experience for someone coming from an urban, gun-control background, he described hunting in Georgia. There, he received gun safety instructions from an eight-year-old and hunted alongside a diverse group that bore no resemblance to coastal stereotypes of rural white men. 

As an agnostic Jew from Washington, D.C., Stern's prior exposure to evangelicals was limited to pop culture references like the movie *Footloose* and figures like Jerry Falwell, who had passed away a decade prior to his project. This unfamiliarity changed when he attended the Urbana Conference alongside roughly 15,000 evangelical youths. Expecting cinematic caricatures, he instead found young people discussing ways to welcome and aid refugees, promote campus diversity, and dedicate their lives to feeding the poor and housing the homeless. Witnessing this group firsthand demonstrated to him that with 50 million evangelicals in existence, there are 50 million distinct stories, making broad generalizations impossible.

Stern also observed that media professionals often cluster together, reinforcing their own confirmation biases, stereotypes, and groupthink. He views this as a profound and difficult hurdle for networks like CNN and others to recognize and overcome. Furthermore, he noted that in the era of Trump, conflict has proven financially advantageous for the media. President Trump's criticisms of outlets like the "failing New York Times" are met with responses from the publication, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that ultimately benefits the bottom line of both parties involved, which he considers a significant issue.

TORONTO (Reuters) - Wednesday afternoon departures headed to the United States from Toronto's primary international airport faced delays following an event that forced certain travelers to undergo customs screening all over again, according to a representative. 

Beverly MacDonald, a spokesperson for Toronto Pearson International Airport, stated via email that a security breach took place in Terminal 3 not long after 3:30 p.m. (2030 GMT). 

She noted that while authorities looked into the matter, boarding procedures were paused and specific travelers were directed back through U.S. Customs for reprocessing, noting further that the situation was cleared up near 5 p.m. (2200 GMT). 

The security lapse happened when individuals getting off an incoming flight from Calgary mistakenly gained entry to a bypass route leading directly into the U.S. departure zone, explained Lauren Stewart, a representative for WestJet Airlines Ltd (WJA.TO), in an email message to Reuters. 

Based on details provided by the airport's official website, Terminal 3 handles U.S.-bound services operated by Delta Air Lines Inc (DAL.N), American Airlines Group Inc (AAL.O), WestJet, and Alaska Air Group Inc (ALK.N).

WARSAW (Reuters) — Prime Minister Beata Szydlo announced on Tuesday that she will unveil a government shake-up in the near future, though she chose not to address rumors suggesting her own position could be in jeopardy. There has been widespread chatter in financial markets and media outlets regarding a potential overhaul, as the ruling Law and Justice (PiS) party reportedly considers removing certain ministers who are dragging down its generally favorable polling numbers ahead of the 2018 regional contests. 

The weekly publication Sieci Prawdy reported on Monday that the 54-year-old Szydlo might step down in favor of Jaroslaw Kaczynski, the leader of the conservative PiS party to which they both belong. Meanwhile, the tabloid Fakt published a report on Tuesday indicating that while Szydlo is expected to retain her post, officials like Foreign Minister Witold Waszczykowski and Environment Minister Jan Szyszko—who struggle with low public approval—could be ousted. 

Kaczynski, aged 68 and widely recognized as a polarizing figure who ranks among the least trusted political figures in the country, wields immense power from behind the scenes. Press reports have suggested he might be eyeing Szydlo's premier role with an eye on the 2019 national elections. 

Speaking to the private television network TVN 24, Szydlo stated that she wished to put an end to ongoing rumors about cabinet modifications, noting that her choices would be revealed shortly. She emphasized that the determination has been made to alter the cabinet composition, and mentioned that she consulted with Kaczynski, describing that step as completely normal. When questioned regarding the potential of her own exit, Szydlo declined to engage in guesswork and asserted that she neither feels exhausted nor burned out. Public surveys consistently place her as the second-most trusted political figure in the nation, trailing only President Andrzej Duda.

Jaroslaw Flis, a sociologist affiliated with Jagiellonian University in Krakow, noted that a more restricted shake-up targeting only a handful of ministers would likely stem from a natural impulse to clear out the administration's weakest performers. 

The current PiS administration has polarized public opinion, steering Warsaw toward friction with the European Union over initiatives like expanding oversight of the judicial system and public broadcasting, which opponents argue threaten democratic norms. Nevertheless, the party maintains robust public support. According to findings from state polling agency CBOS, 44 percent of participants identified as backers of the administration, marking the highest level of support seen in six years.

ANKARA (Reuters) - State television reported that numerous Iranians participated in demonstrations nationwide on Friday to protest U.S. President Donald Trump's recent choice to acknowledge Jerusalem as the capital of Israel. 

Ever since the 1979 Islamic revolution, hostility toward Israel and backing for Palestinians has remained a core pillar of Iranian foreign policy. Iranian leadership has strongly criticized Trump's declaration, which also encompasses shifting the American embassy to Jerusalem. Footage broadcast on state television showed demonstrators carrying Palestinian banners and flags, displaying signs that declared "Quds belongs to Muslims"—employing the Arabic term for the city—while shouting slogans such as "Death to America" and "Death to Israel." Local media outlets noted that effigies of Trump were set on fire in multiple municipalities. 

Iran does not acknowledge the existence of the Jewish state, viewing the entirety of the holy land as Palestinian territory. The country routinely advocates for Israel's elimination and provides support to various militant Islamic organizations opposing it. 

Labeling both the United States and Israel as oppressors, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei stated earlier on Wednesday that Trump's announcement demonstrated failure and incompetence. 

The backlash against the U.S. policy has brought together Iran's pragmatist and hardline political groups. Both hardline Revolutionary Guards commanders and pragmatist President Hassan Rouhani called upon citizens to participate in countrywide "Day of Rage" demonstrations. 

Amid chants of "Death to the Devil," demonstrators destroyed photographs of both Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by fire. 

Rouhani characterized the U.S. policy shift as highly dangerous, provocative, wrong, and illegitimate. Meanwhile, state TV coverage showed senior cleric Ayatollah Ahmad Khatami telling the congregation during Friday prayers at Tehran University that the global Muslim community must band together against Israel. 

During those same Friday services in the capital, attendees chanted, "We will not leave Palestinians alone," according to television broadcasts. Additionally, IRNA, Iran's official news agency, quoted army chief Major General Mohammad Bagheri, who termed the Jerusalem decision unwise and warned it could heighten instability throughout the volatile Middle East.

A group of nine former United States permanent representatives to the United Nations submitted a letter to lawmakers on Tuesday, cautioning that severe budget cuts to the international organization would undermine American standing abroad and hand over leadership opportunities to adversarial nations. 

The bipartisan group of signatories—consisting of Andrew Young, Donald McHenry, Thomas Pickering, Edward Perkins, Madeleine Albright, Bill Richardson, John Negroponte, Susan Rice, and Samantha Power—represented administrations from both major political parties. 

Speaking to the press, Albright stressed that reducing financial support for the organization harms national security and global standing, noting that countries like Russia and China are eager to step into any vacuum left behind. 

Lawmakers were pressed in the correspondence to steer clear of deep budgetary reductions and instead allow the current U.S. envoy, Nikki Haley, alongside U.N. leader Antonio Guterres, adequate time to pursue organizational reforms aimed at improving efficiency and responsiveness. 

As the organization's primary financial backer, the United States currently covers 22 percent of the $5.4 billion core operating expenses and provides 28.5 percent of the $7.9 billion dedicated to peacekeeping missions, with all member states agreeing upon these assessments through the General Assembly. 

Characterizing the American financial burden as inequitable, President Trump has advocated for unspecified cuts to U.N. operations and agencies, alongside the implementation of a strict 25 percent ceiling on peacekeeping contributions. 

Anonymous concerns have also been raised within diplomatic circles regarding the potential fallout of a withdrawal of American financial backing. One high-ranking diplomat remarked that pulling back could inadvertently result in a "China first" outcome rather than an "America first" approach by surrendering influence. 

During a White House luncheon on Monday with envoys from the Security Council, Trump indicated that financial contributions could be justified if the institution successfully implements operational overhauls. Remarking to the fifteen diplomats present, he stated that effective performance makes the budget secondary, describing the costs as minimal relative to the significance of their mission. 

Earlier in the week on Friday, Guterres held his inaugural meeting with Trump at the White House following the recent transition of power for both officials. 

Meanwhile, the State Department announced earlier this month that financial support for the United Nations Population Fund—an agency operating across more than 150 nations to support maternal health, child welfare, and family planning—would be terminated, prompting Guterres to caution that the decision carries the potential for severe consequences.

The stated goal is to halt what they describe as an ongoing push by a coalition—including Obama, Holder, Sharpton, Soros, BlackLivesMatter, the Black Panthers, Louis Farrakhan, Black Liberation Theology, CAIR, liberal academia, the Socialist Party, the Democrat Party, Anarchists, and the Communist Party—to keep race at the forefront. Proponents maintain they are safeguarding the interests of white students whom they believe are becoming marginalized within campus life and political discourse. Conversely, allegations persist that the entire phenomenon is an elaborate trolling campaign directed at universities and media outlets by participants on online forums such as 4chan and 8chan.

Should the movement prove to be a hoax, observers note it is a sophisticated one, given that members have actively contacted news.com.au to articulate their desire to advocate for the interests of white students. Peggy Mast, the Speaker Pro Tem and third-ranking Republican in the Kansas House representing Emporia, published the controversial message on her Facebook profile. "Great quote from Hitler in the video," Mast posted on a Thursday morning, alongside a message that lacked any accompanying video. "Please listen to it closely. His words are profound! Let's start using discernment." 

Christie Kriegshauser, who serves as chief of staff to House Speaker Ray Merrick, immediately questioned the logic behind the post. "Sorry, I'm confused," Kriegshauser replied publicly, asking about the missing video and how a Hitler quote could be considered great.

Insisting she "was not in any way agreeing with Hitler's words," Mast maintained that her intention was to draw a comparison between the dictator and Planned Parenthood.

The linked material featured footage of anti-abortion activist Gianna Jessen delivering congressional testimony that targeted Planned Parenthood. During that testimony, Jessen had referenced Hitler to argue that the women's health organization employed identical propaganda methods. The specific Hitler quote mentioned was: "The receptivity of the masses is very limited, their intelligence is small, but their power of forgetting is enormous. In consequence of these facts, all effective propaganda must be limited to a very few points and must harp on these in slogans until the last member of the public understands what you want him to understand by your slogan."
