WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Following President Donald Trump’s decision to withhold certification of the Iran nuclear accord, newly drafted Senate legislation proposes stringent conditions for the agreement. Should it become law, the bill would bring back sanctions if Tehran blocks inspectors from accessing any facilities or tests a ballistic missile capable of delivering a warhead. 

Authored by Republican Senators Tom Cotton and Bob Corker with backing from the Trump administration, the proposal faces pushback from critics who warn its passage could cause the United States to breach the international pact. Reuters reviewed the legislative draft on Tuesday, which began taking shape around the time Trump made his October 13 announcement rejecting formal certification of Iranian compliance and urging lawmakers to strengthen the accord. 

To secure the necessary votes for passage, Corker has been holding discussions with Senate Democrats, who maintain that the U.S. must collaborate with the deal's European co-signatories prior to implementing alterations. Alongside Russia and China, European nations including the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and the EU itself were signatories to the agreement. They have cautioned that Trump's approach threatens U.S. standing internationally and could fracture relations with Washington. 

As head of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Corker emphasized to Reuters last week that the administration needs to maintain close cooperation with European partners while formulating its updated Iran strategy. 

The proposed legislation takes the form of an amendment to the 2015 Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act. It expands the mandatory government evaluations regarding Iranian compliance to encompass additional criteria, ranging from trade activities to determining whether U.S.-licensed commercial airplanes are being utilized for non-civilian tasks. 

Furthermore, the measure would immediately reinstate the sanctions that were previously removed under the accord—a process known as a "snap back"—if Iran's timeline for potentially producing a nuclear weapon shrinks to under a year. 

Complicating the legislative path is an ongoing feud between Trump and Corker, which intensified when the president criticized the senator for the creation of the accord during the administration of former President Barack Obama. While global leaders have pressed Trump to preserve the pact, it faced unanimous opposition from congressional Republicans at the time, including Corker. In response, Corker criticized the president's handling of the office and accused him of damaging vital global partnerships. A spokesperson for Corker did not immediately provide a statement regarding whether this political fallout would impact the future of the Iran bill.

SAN FRANCISCO (Reuters) — Documents reviewed by Reuters reveal that roughly twenty major corporations, hailing from the tech sector and beyond, are getting ready to form a coalition pushing for laws that would grant young undocumented immigrants a route to permanent legal status. The newly formed Coalition for the American Dream plans to press Capitol Hill to enact bipartisan measures this year to secure the right for these individuals—widely known as “Dreamers”—to stay and work in the country. Among the participants named in the paperwork are prominent American enterprises such as Alphabet’s Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Facebook, Intel, Uber, IBM, and Marriott International, with Reuters breaking the story. While Amazon, Intel, Uber, and Univision Communications acknowledged their involvement, the remaining firms did not issue immediate responses, and organizers noted that the rollout plans remain subject to change.

Intel representative Will Moss expressed support in an official statement, noting the company is glad to partner with others to press lawmakers for protections for Dreamers. Similarly, Uber spokesperson Matthew Wing highlighted the company's backing for the initiative, pointing out that they stand with Dreamers and have previously hosted town hall meetings, offered legal aid, and set up an online resource hub specifically for drivers who are Dreamers. 

This legislative push follows President Donald Trump’s announcement in September winding down the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, program by March. Put in place in 2012 by the Obama administration, the initiative has granted work authorization to roughly 900,000 undocumented individuals. Following the Trump administration's decision, an earlier plea urging congressional action to safeguard Dreamers drew signatures from about 800 businesses, an effort organized by FWD.us, a pro-reform advocacy group co-established by Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg in 2013. A significant portion of the corporations backing that prior appeal are now listed as participants in this latest alliance.

An internal email reviewed by Reuters indicated that the coalition has explored placing advertisements in media outlets, though those strategies could still shift. Recruitment materials being circulated to bring other businesses on board describe Dreamers as integral members of the community who contribute to the economy and national defense, while a registration document for the initiative notes that DACA recipients are employed by 72 percent of the top 25 Fortune 500 corporations.

During his presidential campaign, Trump made strict border enforcement and the construction of a southern border wall central pillars of his platform, and he has ultimately placed the responsibility of determining DACA's future onto lawmakers. A legislative window could open as soon as December, when lawmakers are required to approve federal funding legislation to avert a government shutdown, leading Democrats to weigh making protections for Dreamers a mandatory condition for supplying the votes needed to keep federal operations running. Todd Schulte, the head of FWD.us, noted during a Thursday interview—where he chose not to speak about the new coalition directly—that no lawmaker wants to face headlines over the holidays about DACA recipients spending their final season in the United States, adding that this pressure campaign will only intensify as the year draws to a close.

The arrest follows an anti-corruption investigation that linked him to suitcases and boxes containing over 51 million reais, equivalent to $16.52 million, after investigators discovered his fingerprints on the hidden money. Until November, Vieira Lima had managed legislative relations for President Michel Temer.

Prosecutors claimed he attempted to dissuade businessman Lúcio Funaro—who provided services to politicians aligned with Temer—from entering into a plea agreement with authorities. In the official decision sanctioning the arrest, Judge Vallisney de Souza Oliveira stated that the measure was required to prevent the former minister from engaging in additional illegal acts.

Earlier in the week, law enforcement personnel spent hours tallying the massive sum discovered inside an apartment located in Salvador, marking the largest cash confiscation in the history of the country. When Vieira Lima stepped down from his ministerial position in November, he represented the fifth cabinet departure from the administration stemming from corruption accusations. President Temer subsequently faced corruption charges brought by the nation's chief prosecutor, though he successfully survived the vote in the lower house of Congress in August.

ZURICH (Reuters) - On Wednesday, the man expected to become Switzerland's new foreign minister advocated for a reset in the difficult negotiations regarding relations with the European Union, which stands as the neutral nation's primary economic partner. 

Ignazio Cassis, aged 56, was chosen by parliament, marking the first time in nearly two years—specifically 18 years—that a minister has hailed from the Italian-speaking Ticino canton. Once the four-party coalition cabinet distributes departments on Friday, Cassis is widely anticipated to take over as the country's leading diplomat. The physician, who speaks multiple languages and represents the business-friendly Liberal Democrats, is stepping into the role previously held by Didier Burkhalter, whose resignation was made public in June.

Assuming Cassis assumes control of the foreign portfolio—as cabinet assignments are determined by seniority—he will take charge of managing various unresolved economic and political matters concerning the EU. The bloc in Brussels is pushing for an overarching framework agreement to substitute the existing web of over 100 bilateral agreements that currently regulate the relationship. Nevertheless, major Swiss political factions have grown hesitant about this prospect, particularly with the approach of the United Kingdom's departure negotiations with Brussels.

During his acceptance speech, Cassis drew attention by referencing Marxist thinker Rosa Luxemburg on the importance of valuing differing viewpoints. Speaking to the press afterward, he argued that the conversation surrounding EU relations needs to move away from what he described as a poisoned lexicon. He emphasized the necessity of having the bravery to initiate a fresh chapter, pointing out that the precise contents of a framework treaty remain unclear as both sides attempt to restructure their connections. According to Cassis, language forms our environment, and when the discourse becomes tainted by words, those words must be altered.

Leaders such as European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker and German Chancellor Angela Merkel have maintained that agreeing to a new treaty is a prerequisite for any future trade agreements involving Switzerland. Previously, the Alpine nation narrowly averted a diplomatic collision with the EU following a 2014 public vote favoring immigration caps, as lawmakers ultimately implemented a framework prioritizing domestic job seekers already listed with local employment agencies. 

Any hesitation by the Swiss to advance a new agreement before the UK's talks with the EU gain full momentum risks plunging ties into a severe freeze, potentially halting advancements on pending commercial matters. Meanwhile, the nationalist Swiss People's Party, which holds the position of the nation's biggest political force, remains firmly against any agreement that would grant the European Court of Justice jurisdiction over arbitrating conflicts.

BRUSSELS (Reuters) - Nearly two decades ago, the European Union reacted with extreme hostility when an Austrian chancellor integrated the far-right into the nation's government, with certain EU figures even suggesting a boycott of Tyrolean ski slopes as a form of protest. This Monday, however, the strong possibility that Sebastian Kurz’s center-right might bring the Freedom Party back into a Vienna administration elicited little more than a whisper in Brussels. This muted response highlights both the evolution of the FPO away from its neo-Nazi origins and a broader rightward drift across Europe, particularly regarding immigration. A senior EU official noted that an Austrian government steered by an advocate of strict border controls and including the FPO would have triggered "an earthquake" across the continent just a couple of years ago. 

However, in the wake of the 2015-16 crisis that saw over a million refugees and migrants arriving by sea in Greece and Italy—frequently traveling onward to Germany through Austria—opponents of open borders have successfully steered European politics in their direction. Another Brussels insider remarked, "They’ve built setItems the theater that we are all playing in now." A pragmatic agreement with Turkey to stem the flow of Syrian refugees, more aggressive detention and deportation measures for unsuccessful asylum applicants, the reduction of rescue vessel operations, and partnerships with Libyan authorities have all driven a significant drop in new arrivals. In Germany, where ideological allies of the FPO weakened Chancellor Angela Merkel during the previous month's election, her famous 2015 refugee welcome has been replaced by backing for strengthened border security.

European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker extended his congratulations to the 31-year-old Kurz following Sunday's election win, touching upon anxieties regarding a eurosceptic administration in Vienna. The head of the Brussels executive branch expressed hope that Kurz would successfully build a "stable, pro-European government." Meanwhile, Juncker’s spokesperson declined to confirm whether the Commission was urging Kurz to exclude the FPO—unlike the approach taken by EU leaders when Chancellor Wolfgang Schuessel partnered with the party, then headed by Joerg Haider, back in 2000. 

Nearly 18 years ago, in February 2000, Juncker served as Luxembourg's prime minister and joined 13 other EU leaders in virtually ignoring Schuessel and his ministers for a half-year, subsequently amending EU treaties to establish mechanisms for penalizing wayward member states. Strong rhetoric abounded at the time. The Belgian foreign minister—father to current premier Charles Michel—even urged travelers to avoid winter vacations in Austria. 

By contrast, current Belgian Foreign Minister Didier Reynders joined numerous peers at an EU gathering in offering polite congratulations to their absent young Austrian counterpart, expressing anticipation of cooperating with his upcoming administration. Not a single official brought up the punitive suspension powers the EU adopted after failing to sway Schuessel. Instead, fellow ministers uniformly praised Kurz’s pro-EU stance. Johannes Hahn, a party colleague of Kurz who represents Austria on Juncker’s Commission, stated that whatever coalition Kurz assembled would maintain "a very pro-European agenda because all the major political parties are very much committed to the European Union."

This shift mirrors the transformation of the FPO under Heinz-Christian Strache, who has softened his anti-EU rhetoric and distanced the party from anti-Semitism while maintaining critiques of Islam. The sole strong condemnation outside of mild reactions came from the far-left leader within the European Parliament. Gabi Zimmer asserted that the election results ought to "strike fear into everyone" and charged Kurz with utilizing "bigotry and prejudices" to triumph over a faction led by a "neo-Nazi."

Nevertheless, Kurz confronts a vastly different Europe than the one that previously isolated Schuessel. The political landscape has tilted toward conservatives, a stark contrast to 2000 when left-leaning administrations governed countries like Germany, France, Britain, and Italy. Furthermore, the EU's expansion into the former communist east has integrated numerous leaders, notably in Poland and Hungary, who openly oppose immigration, particularly from Muslim populations. Kurz received a notably enthusiastic commendation from his Hungarian counterpart. Additionally, a growing number of governments—in France, the Netherlands, Nordic nations, and now Germany—grapple with the same challenge Schuessel faced regarding a popular far-right movement. 

This reality has fostered a reluctance to reprimand EU counterparts over tactics used to manage such political insurgencies, although leaders will expect Kurz to keep the FPO in check, mirroring past efforts to justify readmitting Schuessel into their diplomatic circle. That historical lesson—learned after rushing to rhetorical opposition without a viable exit strategy and failing to move Schuessel—explains the current hesitation to suspend Hungary or Poland over democratic shortcomings. As one EU official summarized, "Austria in 2000 showed us how not to go in without an exit strategy."

A federal judge sitting in Texas handed down an order on Saturday putting the brakes on an Obama administration initiative that aimed to broaden anti-bias protections under the Affordable Care Act to cover abortion services and transgender healthcare. The ruling comes in favor of a coalition consisting of Texas, seven additional states, and three faith-based healthcare organizations that contested the directive. According to the judge, the contested rule categorized sex discrimination as encompassing both "termination of pregnancy" and "discrimination on the basis of gender identity." 

Just 24 hours prior to the scheduled implementation of the regulation, U.S. District Judge Reed O'Connor granted the injunction, concluding that the measure runs afoul of the Administrative Procedure Act, which regulates federal rule-making procedures. Furthermore, the judge determined that the challengers stood a strong chance of succeeding on their argument that the policy breaches the Religious Freedom Restoration Act by infringing upon the rights of private medical providers. 

In his 46-page written opinion, O'Connor noted the plaintiffs' contentions that the mandate would compel them to offer medical coverage and perform procedures related to abortions and gender transitions, despite any medical judgment or religious objections to the contrary. O'Connor previously issued a comparable injunction back in August against a different federal policy that would have mandated public schools to permit transgender students access to the restrooms corresponding with their gender identity, a directive opposed by 13 states. 

Questions remained regarding whether the outgoing administration, facing only 20 days remaining in its term, would pursue an appeal against this newest judicial block. Katie Hill, speaking as a White House spokeswoman, criticized the outcome. She described the ruling as a disappointing hurdle, though expressing hope that it would prove short-lived, maintaining that every individual deserves access to affordable, high-end healthcare free from bias, regardless of sexual orientation, sex, or gender identity.

Enacted in 2010, the Affordable Care Act—frequently referred to as Obamacare—contains provisions prohibiting insurers from denying coverage or levying higher costs based on factors such as race, age, disability, sex, or national origin. The specific regulation at the center of Saturday's dispute was formulated by the Department of Health and Human Services to carry out those statutory anti-discrimination measures, explicitly integrating transgender care and abortion services into the definition of sex bias. 

The court document outlined that the regulation defined gender identity as a person's internal understanding of their gender—which could align with male, female, a blend of both, or neither—and which might differ from the sex they were assigned at birth. Under the leadership of Texas, various Republican-governed states have spearheaded numerous legal challenges against social initiatives championed by President Barack Obama, most prominently his 2014 executive order providing deportation relief and work authorization to millions of undocumented immigrants, a program that was ultimately blocked by the courts. Nevertheless, the Supreme Court upheld the broader Affordable Care Act—the signature legislative achievement of the administration—through decisions handed down in 2012 and 2015.

While the Cuban government has maintained its innocence and denied any role in the matter, the U.S. State Department has refrained from directly blaming Havana. However, as a consequence of the situation, two Cuban diplomats were ordered to depart Washington earlier in May.

text:
UNITED NATIONS (Reuters) - The United States faced deeper isolation on Monday after single-handedly blocking a United Nations Security Council resolution demanding the reversal of President Donald Trump's designation of Jerusalem as Israel's capital. While the other 14 members of the council backed the measure brought forward by Egypt—which avoided explicitly naming Trump or the U.S. while voicing "deep regret at recent decisions concerning the status of Jerusalem"—Washington exercised its veto.

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley reacted to the outcome by calling it an insult that would not be forgotten, noting it was the first time in over six years that the U.S. had used its veto power. Defending the move, Haley stated that protecting American sovereignty and the nation's position in the Middle East peace process was not embarrassing for the U.S., but rather should embarrass the rest of the Security Council.

The proposed text asserted that any actions or decisions aimed at altering the demographic makeup, status, or character of Jerusalem hold no legal standing, are considered null and void, and must be canceled in line with prior Security Council resolutions. This came on the heels of Trump’s sudden departure from decades of American foreign policy earlier in the month, which sparked widespread anger among Palestinians and across the Arab world, alongside apprehension from Western partners of Washington.

Prior to the vote, U.N. Middle East peace envoy Nickolay Mladenov briefed the Security Council, warning that tensions had escalated since the American announcement, marked by a rise in confrontations between Palestinians and Israeli security forces as well as rocket fire originating from Gaza. Alongside the capital recognition, Trump has announced intentions to relocate the American embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, prompting the U.N. draft resolution to urge all nations against setting up diplomatic missions in the city.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu shared a video message on his Facebook account expressing gratitude to both Trump and Haley for the veto. Israel views Jerusalem as its undivided and eternal capital and pushes for all embassies to be located there, whereas Palestinians claim the eastern portion of the city—seized by Israel in a 1967 conflict and subsequently annexed in an action lacking international recognition—as the capital for a future independent state.

In the wake of the veto, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry announced that Arab nations, which previously agreed earlier in the month to pursue the Security Council measure, would convene to assess developments and decide on subsequent actions. Meanwhile, Palestinian Foreign Minister Riyad al-Maliki stated that Palestinians intend to push for an uncommon emergency special session of the 193-member U.N. General Assembly regarding the Jerusalem announcement. 

Based on a resolution from 1950, such an emergency session allows the General Assembly to review an issue and provide members with recommendations for collective action if the Security Council is unable to reach a decision. This mechanism has only been utilized 10 times previously, with the most recent occurrence taking place in 2009 to address Israeli military actions in occupied Palestinian territories. Although any decisions resulting from such a session lack legal binding, they carry significant political influence.

While President Trump faced widespread criticism for prioritizing attacks on NFL players and news outlets over the plight of American citizens on the island, Pence was dispatched for damage control to comfort survivors.

Burgos confronted Pence directly, urging him to look beyond San Juan and witness the true extent of the devastation inland where entire towns remained inaccessible. 

Burgos further criticized the administration by referencing President Trump's controversial remarks suggesting officials should feel proud of the initial low casualty count. She pointed out that the official figures were unreliable because widespread communication blackouts made it impossible to know the actual number of fatalities. When another voice off-camera chimed in to update the death toll to thirty-four, Burgos reiterated that the current outside estimates were inadequate.

Caught off guard, Pence offered little response beyond a brief "Good to talk," though Burgos continued pressing him to travel to the center of the island where the destruction was worst. Pence offered a vague agreement before asking if she and her family would be alright to return home, a query that critics argued demonstrated a continued lack of understanding regarding the severity of the crisis and a failure to commit to meaningful action.

During a Tuesday broadcast, Morning Joe co-host Joe Scarborough made a striking on-air statement, conceding that the economic theory of trickle-down economics is a falsehood that has exclusively served to enrich the wealthy. While attempting to account for the massive conservative support behind Republican primary leader Donald Trump, Scarborough pointed out that for three decades, Republican politicians have misled their base by promising that tax cuts for the rich would eventually benefit everyone else. 

This reality is starkly illustrated by the expanding wealth gap over the past thirty years, which has left the richest one percent possessing a larger share of the nation's wealth than the lower fifty percent combined. As the wealthy accumulate more money and the impoverished grow poorer, the once-strong American middle class is steadily vanishing. Scarborough acknowledged the shortcomings of his former party, noting that for thirty years, Republicans have failed to offer an economic message that resonates with working-class Americans in the way Donald Trump's platform does. 

He pointed out that the GOP continually pushes for capital gains tax cuts that will never apply to the thousands of people cheering at Trump rallies, nor will the elimination of the death tax impact them. Furthermore, he noted that the praised free trade agreements never actually benefit the individuals attending these rallies. The former GOP congressman explicitly stated that trickle-down economics has failed, pointing out that wealth simply never reaches the working class. 

According to Scarborough, the people in Trump's audiences are the very ones who lost their jobs when employment was relocated to Mexico and other foreign countries, while the Republican donor class profited immensely as their capital shifted overseas to generate higher returns. He observed that voters this election cycle are even willing to support a candidate who defends Planned Parenthood if they believe that candidate offers an economic strategy with a better chance of helping them in the future. 

The decades-long GOP promise that cutting taxes on the elite would resolve the economic worries of everyday Americans has proven entirely false. Instead, trickle-down policies have only led to overseas job losses, leaving citizens empty-handed and far from the prosperity the party guaranteed. This dynamic is comparable to waiting for apples to fall from a tree, only to find the fruit rotten and worthless—assuming the tree doesn't hoard the apples entirely, much like the wealthy hoarding their money today. Ultimately, trickle-down economics stands as an unsuccessful policy that must be abandoned in favor of measures that genuinely support the population, requiring the rich to contribute their proper share so the middle class can reclaim the wealth taken by Republicans and their wealthy backers.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Wednesday marked the release of a recommendation from a congressional commission urging the establishment of a national museum celebrating women’s history, ideally situated on or close to the National Mall in Washington. Supporters pointed out that while the nation's capital boasts institutions dedicated to numerous subjects ranging from espionage and aviation to postal history and African American culture, it currently lacks a space entirely devoted to women. According to the findings released by the all-female, seven-member panel established by Congress two years prior, the country requires and has earned a physical national institution highlighting the historical contributions and experiences of American women. 

Bringing the museum to fruition would require roughly ten years dedicated to securing financial backing, building community support, and constructing the facility. The document estimates that a structure spanning between 75,000 square feet (6,900 square meters) and 90,000 square feet (8,400 square meters) would carry a price tag ranging from $150 million to $180 million, financed through private donations. Additionally, the commission suggested that lawmakers contribute land at no cost or make an existing structure available for the project. 

Under the proposal, the institution would integrate into the Smithsonian Institution—recognized as the largest museum network globally—and would be supervised by a congressional-appointed board. While private funds would cover construction, the operational and maintenance expenses would be handled by the federal government. 

Three specific locations on or adjacent to the National Mall—the two-mile (3.2 km) stretch often dubbed "America's front lawn" running from the Lincoln Memorial eastward to the U.S. Capitol—were put forward by the panel. The first option sits directly across from the recently opened National Museum of African American History and Culture. The second choice points to the historic, 19th-century Arts and Industries Building situated on the Mall, while the final option designates a location within the U.S. Capitol grounds. 

Although a legislative declaration in 2003 barred new construction on the Mall, an exception was previously granted for the African American museum. Given that the area is already densely packed with memorials and exhibition spaces, urban planners in Washington are actively exploring alternative ways to honor significant American figures and milestones outside of this central zone.

text: COPENHAGEN (Reuters) - Police in Denmark stated on Wednesday that the inventor accused of killing Swedish reporter Kim Wall on his submarine never actually claimed she perished from carbon monoxide poisoning, thereby revising a previous announcement. Speaking to Democratic donors in California on Thursday, President Barack Obama addressed the Supreme Court's recent choice to temporarily halt his administration's Clean Power Plan, describing the ruling as unusual while maintaining an optimistic outlook regarding the ultimate legal outcome. In his initial public comments concerning the judicial action, Obama asserted that the administration stands on solid legal ground. Meanwhile, back in Washington, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Gina McCarthy delivered a message to state environmental and energy officials assuring them that the decision would not decelerate their progress.

The high court's Tuesday ruling represented a setback for the initiative, which serves as the foundation of Obama's climate strategy and supports the greenhouse gas reduction commitments he made previously in Paris. During his remarks, Obama pointed out that the Supreme Court previously mandated that the EPA must regulate carbon emissions under the Clean Air Act if scientific evidence demonstrates they threaten public welfare. Addressing concerns from individuals who believed the court had completely invalidated the regulation, the president urged supporters not to lose hope, clarifying that such claims are incorrect.

McCarthy sought to lift the spirits of state regulators responsible for implementing the guidelines, expressing assurance that the initiative will overcome its current legal hurdles. Emphasizing a resilient attitude, she encouraged the audience to dust themselves off, renew their commitment, and demonstrate their dedication to the American public, punctuating her remarks with fist pumps. Characterizing the judicial stay as merely a minor interruption in a multi-year collaborative process between the EPA and state governments, McCarthy defended the initiative aimed at reducing carbon pollution from domestic power plants by nearly a third—specifically thirty-two percent below 2005 levels—by the year 2030. The Supreme Court's directive pauses the rollout of the regulation while pending lawsuits proceed through the courts. Reiterating the mandate, Obama noted that the judiciary previously established the EPA's obligation to curb carbon emissions hazardous to public health, a danger he emphasized can be clearly demonstrated. Securing progress against climate change remains a vital component of the president's agenda as he navigates his final year in office.

BERLIN (Reuters) — According to a document reviewed by Reuters on Wednesday, German intelligence services have issued warnings to domestic businesses regarding ongoing efforts by Iran to bypass trade restrictions on dual-use products utilized in rocket and missile programs. The BfV, Germany's domestic intelligence agency, emphasized in the advisory that transactions involving specific technologies continue to be prohibited, notwithstanding the lifting of sanctions resulting from the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement. 

The advisory explicitly noted that Tehran maintains an aggressive rocket and missile initiative that stays completely outside the scope of the sanctions relief. While the advisory mentioned that recent occurrences prompted the reminder, no specifics were provided. On Monday, German Foreign Minister Sigmar Gabriel informed the press that Berlin maintains its apprehension regarding Iranian actions in the Middle East and its missile advancements, while simultaneously affirming that Tehran continues to adhere to the nuclear accord. 

As U.S. President Donald Trump approaches a decision to decertify the nuclear agreement, European nations are working urgently to formulate a set of incentives that would preserve the accord. The historic agreement required Iran to suspend its nuclear activities for a decade and a half in return for the removal of economic penalties. President Trump is anticipated to announce this week that Tehran is failing to meet the terms of the treaty and will present a rigorous new policy approach toward the country.

The BfV filing indicated that German security services are maintaining active and deep investigations into whether Iranian entities are attempting to bypass current laws to obtain technology and expertise within Germany. A previous report released by the agency in June noted a sharp decrease in Iranian procurement efforts targeting the nuclear program, while procurement attempts aimed at missile development stayed steady. The report omitted specific figures regarding the volume of these acquisition efforts.

Separately, North Rhine-Westphalia—Germany's industrial center and most heavily populated region—published its 2016 intelligence findings on Tuesday. The regional report documented 32 procurement efforts linked probably or certainly to proliferation during 2016, marking a significant drop from the record-setting 141 attempts recorded the previous year. The vast majority of these procurement activities targeted Iran's missile efforts, alongside a small number connected to Pakistan, according to the document.

State authorities successfully blocked the vast majority of these transactions from being fulfilled, as regional intelligence personnel alerted businesses promptly or the targeted companies themselves identified suspicious purchase orders. The report detailed that Tehran frequently employs front corporations for these acquisitions, routinely routing shipments through nations such as Turkey, China, and the United Arab Emirates.

text:
Trump has spent a considerable amount of time complaining that Puerto Rico's devastated infrastructure makes the recovery effort slow and disorganized, stating that a response and recovery effort like this has probably never been seen before. He remarked that it is an island surrounded by water, specifically big water and ocean water, and called it a thing called the Atlantic Ocean, describing it as tough stuff. These excuses echo his past remark about how nobody knew healthcare could be so complicated. Under the current administration, statements claiming the situation is really difficult and that they are doing all they can often translate to a lack of genuine care unless there is a way to boost their own image. However, are logistical hurdles truly driven by Puerto Rico being an island, especially considering Florida and Texas were also ravaged by hurricanes? Current evidence points elsewhere, as essential supplies sit locked in shipping containers due to a shortage of truck drivers and obstructed roadways. One must question why additional personnel have not been deployed to assist the local government in clearing roads, restoring supply lines, and delivering aid where it is most urgent. An observer even noted that the personnel currently present appear more focused on modeling their uniforms, implying a severe lack of direction and purpose on the ground—a failure that falls squarely on the federal government rather than Puerto Rico.

In contrast, the handling of natural disasters on islands by the Obama administration tells a different story. Back in 2010, Haiti—located in the Caribbean near Puerto Rico, rather than the Atlantic—suffered a catastrophic earthquake. Even though the earthquake struck with zero warning, whereas there was ample advance notice for Hurricane Maria, President Obama mobilized the military as if preparing for war, as reported by the Washington Post. Just two days later, 8,000 troops were en route to the stricken nation. Within two weeks, the ground presence reached 22,000 troops, supported by 300 military helicopters dropping supplies and 33 Navy ships assisting the mission. By comparison, eight days after Hurricane Maria hit Puerto Rico, only 4,400 troops and 1,000 Coast Guard members were deployed for relief, with a mere 50 helicopters delivering supplies.

The morning after the Haiti earthquake, Obama instructed military leadership to execute a robust and immediate response in Port-au-Prince, providing the entire government with a clear sense of purpose. Rajiv Shah, who headed USAID during the disaster, pointed out that the government managed to act more swiftly in a foreign nation without any early warning than a better-equipped agency managed in a domestic territory. While the Posse Comitatus Act restricts military actions within U.S. states and territories—unlike foreign nations like Haiti, where military responses face different constraints—over 17,000 troops from 23 states were deployed to Florida following Hurricane Irma. Meanwhile, the administration continues to claim that Puerto Rico is not asking for much, even as locals exhaust their supplies of food and clean water, and the mayor of San Juan breaks down in tears over administration claims that the response has been successful. 

Complicating factors certainly exist, but the White House is displaying an unacceptable level of apathy and incompetence during crises where lives are being lost. Obama's actions demonstrated that being an island is far less of a barrier to effective relief than the current administration claims.

CHICAGO (Reuters) — Amid falling crop prices that are heavily pressuring sector profits, American agricultural organizations are actively seeking ongoing dialogues with the presumptive major-party presidential candidates to shape their respective farm policies. 

On Friday, delegates from roughly twelve trade groups—such as the National Farmers Union and the American Farm Bureau Federation—traveled to New York for a briefing at Hillary Clinton’s campaign headquarters. Participants reported on Wednesday that this marked the coalition's initial engagement with Clinton’s team, covering topics such as farm labor, agricultural trade, and mandatory labeling for foods with genetically modified ingredients. 

This gathering initiated a broader effort by the industry to extract clearer positions from both Clinton and her Republican opponent, Donald Trump, regarding agribusiness and agricultural issues. Organizers are currently attempting to schedule a comparable meeting with the Trump campaign. 

CropLife America CEO Jay Vroom, who participated in the discussions, noted that both sides concurred the session would only be considered a success if it served as the foundation for ongoing dialogue. 

According to these organizations, the candidates' stances on agriculture carry immense weight because U.S. net farm income is projected to hit its lowest point since 2002, primarily driven by falling grain prices. Such a drop would place incomes 56 percent below the recent peak of $123.3 billion recorded in 2013. 

Tom Bryant, who serves as the membership director for the National Farmers Union, expressed that given these economic conditions, the sector is understandably anxious about the direction of farm policy as preparations begin for the upcoming congressional farm bill. 

Tyrone Gayle, a spokesman for Clinton, stated that if she wins the presidency, she will work to boost profitability and agricultural production for family farms. Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Trump did not offer an immediate reply when asked for comment. The discussions also featured Matt Paul, a former spokesman for the U.S. Department of Agriculture who is now collaborating with the Clinton campaign. 

This meeting took place just one day after the unexpected British referendum to leave the European Union, a vote that found significant backing in various low-population areas. 

Chandler Goule, the incoming chief executive officer of the National Association of Wheat Growers, pointed out that agricultural leaders connected the EU vote to the domestic political landscape, arguing that rural America will mobilize for the upcoming race and ultimately decide the outcome of the presidential election. With Clinton and Trump established as the presumptive nominees, Goule emphasized that the time has arrived to secure more specific, detailed policy commitments.

THE ULTIMATE COMMUNITY ORGANIZER: IS YOUR NEIGHBORHOOD TOO WHITE? IS IT TOO RICH? Obama Plans To ‘Fix’ Them Using Government to Force Diversity

According to the administration, housing choices remain restricted in far too many areas due to discrimination, market operations, and investment decisions made by capital holders—a phrase pulled directly from an official HUD document. To address this, the president has directed the Department of Housing and Urban Development to introduce a directive named Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing, aimed at compelling local neighborhoods to become more diverse.

Naturally, this initiative means the government will need to tackle the broader issue of income inequality, given that underprivileged Americans and illegal aliens might lack the financial resources required to settle into wealthier suburbs and communities. Socialism has arrived, and unless a member of Congress steps up to challenge the president, the fruits of hard-working Americans' labor risk being seized by government coercion. This is the outcome of placing a community organizer in the White House, as he attempts to restructure neighborhoods straight from Washington.

Under this new policy, federal authorities will gather extensive data concerning the racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic characteristics of numerous local municipalities, searching for any disparities related to race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, or disability regarding access to community assets. Communities producing unfavorable outcomes will then be targeted, utilizing billions in federal grants to pressure or compel them into altering their housing and zoning regulations.

Housing discrimination has already been outlawed since 1968, making this initiative distinct from simply preventing such practices. It remains illegal to refuse a loan or block a home purchase based on race, creed, or color. However, socioeconomic status is and should remain a separate issue; purchasing an upscale suburban home requires the financial means to do so, though the administration apparently views this as unfair discrimination by capital holders. Granting federal bureaucrats control over local community management undermines freedom, as local autonomy remains vital to liberty. As Milton Friedman observed in *Capitalism and Freedom*: “If I don’t like what my local community does, be it in sewage disposal, zoning or schools, I can move to another local community. . . . If I don’t like what my state does, I can move to another. If I do not like what Washington imposes, I have few alternatives in this world of jealous nations.” Washington lacks any authority to dictate zoning and housing rules to countless local municipalities.

This policy could surface as a factor in the presidential campaign, particularly since HUD Secretary Julian Castro—tasked with rolling out the initiative—frequently appears on shortlists for Hillary Clinton's running mate. Furthermore, as Stanley Kurtz of the National Review notes, gathering the necessary data will require time, meaning decisions regarding its application will ultimately fall to the incoming president.

Communities nationwide will understandably react with outrage to this regulation. The federal government has no business dictating whether a neighborhood has too many Caucasian residents, too many Jewish residents, or an excess of married couples. Even so, Republicans must proceed cautiously, as Democrats hope the GOP will oppose the rule, allowing them to frame Republicans as defenders of wealthy, white suburbs who seek to exclude impoverished people of color.

Conservatives must emphasize a clear message: every American, regardless of race, color, or creed, should enjoy the freedom to reside wherever they choose. Achieving this requires fostering economic opportunities at the lower end of the spectrum, enabling individuals to secure better jobs and education so they can eventually afford superior neighborhoods.

Throughout the current administration, such opportunities have dwindled for those at the bottom of the economic ladder. Despite rhetoric surrounding inequality, the poor have grown poorer while the wealthy have enriched themselves. Data from the recovery period shows that households in the top 5 percent—those averaging incomes above $320,000—were the sole group to experience income growth between 2009 and 2013. Conversely, the bottom 20 percent suffered the most, enduring an average 7 percent drop in real income. As Arthur C. Brooks, president of the American Enterprise Institute, points out: “Our putatively progressive president has inadvertently executed a plutocratic tour de force.” Allowing Washington to oversee the housing and zoning decisions of local municipalities will not resolve this dynamic. Instead of compelling local governments to construct affordable housing within affluent areas, the real solution lies in reviving upward mobility so a greater number of people can naturally afford to live in those neighborhoods.

Via: Washington Post

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — President Donald Trump’s plan to achieve a balanced federal budget within ten years relies heavily on hitting a consistent 3 percent yearly economic expansion—a target from his campaign—alongside an undefined “feedback” mechanism projected to slash yearly government deficits by massive sums. Economists and the Federal Reserve view these forecasts as an ambitious gamble, pointing out challenges like an aging population and sluggish productivity growth. Furthermore, the strategy depends on maintaining low inflation, minimal interest rates, and full employment, essentially banking on a ten-year stretch entirely devoid of severe economic disruptions or even the typical mild recessions associated with standard market cycles.

Administration data made public on Monday evening indicate that gross domestic product growth is projected to climb to 3 percent per year by the conclusion of Trump's initial term and maintain that pace through at least 2027. This optimistic outlook comes despite an annualized first-quarter growth rate of just 0.7 percent, whereas the Federal Reserve projects overall growth for the year closer to 2.1 percent. The administration contends that this robust expansion will drive roughly 5 percent annual increases in tax revenue, notwithstanding the president's pledges that forthcoming tax reductions will stimulate investment and employment.

Additional assumptions built into the budget include inflation meeting the Federal Reserve's 2 percent target and remaining steady, contrasting with current Fed projections sitting slightly below 2 percent. The administration also estimates that the unemployment rate will tick up slightly from its 4.4 percent level, ultimately settling at a long-term average of 4.8 percent. Government figures indicate that without the projected acceleration in growth and an entirely stable macroeconomic backdrop, annual deficits would swell by as much as $500 billion, hovering near their current levels. This calculation factors in a so-called economic feedback effect that is anticipated to shrink the federal shortfall by up to $496 billion annually by 2027, though the initial release provided no specific explanation regarding how this feedback functions.

By comparison, the final budget proposal under President Barack Obama projected annual growth of 2.6 percent, a figure that professional economists and central bank officials already viewed as overly optimistic. Federal Reserve policymakers currently estimate the long-term trend for U.S. growth to be near 1.8 percent. Meanwhile, a quarterly survey conducted by the Philadelphia Fed shows that Wall Street analysts factoring in potential tax-cutting measures anticipate growth reaching 2.3 percent by 2020. 

In a client note published on Sunday, UniCredit chief economist Erik Nielsen remarked that the comprehensive fiscal scenario pushed by the administration was never grounded in realistic expectations. Historical data shows that U.S. economic growth has averaged 1.9 percent annually since the year 2000. Over a ten-year period, compounding the gap between that historical average and the administration's 3 percent target accounts for an additional $2 trillion each year in economic activity that would otherwise bypass spending, investment, and taxation.

The fiscal blueprint also banks on prolonged low interest rates, projecting that the yield on the 10-year Treasury note will rise to 3.8 percent and stay level—a crucial variable for estimating government borrowing expenses. Although the 10-year yield has averaged close to that threshold over the course of the century and currently sits well below it, periods of accelerated economic expansion typically trigger higher interest rates driven by tighter monetary policy and shifts in demand for U.S. debt securities.

The Last Time This Happened, It Signaled The Global Financial Crash Of 2008. Now, It’s Happening Again.

A sharp collapse in this specific trade metric previously foreshadowed the onset of the worldwide financial crash of 2007 and 2008. At present, the exact same phenomenon is recurring, though the gauge has now plunged to an all-time low. 

The Baltic Dry Index measures the expenses associated with transporting dry commodities globally. Traditionally, the index functions as an indicator for worldwide economic health because declining prices indicate shrinking trade volume, which subsequently signals an impending economic downturn. 

Late in 2013, the Baltic Dry Index reached a strong level of 2,330, and even as recently as last August, it maintained a solid figure of 1,222. However, it recently plummeted to a mere 354.

Image via Business Insider

This dramatic drop warrants serious concern because the previous instance preceded the 2008 global financial crisis—an event from which numerous economies still struggle to recover—and at that time, the index remained above 600. 

As Business Insider points out, multiple other instances exist where the index has signaled major corrections in the world economy. Operating in its modern form since 1985, the Baltic Dry Index experienced an initial substantial drop in mid-1986, roughly a year ahead of the 1987 Black Monday market crash. Later, in 1999, the index dropped to 12-year lows shortly before the dot-com bubble ruptured, and it fell to another significant low in 2001, coinciding with a United States economic recession that persisted until 2003.

Does this guarantee a crash matching the magnitude of 2008? Not necessarily, as it would be unwise to claim this indicator is entirely foolproof. Even so, combined with other economic warning signs, it demands careful consideration.

William White, the former chief economist at the Bank for International Settlements located in Switzerland, has cautioned that a massive wave of debt is approaching the global economy, stating that current conditions are worse than those of 2007. He noted that policy makers have effectively depleted their macroeconomic ammunition to combat economic downturns, leaving only the question of whether society will confront reality in an orderly manner or face a disorderly outcome.

White is far from alone in his assessment, as major financial institutions such as Goldman Sachs and the Royal Bank of Scotland have also delivered grim warnings regarding an approaching financial crisis. Furthermore, Baltic Exchange CEO Jeremy Penn remarked to The Telegraph that conditions have reached a point where individuals struggle to recall any period matching this level of difficulty, surpassing the 1990s, 1980s, and 1970s, to the extent that terms like living memory become applicable. Ultimately, disregarding these signals comes with significant risk.

Bernie Sanders Could End Up Winning Iowa

21st Century Wire reports that the Democratic primary in Iowa went down as one of the tightest contests ever, with mainstream outlets claiming Hillary Clinton triumphed by a razor-thin margin of just 0.3%. Yet, questions remain regarding whether Clinton truly emerged victorious. 

The National Review suggests the outcome is far from settled. Beltway journalist Quinn Hillyer points out that when looking at the ultimate tally of state convention delegates—excluding the seven secured by Martin O’Malley—Clinton ended up with 699 while Sanders held 695. However, based strictly on direct voter choices, Sanders actually led with 695 to Clinton's 693, alongside six ties. While Clinton currently heads to the state convention holding four more committed delegates than her rival, her lead came not from ballots cast by voters, but rather through a strange sequence of coin tosses. 

History shows precedent for such shifts; four years prior in 2012, major news networks initially declared Mitt Romney the winner of the GOP Iowa primary, only to issue a retraction later after realizing Rick Santorum had actually captured the caucus majority. Even then, neither Romney nor Santorum secured the bulk of Iowa's delegates heading into the national gathering. That distinction belonged to party outsider Ron Paul—a reality that mainstream American television networks largely swept under the rug. Paul pulled off this feat because his team grasped the true nature of the Iowa Caucuses as a massive statewide straw poll, executing a remarkably fierce delegate approach. The fallout within the Republican party was severe enough that the Republican National Convention subsequently created new rules to address the "Ron Paul Problem," ensuring outsider candidates could no longer establish a state-level presence without establishment backing.

Similarly, should Bernie Sanders manage to execute effective grassroots work focused on a robust county-level delegate plan, followed by capturing at least five of the seven uncommitted delegates left behind by the departed Martin O’Malley during the upcoming Iowa State Convention, Sanders might still turn out to be the true delegate victor in Iowa.

Collins marked just the second Republican in the chamber to sit down with Merrick Garland since the moderate appeals court judge was put forward last month to succeed the late Justice Antonin Scalia, who died on February 13. 

The sixty-minute discussion unfolded while GOP senators deal with heavy demands from conservative groups to support Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell's strategy of obstructing any selection put forth by Obama. Following the talk, Collins expressed to journalists that the encounter strengthened her belief that the procedure ought to move forward, adding that public sessions in front of the Judiciary Committee should be the upcoming phase. 

Roughly two hours afterward, McConnell countered by telling the press that it is certain neither proceedings nor votes will take place regarding Garland. Both McConnell and Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley maintain that the open seat left by Scalia ought to be filled by whoever succeeds Obama in the presidency, with the election scheduled for November 8 and the inauguration set for January 20. With an even 4-4 ideological split currently dividing the bench between conservatives and liberals, the next justice could shape the court's balance for a long time. 

Describing Garland as highly knowledgeable, reflective, remarkable, exceptionally intelligent, and deeply aware of the constitutional boundaries separating the executive, legislative, and judicial branches, Collins offered high praise. Meanwhile, the administration announced that Garland is scheduled to sit down next week for courtesy discussions with GOP Senators Kelly Ayotte, Rob Portman, Lisa Murkowski, and Jeff Flake. 

Garland previously held talks last week with Illinois Senator Mark Kirk, who criticized members of his own party as close-minded for declining to evaluate the pick. Additionally, a spokesperson for Grassley stated on Monday that the committee chairman invited Garland to a breakfast gathering so he can personally articulate the rationale behind withholding hearings. 

Democrats continued criticizing the GOP blockade, with Senate Democratic whip Dick Durbin pointing out that if McConnell maintains his position, Garland will become the initial high court nominee in American history to be refused a hearing. Conversely, Flake suggested that if a Democrat secures the presidency, the Senate ought to approve Garland swiftly during a legislative session following the election, as certain conservatives worry that Democratic front-runner Hillary Clinton might put forward someone far more liberal than Garland. 

However, Senator Lindsey Graham, a fellow Republican on the Judiciary Committee, brushed aside the notion of a post-election lame-duck approval for Garland, asserting that confirmation is out of the question and questioning the point of holding a hearing solely to berate the nominee.

Factbox: What do the new U.S. sanctions on Russia target?

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - This week, U.S. President Donald Trump gave his signature—albeit reluctantly—to a comprehensive sanctions package directed at Russia, North Korea, and Iran. Ahead of a weekend meeting in Manila between U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at a regional gathering, the following outlines the key components of the new measures against Moscow:

* Lawmakers instituted a legislative review mechanism empowering Congress to halt any attempt by President Trump to roll back or terminate the restrictions on Russia. The legislation was advanced by members of Congress to penalize Moscow for its purported meddling in the 2016 American presidential election, the seizure and annexation of Crimea from Ukraine, and its participation in the civil conflict in Syria.

* Under the new rules, the sitting president is required to deliver a detailed report to the relevant congressional committee outlining the justification for any proposed relaxation of penalties, alongside an assessment of how such a move would impact American national security. Legislators are granted a minimum of thirty days to conduct hearings and subsequently cast votes regarding the adjustment. Should Congress pass a joint resolution of disapproval, the executive branch is legally blocked from altering the penalties.

* Fresh economic penalties are directed at organizations engaging in commerce with the military or intelligence sectors of Russia, firms participating in offshore oil ventures connected to Russia, and entities taking part in the building of Russian gas or oil pipelines located within the country. This broad reach across multiple Russian industrial sectors threatens to inflict additional damage on an economy that was previously battered by penalties enacted in 2014 following the annexation of Crimea.

* Additional penalties are applied to any group or individual participating in cyber attacks on behalf of Moscow, as well as organizations owned by or operating for such entities. While the president retains the authority to grant waivers for these specific measures if deemed vital to national security, such actions remain subject to congressional oversight.

* Six distinct executive orders previously issued by President Barack Obama have now been formally codified into law, ensuring that Trump cannot unilaterally undo them through executive action. Enacted between 2014 and 2016, these earlier actions focused on Russian defense, financial services, energy, and additional sectors as a response to the Ukraine incursion, the seizure of Crimea, and election meddling and cyber operations directed at the United States.

* Furthermore, the legislation mandates a coordinated government report detailing prominent Russian oligarchs and senior political figures, which must include estimates of their fortunes, revenue sources, potential links to corruption, and their ties to Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

Simon responded that Jackson Lee's statement accused her of racism, pointing out that she had no knowledge of who was in her seat when complaining at the gate about it being given away, as terminal views into seated areas are impossible. Approximately five minutes after capturing the photo onboard, Simon reported that another flight attendant sat beside her to ask if she intended to be a problem, prompting Simon to reply that she merely wished to return home.

When Simon requested the identical free meal and beverage privileges associated with her first-class ticket alongside the $500 voucher, she asserted that the gate agent mocked her by stating, "And I want a Mercedes Benz, but I'm not going to get it." The gate agent initially offered $300—amounts Simon noted people typically receive in greater sums for voluntarily surrendering seats on overbooked flights—and eventually presented an ultimatum to accept the $500 or have the plane depart without her.

A law professor raised the question of whether the House Ethics Committee ought to investigate whether the Texas Democrat pressured the airline to secure her first-class seat, suggesting the committee examine what pressure Jackson Lee may have applied and how United accommodated her, while placing United under oath because claims that Simon canceled her own reservation are unbelievable.

Although multiple major news outlets relying on an Associated Press source reported that United Airlines issued an apology for their mistake, Simon publicly challenged these reports and demanded corrections, stating that United had not apologized to her. She clarified that on December 23, a low-level call center employee expressed a verbal apology over the phone, while the voucher served as compensation for her canceled flight and the reassignment of her seat to Jackson Lee. Simon insisted that media outlets correct their coverage to show that corporate United never apologized, and that the $500 voucher originated from an exasperated gate agent rather than serving as an apology.

During a Sunday television appearance, Senator Bernie Sanders criticized Donald Trump, accusing him of betraying working-class voters who backed his presidential campaign. 

Sanders' remarks followed a Friday meeting where Trump spoke with Wall Street bankers and stated his intention to dismantle the Dodd-Frank regulations, which were designed to prevent financial institutions from mistreating consumers. During that meeting, Trump explained that the rules make it difficult for his acquaintances and friends to borrow money for their businesses because banks are restricted by the current regulations. 

Throughout his campaign, Trump frequently criticized Hillary Clinton for her connections to major financial institutions. However, he has since filled his administration with individuals formerly employed by Goldman Sachs. 

Appearing on CNN's program hosted by Jake Tapper on Sunday, Sanders expressed strong criticism of the president's actions. Calling Trump a fraud, Sanders pointed out the contrast between the president's current association with Wall Street figures and his campaign rhetoric. He reminded viewers that Trump had previously campaigned on taking on Wall Street and accusing financial players of wrongdoing, only to later appoint billionaires and a chief financial adviser from Goldman Sachs while moving to dismantle consumer protection legislation.

Sanders also highlighted Trump's prior campaign pledges to bring back Depression-era laws like Glass-Steagall, which had placed restrictions on the financial sector to avert banking practices similar to those that triggered the 2008 Great Recession. 

In addition, Sanders targeted Trump over his cabinet appointments, arguing they contradict his previous promises to safeguard Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid. According to Sanders, despite campaigning on protecting these safety-net programs from cuts, the president has chosen nominees intent on dismantling them. Concluding his remarks, Sanders suggested that Trump staged an effective performance to mislead the electorate and predicted that the administration would ultimately abandon the middle and working classes.

The requirement stems from the National Defense Authorization Act, a defense policy legislation that President Barack Obama enacted in November, which set a Feb. 15 deadline for the administration to present its counter-militant roadmap to lawmakers. Earlier on Thursday, however, Republican congressional leaders noted they had received no signals that the document was about to arrive, even with the deadline fast approaching.

In an emailed statement provided on the condition of anonymity, the defense official mentioned that the agency recognizes the report's existence and is collaborating closely with various interagency departments to fulfill this legal obligation under the NDAA, anticipating the delivery of the final document to Capitol Hill shortly.

Currently, the U.S. spearheads an ongoing military offensive targeting the extremist faction, which has taken control of extensive regions across Iraq and Syria. Congressional Republicans have repeatedly found fault with Obama's handling of Islamic State, arguing that his initial underestimation of the danger allowed the militant network to expand its influence and power.

MANILA (Reuters) - Disaster authorities and the coastguard reported that a Philippine ferry carrying 251 people overturned in severe weather on Thursday close to Manila, leaving four dead and seven unaccounted for. Maritime incidents frequently occur in the Philippines due to the heavy reliance on inter-island boat travel. Although these vessels frequently exceed passenger limits, the coastguard confirmed that the ferry was not overcrowded and possessed a maximum capacity of 286 passengers. Several hours after the vessel capsized and sank roughly eight miles away from Real town located in Quezon province, rescue boats dispatched by the coastguard alongside local fishermen managed to pull 240 individuals from the water. 

Coastguard spokesman Captain Armand Balilo stated that search and rescue efforts will persist until every passenger and crew member is located. The majority of the survivors were transported to Dinahican port, while the fatalities consisted of two men and two women who drowned. Having departed from a port in Real around daybreak, survivors recounted to reporters that weather conditions deteriorated three hours into the journey, bringing powerful winds and massive waves. The vessel quickly started filling with water before overturning and sinking within minutes. 

Emergency management officials noted that the ongoing search operations faced significant obstacles due to torrential rain and towering waves whipped up by a tropical storm impacting the southern region of the country. The tropical storm was anticipated to hit the southern island of Mindanao either late Thursday night or early Friday morning. In advance of the storm, which featured central winds reaching 65 kph (40 mph), the weather bureau issued warnings regarding widespread flooding and landslides across the archipelago.

text:
WASHINGTON — Rex Tillerson, the nominee for secretary of state, took stances during his Wednesday confirmation proceedings that conflicted with several core foreign policy positions held by President-elect Donald Trump, touching on topics such as climate change, trade agreements, nuclear proliferation, and ties with Mexico. Appearing before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee for a marathon nine-hour session, the former Exxon Mobil chief executive stated that current U.S. sanctions against Russia ought to be maintained for the time being, and agreed that NATO members had valid reasons to feel threatened by Moscow's escalating aggression. 

Russia remained a central focus throughout the proceedings, driven by bipartisan anxiety over the 2014 annexation of Crimea, involvement in the Syrian civil war, and meddling in the American presidential election. Lawmakers also pressed the nominee on the Islamic State threat, human rights issues, Beijing's actions in the South China Sea, and whether he could successfully separate himself from his extensive background at the oil giant to lead the State Department. 

Addressing his divergent views from the incoming president, Tillerson maintained that these differences would not necessarily create friction with the White House. He characterized himself as transparent and open, explaining that Cabinet members would have opportunities to debate matters before a final presidential determination is made. 

In clear contrast to Trump's past statements, Tillerson asserted that allowing additional U.S. allies to acquire nuclear weapons would be unacceptable. When Democratic Senator Edward Markey inquired about Trump’s previous interview remarks suggesting he would not oppose nations like Japan pursuing nuclear arms, Tillerson answered directly that he disagreed. Furthermore, he stated he did not support the creation of a Muslim registry, noting he opposed targeting specific groups, and clarified that he did not oppose the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade agreement—which Trump has heavily criticized—though he conceded the negotiated pact might not fully serve American interests. 

At the same time, Tillerson aligned with Trump by leaving the door open for significant revisions to Obama-era initiatives, including trade policies concerning Cuba and the Iran nuclear agreement, which he argued should be subjected to a comprehensive review. 

Amid occasional interruptions by demonstrators, the 64-year-old nominee is widely anticipated to secure confirmation within the Republican-led Senate. However, senators repeatedly voiced unease regarding his past connections to Russia through Exxon Mobil, particularly given Trump’s stated objective to foster closer ties with Moscow. Tillerson declined to label Russian leader Vladimir Putin a war criminal and kept options open regarding potential adjustments to sanctions, mentioning he had not yet reviewed classified intelligence on election interference. “I would leave things in the status quo so we are able to convey this can go either way,” Tillerson remarked, advocating for candid discussions with Moscow to clarify its motivations. 

He attributed Russian hostility toward Ukraine dating back to 2014 to a lack of American leadership, arguing that stronger deterrent measures should have been deployed. “I’m advocating for responses that will deter and prevent further expansion of a bad actor’s behavior,” he stated. While acknowledging it was a fair assumption that Putin knew about efforts to disrupt the U.S. election, Tillerson admitted he had not conferred with Trump on Russia policy, a fact Democratic Senator Robert Menendez termed remarkable. 

During a sharp exchange, Republican Senator Marco Rubio challenged Tillerson on whether Putin bore responsibility for war crimes stemming from military campaigns supporting the Syrian government in Aleppo. Tillerson responded that the label involved extremely serious charges requiring substantially more information before drawing a conclusion. Rubio, a former rival for the Republican presidential nomination, pushed back, asserting that ample evidence was already publicly available regarding military actions in Syria, and expressed disappointment at the nominee's reluctance to acknowledge what he deemed globally accepted facts. 

Tillerson similarly avoided taking firm stances on human rights abuses in nations like the Philippines and Saudi Arabia, stating he preferred to examine the facts first. Following the hearing, Rubio told reporters he remained undecided on whether to support the nomination. As one of 11 Republicans on the 21-seat panel, Rubio's vote is vital for securing the committee's approval.

Regarding the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement—in which Tehran curbed its nuclear program in exchange for the lifting of economic sanctions—Tillerson recommended a complete review rather than an immediate outright rejection, despite Trump's conflicting statements and threats to dismantle the pact. On Asian affairs, Tillerson maintained that China should be barred from utilizing artificial islands constructed in contested areas of the South China Sea. Regarding North Korea, which recently claimed proximity to testing an intercontinental ballistic missile, he outlined an approach centered on sanctions and strict enforcement as part of a long-term strategy. 

When questioned about potential conflicts of interest stemming from his tenure at the world’s largest publicly traded oil company, Tillerson pledged to prioritize American interests. He also navigated queries concerning human-induced climate change by stating that risks and serious consequences do exist and warrant action, though he noted that predictive capabilities regarding greenhouse gas impacts remain very limited. This contrasted with Trump's past characterization of global warming as a Chinese hoax and threats to withdraw from the Paris climate accord. 

Describing Mexico as a long-standing neighbor and friend, Tillerson offered a view distinct from Trump's campaign rhetoric, which included plans for a border wall and controversial characterizations of Mexican migrants. 

Throughout the proceedings, Tillerson maintained a calm and measured demeanor, rarely relying on notes. Addressing past actions, he recalled opposing the 2014 sanctions against Russia over Crimea because he believed they would prove ineffective. While he maintained he never personally lobbied against the measures and was unaware of Exxon Mobil doing so directly, he later conceded that he had spoken with U.S. Treasury Secretary Jack Lew regarding discrepancies between American and European sanctions policies. Democratic Senator Chris Murphy confronted Tillerson over the matter, arguing that contacting a U.S. senator to voice concerns about the measures effectively constituted lobbying, which regulatory filings show the company did engage in regarding energy-related matters following the annexation of Crimea.

Law enforcement officers in Kiev placed Mikheil Saakashvili, the ex-president of Georgia, back into custody on Friday. The move quickly sparked fresh demonstrations in the heart of the Ukrainian capital by followers who had previously helped him escape from police custody earlier in the week. This event marks the latest chapter in an ongoing political conflict between the Ukrainian government and Saakashvili, who shifted from an ally of President Petro Poroshenko to a vocal opponent demanding his ouster and alleging official corruption. 

Yuriy Lutsenko, the General Prosecutor, announced via a Facebook update that the opposition figure was being held at a temporary facility, noting he faces suspicions of aiding a criminal organization. Lutsenko emphasized that law enforcement had taken care to prevent bloodshed and extreme violence during the operation. 

The renewed detention comes on the heels of bizarre events earlier in the week, which featured Saakashvili climbing onto a rooftop to evade authorities and later being liberated from a police van by demonstrators following violent confrontations with large numbers of riot police on Tuesday. 

Davit Sakvarelidze, an ally and fellow Georgian who previously lost his job as a high-ranking Ukrainian prosecutor in March, urged capital residents to mobilize and protest the arrest. Speaking to NewsOne near the central detention facility, Sakvarelidze accused Poroshenko of surpassing all previous limits and sealing his legacy as a dictator targeting political rivals. 

By 2200 GMT, several hundred demonstrators had congregated close to the detention center, located near the parliament building. Surrounded by a heavy presence of riot police, the crowd chanted slogans such as "Shame!" and "Kiev, get up!" 

Saakashvili initially arrived in Ukraine to serve as a regional governor in 2015 at the personal request of Poroshenko, though the relationship eventually deteriorated. The politician has consistently rejected all accusations against him. 

This ongoing standoff risks bringing international embarrassment to Ukraine's pro-Western leadership, particularly as they already face mounting pressure from international backers and domestic reformers regarding perceived stagnation on reforms and pressure on anti-corruption agencies. Addressing the situation on Friday, President Poroshenko insisted that the legal proceedings against Saakashvili are entirely valid and urged him to cooperate fully with investigators, warning that running away would destroy his credibility. 

Following his initial escape from custody, Saakashvili had urged supporters to attend an anti-Poroshenko rally in Kiev scheduled for Sunday. However, he maintained a low profile over the preceding days, reportedly falling ill after staying in a makeshift protest encampment outside the parliament building. 

Prior to Friday's action, police attempted a raid on the camp on Wednesday to retake the former Georgian leader, which similarly resulted in violent skirmishes with his supporters. Despite having a dedicated group of followers, Saakashvili commands modest backing throughout the wider country. Findings from an October poll conducted by the Razumkov Centre, a think-tank based in Kiev, indicated that only 1.7 percent of the electorate would back his Movement of New Forces party at the ballot box. While his supporters view him as a courageous fighter against graft, detractors argue that his public speeches lack substance.
