Sarah Palin And Other Conservatives Fly Into A Panic After Seeing UN Vehicles On The Road (SCREENSHOTS)

Right-wing circles frequently view everyday occurrences through the lens of conspiracy, with a prevailing delusion focused on the notion that the United Nations intends to seize control of the United States and strip citizens of their firearms. Consequently, when a motorist belonging to this political persuasion spotted a shipment of UN vehicles being hauled from a domestic manufacturer toward an overseas shipping point, they panicked and rushed to social media with warnings of an impending UN takeover. 

"Can't begin to tell you how many of these I passed today on 81 near Lexington VA," posted conservative Jeff Stern, accompanied by pictures of the trucks riding on trailers. 

This post sparked widespread hysteria among right-wing commentators, echoing the kind of frantic bunker-building and weapon-stockpiling seen among Texas conservatives during the Jade Helm military training exercise. Stern observed the transport on Interstate 81 close to Lexington, Virginia—a detail that some individuals mistakenly associated with Lexington, Kentucky, thereby fueling rumors of sightings across both states. Matters escalated further when the Daily Mail sensationalized the situation by questioning whether the UN had arrived in anticipation of an economic collapse, inadvertently driving even more anxiety among anxious conservatives.

The panic extended to standard vehicle specifications, such as bullet-resistant windows and poison gas seals. Given the global deployment zones of UN personnel, these protective measures are standard and entirely practical; comparable American military equipment features identical defenses for identical reasons. 

Snopes reached out to the creator of these specific units and obtained a logical rationale regarding the transit. In contrast to the Daily Mail's approach, inquiries directed to Alpine Armoring—the company identified in the report—clarified the situation. A representative from Alpine explained that these specific units were bought by the United Nations for deployment outside American borders. Because various defense contractors maintain operations in the Washington, D.C. area, which encompasses Virginia, for straightforward logistical purposes, the spokesperson verified that the trucks were bound for international service.

Following production, these UN units must be moved to domestic ports for export. Driving them directly to departure points would accumulate thousands of miles prior to loading onto cargo vessels or aircraft, making flatbed transport a logical choice. It follows that these same vehicles could plausibly appear in other Southern states along transit routes toward shipping terminals in the South.

Naturally, reason failed to prevail among conservatives, who shared Stern's update upwards of 120,000 times alongside reactionary commentary. Sarah Palin herself amplified the widespread hysteria by endorsing the notion that the UN had arrived to confiscate domestic firearms. The sheer scale of the absurdity remains striking.

text:
WASHINGTON AND GREEN BAY, WIS. — Amid declining poll numbers against his Democratic rival, Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump argued during a campaign stop on Monday that the upcoming November 8 contest is “rigged,” pointing to studies he contends demonstrate widespread voter irregularities. Despite the businessman's claims, Republican legal experts have labeled his assertions completely unfounded. 

Speaking to supporters at a Wisconsin rally in Green Bay, the GOP nominee warned that efforts to manipulate the outcome might occur directly at polling locations, asserting that numerous municipalities suffer from widespread corruption and frequent voter fraud. To back up his claims, Trump referenced a 2012 analysis by the Pew Charitable Trusts that advocated for voter registration updates due to millions of inaccurate entries. He also pointed to a 2014 Washington Post piece co-authored by two political scientists, which suggested non-citizen voting could have swung a small number of close 2008 races, though the researchers admitted their sample size was quite limited.

Conversely, multiple investigations have demonstrated that electoral fraud in the United States remains exceedingly uncommon. Chris Ashby, a Republican campaign attorney, characterized Trump's warnings as dangerous and capable of inciting civil disturbance. During an interview, Ashby explained that declaring an election fixed essentially tells supporters that their ballots hold no value, noting that such rhetoric could provoke unrest at voting sites. These warnings have prompted some party members to urge the candidate to drop the rhetoric, particularly as mail-in and early voting are already underway across numerous jurisdictions.

Mark Braden, a former chief counsel for the Republican National Committee and partner at Baker and Hostetler, argued that nationwide election manipulation is practically impossible given the complex network of safeguards currently in place. In an interview, Braden emphasized that the American framework relies heavily on bipartisan oversight and local volunteers, a system he credits with functioning exceptionally well over the years due to grassroots involvement.

Additionally, Trump seized upon FBI documents released on Monday, describing them as proof of severe corruption. The records included statements from an FBI official alleging that a high-ranking State Department representative attempted to pressure the bureau in 2015 to remove classified markings from an email originating on Hillary Clinton’s private server. Clinton’s reliance on that private setup throughout her tenure as secretary of state between 2009 and 2013 has consistently drawn accusations of poor national security judgment. Denouncing the situation as worse than the Watergate scandal, Trump also unveiled an ethics platform promising a five-year lobbying ban for departing administration officials if he wins the presidency.

Meanwhile, Clinton campaign manager Robby Mook dismissed Trump's attacks on the electoral process as a sign of desperation from a candidate who recognizes he is behind. Citing current RealClearPolitics polling averages, Clinton holds a 7.1 percentage point advantage nationally, standing at 46 percent compared to Trump's 38.9 percent.

Efforts to push back against the nominee's fraud allegations also came from within his own party. AshLee Strong, a spokeswoman for House Speaker Paul Ryan—the nation's highest-ranking elected Republican—stated that Ryan maintains absolute trust in the states' ability to execute a secure election. In Ohio, a key battleground, the state's Republican chief election officer likewise rejected claims of widespread problems. Ohio Secretary of State Jon Husted assured CNN that he personally oversees the state's voting procedures and guarantees they will not be compromised.

Research consistently underscores the extreme rarity of such issues. A New York University School of Law Brennan Center report titled “The Truth About Voter Fraud” estimated incident rates between 0.00004% and 0.0009%. Similarly, an August investigation by the Washington Post identified only 31 credible instances of voter impersonation out of more than a billion ballots cast between 2000 and 2014, with Arizona State University publishing comparable findings in 2012 and 2016. While several conservative-led states have enacted stricter identification mandates aimed at stopping fraud, courts have struck down multiple provisions over rulings that they intentionally suppressed minority turnout.

Trump’s presidential bid has faced intense turbulence following the publication ten days prior of a 2005 video featuring the candidate making crude remarks about non-consensual kissing and touching of women. Although multiple women have subsequently stepped forward with complaints regarding similar conduct, Trump has denied all accusations, accusing the press of attempting to manipulate voter perceptions with sensationalized headlines about fabricated incidents.

The controversy returned to the forefront on Monday as Melania Trump addressed the "Access Hollywood" tape publicly for the first time. The former model, who has largely remained away from the campaign trail, told CNN she was taken aback by her husband's language, suggesting he was nudged into making crude remarks that she described as typical “boy talk.” She further claimed that the accusations of unwanted physical contact were coordinated by political opponents and criticized the media for failing to vet the accusers. In a separate discussion with the Fox News Channel, she confirmed she had accepted his apology for the recorded comments, stating that the remarks were offensive and inappropriate, but emphasized that they have forgiven him and are moving forward.

BEIJING (Reuters) - Military exercises by China's air force recently involved sending bombers and additional warplanes across a pair of vital passages close to Taiwan, as well as traversing the disputed waters of the South China Sea, according to state media reports released on Thursday. 

Xinhua, the official news agency, reported that various jets alongside multiple H-6K bombers executed a "combat patrol," passing through the Miyako Strait located in Japan's southern region and the Bashi Channel situated between the Philippines and Taiwan, in addition to flying over the South China Sea. 

Shen Jinke, an Air Force spokesman cited by Xinhua, did not specify the exact start date of the exercises, though he confirmed that all participating aircraft concluded their patrols on Thursday. These maneuvers were designed to sharpen actual combat capabilities at sea and develop the military's strategic battle tactics, according to Shen. 

Beijing has grown more assertive regarding territorial claims in both the East and South China Seas. Furthermore, concerns persist regarding Taiwan, which is governed by an administration Beijing suspects of pursuing formal independence. 

The Chinese leadership has consistently refused to renounce the potential use of military force to place the democratic island under its governance, cautioning that steps toward formal independence could trigger an armed intervention. 

Presently, China is undertaking a sweeping military modernization effort encompassing the development of stealth fighters and the construction of aircraft carriers, aiming to project military might at significant distances from its coastline. Although Taiwan maintains a well-equipped military relying primarily on American arms, Taipei continues to urge Washington to provide additional advanced technology to strengthen its deterrence against Beijing.

An Iranian nuclear scientist, who provided crucial details to the enemy, was put to death on Sunday by Iran. Shahram Amiri went missing back in 2009 while visiting Mecca in Saudi Arabia. Following a year-long disappearance, he reappeared in the United States in June 2010. Amiri maintained that the CIA abducted him and subjected him to severe psychological pressure to extract sensitive data, asserting that he resisted U.S. attempts to break him. Conversely, the U.S. Government maintained at the time that Amiri defected of his own accord and received millions of dollars in exchange for valuable insights concerning the nation's nuclear program.

The following month, he showed up at the Pakistani embassy's Iranian interests section in Washington DC, expressing a desire to go back to Iran. He secured safe passage home a few days later, initially receiving a hero's welcome upon arrival. However, authorities arrested and prosecuted him for treason in May 2011. Although his relatives thought he received a ten-year prison sentence—which would have allowed for his release in 2022—he actually faced capital punishment. Ultimately, the execution took place on August 7, 2016. 

Gholamhosein Mohseni-Ejei, a spokesman for the Islamic Republic of Iran, stated during his weekly press conference that Amiri possessed confidential military secrets and maintained ties to the Great Satan, which they consider public enemy number one. Mohseni-Ejei noted that a primary court handed down the death sentence, and the Supreme Court upheld it following Amiri's appeal. He added that the CIA believed their activities remained hidden from the Iranian Intelligence Ministry when they brought Amiri to Saudi Arabia.

To most observers, the sequence of events appears quite standard: he published a video stating he shared national secrets with the CIA, the United States verified his actions, and he somehow believed it was safe to head back home. This represents the established historical record, unless the perspective belongs to Tom Cotton.

As it turns out, Amiri's name appeared within recently made-public Clinton emails. Cotton asserted that these messages, which only recently entered the public sphere, triggered Amiri's 2011 arrest and subsequent death sentence. Nine days prior to Amiri's return to Iran, Richard Morningstar, who formerly served as the State Department special envoy for Eurasian energy, wrote that they faced a diplomatic and psychological challenge rather than a legal one, adding that their friend needed a way out and that their person could not accomplish anything anyway, so if he had to leave, it should happen.

During an appearance on "Face the Nation," Cotton strongly criticized Clinton, stating that while he would not comment on potential work done for the United States government, conversations among her top advisors regarding this individual existed within the emails stored on Hillary Clinton's private server. During a telephone conversation on Monday, Russian President Vladimir Putin brought up the concept of sending U.N. personnel to the region with Merkel, proposing that these forces could safeguard monitors from the international OSCE observer mission.

As pressure mounts within Germany to ease European Union sanctions imposed on Russia because of the crisis in Ukraine, Moscow has shown interest in initiatives aimed at easing trade restrictions that have negatively impacted living standards for Russians. 

Speaking to the FUNKE media group on Friday, Merkel remarked that Putin's suggestion to use U.N. forces for the protection of OSCE monitors was noteworthy, adding that she had spoken with him a few days prior about ensuring these troops receive authorization to travel wherever the OSCE maintains a presence across the entirety of the Donetsk and Luhansk areas.

Since the fighting began in 2014, the clashes between Ukrainian troops and Moscow-supported separatists have resulted in a death toll exceeding 10,000. While Western nations maintain that Moscow engineered the hostilities and supplied weapons and personnel, Russia rejects these claims. 

The monitoring personnel are tasked with overseeing compliance with a 2015 peace agreement negotiated in Minsk, though the pact has largely failed to resolve the hostilities despite persistent appeals from Berlin and Paris. 

Certain German political figures have argued that punitive measures against Moscow could be removed if the Minsk accord is put into practice. Christian Lindner, who heads the Free Democrats and could potentially join Merkel's governing coalition following the September 24 elections, went so far as to propose that Berlin acknowledge Russia's annexation of the Crimean peninsula.

Calling Putin's ideas "tender shoots" of advancement, Merkel noted they do not currently provide a justification for relaxing sanctions. She also dismissed Lindner's stance, stating that the annexation violates international law and cannot be condoned.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Testifying before Congress on Thursday, Donald Trump’s nominee for secretary of defense placed Moscow at the very top of his concerns regarding American security. Retired Marine General James Mattis stated that the nation must be prepared to push back against Russia when necessary, though he simultaneously supported the president-elect's desire for improved diplomatic ties. 

Mattis's statements represented yet another instance where a Cabinet choice appointed by Trump distanced himself from the campaign trail rhetoric of the incoming president, who had previously lauded Russian President Vladimir Putin and promised better relations. A day earlier, Rex Tillerson, nominated to head the State Department, also voiced perspectives that diverged from Trump on several major foreign policy matters, including trade pacts, climate change, nuclear proliferation, and ties with Mexico. 

According to Mattis, the American-led global order faces its most severe threats since the Second World War from Russia, China, and militant Islamist groups. He additionally urged lawmakers to eliminate budget caps that he argued were harming military preparedness. 

While expressing openness to diplomatic engagement, Mattis emphasized the necessity of acknowledging the reality of Russian actions, noting a shrinking number of opportunities for bilateral cooperation with Moscow. When lawmakers inquired about primary threats to national interests, he stated that Russia takes precedence. 

Addressing the prospect of new American penalties, Mattis indicated a desire to collaborate with Trump’s national security team in formulating a strategy to hold Moscow accountable for its past behavior. With just eight days remaining before taking office, Trump acknowledged on Wednesday that Russian actors likely carried out cyberattacks against the Democratic National Committee and the email accounts of prominent Democrats during the 2016 election race—a conclusion previously established by U.S. intelligence agencies. 

Alongside cyber warfare and hacking operations, Mattis pointed to treaty breaches, destabilizing foreign operations, and concerning rhetoric emanating from Moscow concerning atomic weaponry as key challenges. He also accused the Russian government of seeking to weaken the NATO alliance. In contrast to Trump, who expressed skepticism toward the alliance on the campaign trail, Mattis offered a robust endorsement, describing NATO as foundational to American defense and asserting that Putin aims to fracture the North Atlantic partnership. 

Republican Senator John McCain, who chairs the committee, declared himself extremely pleased with the nomination, while issuing a sharp warning against overly optimistic approaches to Putin, stating that the Russian leader actively requires the U.S. as an adversary and will never function as an ally. 

Furthermore, Mattis drew attention to Beijing's maneuvers in the South China Sea, where artificial islands outfitted with anti-missile and anti-aircraft defenses have been constructed. He categorized Chinese behavior, alongside Russian actions and extremist threats, as part of a broader challenge to international stability, insisting that relations with Beijing demand careful management. In his view, the global architecture is enduring its heaviest assault since WWII due to Russia, terrorist organizations, and Chinese activities in the region. 

Criticizing the legislative spending restrictions currently in place, Mattis asserted that the U.S. armed forces currently lack the strength required to adequately deter potential foes. Having retired in 2013, Mattis technically falls short of the seven-year civilian requirement for the Pentagon post, necessitating a congressional waiver—an exemption not granted since 1950, though lawmakers appeared ready to approve it. 

Following his testimony, the waiver successfully passed its initial legislative test as the Senate Armed Services Committee voted in favor. The broader Senate subsequently endorsed the waiver by a decisive 81 to 17 margin, underscoring the deep backing Mattis commands among lawmakers. 

Mark Cancian, a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, noted that bipartisan backing would likely help Mattis bypass minimal resistance. Cancian added that Mattis is also viewed by some as a potential check against certain extreme tendencies of Trump. 

At age 66, Mattis has reportedly advised Trump behind closed doors to avoid waterboarding, a simulated drowning method used for interrogation that has been widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations, lawmakers, and senior officials. A similar stance was taken on Thursday by Trump's nominee for the CIA, who testified that he would resist the incoming administration if pressured to adopt such enhanced interrogation methods. 

Turning to the Middle East, Mattis delivered harsh criticism of Iran, warning that Tehran was expanding its harmful regional footprint. In written testimony submitted to the panel, he called Iran the primary destabilizing force in the region with policies running counter to U.S. objectives. Nevertheless, Mattis refrained from repeating Trump's campaign threats to scrap the international nuclear agreement under which Iran restricted its atomic program in exchange for sanctions relief. Characterizing the accord as flawed, Mattis maintained that Washington should still adhere to it, asserting that the United States must honor its commitments.

Events unfolding in Yemen continue to demonstrate that President Trump may ultimately fail to fulfill his prominent campaign pledges regarding foreign military interventions. Observers note how Trump appears to defer to military generals, effectively continuing a flawed policy initiated during the Obama administration. 

Reports indicate that the Department of Defense, headed by General James Mattis, aims to bolster backing for Saudi Arabia and its regional allies. Their objective is to maintain the bombing campaign in Yemen and forcefully install a leadership favored by Washington and Riyadh. 

Following more than two years of military action, Mattis has approached Congress to help formulate authorization that might grant the U.S. formal legal backing for its ongoing participation in the conflict. Critics point out that Mattis is improperly linking the situation in Yemen to operations in Syria and Iraq under the broader umbrella of countering ISIS. 

Many question why Yemen remains a major blind spot for U.S. officials, diplomatic representatives, and mainstream media organizations. Observers argue that the joint U.S.-Saudi campaign violates both domestic and international statutes. 

Legal scholars, such as University of Illinois professor Francis Boyle, characterize the actions of the U.S., Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates as inflicting a genocidal campaign against the Houthis. In response to the deteriorating situation, the Trump administration has proposed implementing additional sanctions. 

Because the conflict began under President Obama, progressive and liberal media outlets, alongside Democratic operatives, largely maintained a silent stance on Yemen throughout 2015 and 2016. Coverage was instead funneled toward Syria, aligning closely with talking points issued by the U.S. State Department and the British Foreign Office. 

Conversely, conservative media and Pentagon-aligned outlets framed the Yemen conflict through a binary lens, attributing the entire crisis to Iranian influence and labeling the Houthis as primary antagonists. Analysts suggest this Iran-centric framing obscured the underlying struggle to control lucrative regional energy reserves while providing a geopolitical justification for international crimes. Figures like CNN's Wolf Blitzer frequently utilized the qualifier "Iranian-backed Houthis," which neoconservatives leveraged to align the intervention with broader U.S. and Israeli strategic interests.

Since the campaign launched in March 2015, foreign policy analysts and commentators like Fareed Zakaria have largely bypassed the carnage in Yemen, choosing instead to focus on narratives surrounding Aleppo and operations in Syria. 

Critics argue that media figures and public relations figures, such as George Clooney, campaign for international action in areas like South Sudan while ignoring the joint actions of the U.S., Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, and the United Kingdom. Observers assert that international bodies, think tanks, Hollywood figures, and mainstream outlets have collectively enabled a severe violation of international law. 

Comparisons have been drawn between Saudi actions in Yemen and the unprovoked military aggression seen prior to World War II, with critics arguing the current precedent is even more dangerous. Furthermore, the United Nations and its leadership face severe criticism for failing to censure Saudi Arabia, drawing parallels to the ineffectiveness of the League of Nations in 1938. 

According to analyses by Trevor Thrall and John Glaser published via Reason, the nearly year-long bombing campaign has created a profound humanitarian crisis, resulting in thousands of deaths—half of whom are civilians. United Nations reports indicate that airstrikes have targeted residential areas, refugee camps, medical facilities, weddings, and religious sites, potentially constituting crimes against humanity. 

Millions of Yemenis remain internally displaced, facing critical shortages of clean water and severe risks of starvation due to a blockade on imports supported by the United States. Throughout these developments, Washington has supplied weaponry, logistical support, and diplomatic cover to the coalition.

The roots of the civil conflict trace back to the 2011 ouster of long-standing U.S. and Saudi ally Ali Abdullah Saleh. Saudi Arabia and the United States subsequently backed a transition centered on Abed-Rabbo Mansour Hadi, who stood as the sole candidate on the ballot. Houthi rebels subsequently initiated an insurgency, capturing the capital of Sanaa in 2014. 

The situation escalated into an intractable proxy conflict when Saudi Arabia initiated airstrikes aimed at defeating the Houthi movement and restoring the Hadi administration. Riyadh views the Houthis as Iranian proxies, and following the diplomatic nuclear agreement between Washington and Tehran, U.S. officials reportedly felt compelled to reassure Saudi allies through military backing. 

Critics contend this involvement compromises both strategic interests and moral standing. By undermining the Houthis and expanding the power vacuum, the intervention has inadvertently strengthened al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, which shares an animosity toward the Houthi movement. Although Saudi Arabia frames its operations as counterterrorism, analysts point to an uneasy alignment between Saudi forces and extremist elements, rendering U.S. assistance counterproductive.

Furthermore, the intervention is viewed as a clear violation of the jus ad bellum principle, which dictates that military force requires just cause and must follow the exhaustion of all diplomatic alternatives. Observers note that Yemen, as the poorest nation in the Middle East, poses no military threat to Saudi Arabia, rendering claims of self-defense or preventive war invalid under international law and the UN Charter. 

While Saudi officials argue the intervention is legal due to an invitation from the recognized Yemeni government, critics challenge the legitimacy of the Hadi administration, describing it as an instrument of Saudi influence. 

Ultimately, analysts argue that justifications connecting the Yemen campaign to the broader war on terror are unfounded, as the military actions tend to empower extremist groups. With no solid legal, moral, or strategic rationale, involvement in the conflict continues to face substantial criticism from legal and foreign policy experts.

HARARE — Zimbabwe’s governing party is preparing to strip President Robert Mugabe of his leadership on Sunday and bring back Emmerson Mnangagwa, the vice-president who had been fired, according to two party insiders who spoke to Reuters on Saturday amid jubilant street celebrations over the unfolding power shift. 

The 37-year-old presidency has effectively reached its conclusion following the military's takeover on Wednesday, which placed Mugabe under house arrest at his compound under the stated objective of removing the "criminals" surrounding him. Catholic priest Fidelis Mukonori, who has acted as a mediator during talks with the leader, was cited by state television as saying that Mugabe is scheduled to meet with military leadership on Sunday. 

Even without an official announcement, enormous crowds flooded the streets of the capital, embracing soldiers, singing, and dancing. The atmosphere drew comparisons to the 1989 fall of Romanian dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, with citizens of all ages sprinting alongside armored vehicles and the troops who intervened to remove the country's sole leader since its 1980 independence. Additional crowds marched toward the president's expansive "Blue Roof" property, though soldiers blocked their approach. 

Confined to his residence, the 93-year-old leader has watched his backing from the populace, security forces, and his own political party vanish in less than three days. Insiders noted that an upcoming ZANU-PF central committee gathering, set for 10:30 a.m. (0830 GMT), is also expected to strip Mugabe’s wife, Grace, of her position leading the party’s Women’s League. 

Speaking from an undisclosed location in South Africa, Mugabe's nephew, Patrick Zhuwao, told Reuters that the president and his spouse were prepared "to die for what is correct" rather than resign and legitimize what he termed a coup. Zhuwao added that Mugabe—who had barely slept since the military intervention but remained in "good" health—was the only person authorized to convene the central committee. While party rules were unclear regarding who holds the power to call such a gathering, unfolding events appeared to render the question moot. 

Across Harare, citizens described the moment as a second liberation for the former British colony, expressing hopes for political and economic transformation following two decades of mounting hardship and repression. 

"These are tears of joy," stated Frank Mutsindikwa, 34, raising a Zimbabwean flag high. "I’ve been waiting all my life for this day. Free at last. We are free at last."

The ousting of Mugabe is expected to create ripples across Africa, where several long-standing rulers—including Joseph Kabila in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Yoweri Museveni in Uganda—face growing demands to step down. The massive gatherings in Harare have lent a semi-democratic appearance to the military action, supporting assertions that the army is merely facilitating a constitutional transfer of authority. This approach helps the military sidestep the diplomatic condemnation and criticism that typically follows a coup. The armed forces were spurred into motion when Mugabe dismissed Mnangagwa, who was Grace Mugabe's primary competitor to succeed her husband ahead of next year's presidential election.

Members of the Zimbabwean diaspora also celebrated the end of the Mugabe era, including hundreds gathered outside their embassy in central London. 

"I’m ecstatic to see people give Mugabe a reality check because he has been in his echo chamber for too long, lying to himself that people still want him," remarked Ruva Kudambo, 37, who initially moved abroad for technology studies and remained. Tasa, a 36-year-old who declined to share his last name, brought his four children—ranging in age from 5 to 9—to the demonstration "because they are the future of Zimbabwe."

While some Africans still view Mugabe as a nationalist hero, the continent's final independence leader, and a figurehead for the battle against decades of colonial rule, many more inside and outside the country condemn him as a dictator willing to use violence to maintain control and devastate a once-promising economy.

According to political insiders and intelligence records reviewed by Reuters, Mugabe's departure is anticipated to clear the path for a transitional unity administration headed by Mnangagwa, a lifelong confidant and former security chief widely known as "The Crocodile." Restoring the collapsing economy will stand as the primary objective, the records indicated. 

The United States, a persistent critic of Mugabe, stated it anticipates a "new era" for Zimbabwe, while Botswana’s President Ian Khama asserted that Mugabe lacked regional diplomatic backing and needed to step down immediately. 

The Herald, the state-run publication that traditionally functioned as Mugabe's faithful vehicle, reported that ZANU-PF formally requested his departure on Friday. The newspaper added that party branches spanning all 10 provinces likewise demanded the resignation of Grace, whose aspirations to succeed her husband drew intense backlash from the military and the broader public. Among Zimbabweans, she is frequently labeled "Gucci Grace" due to her well-documented affinity for shopping, or "Dis-Grace" following an alleged September incident involving an assault on a South African model.

The scenes in Harare mirror the frustration and anger accumulated among the nation's 16 million citizens over nearly twenty years of economic mismanagement, triggered initially by the expropriation of white-owned farms in 2000, which sparked a broader societal collapse. The central bank attempted to print its way out of the crisis by flooding the market with currency, accelerating hyperinflation that peaked at 500 billion percent in 2008. Consequently, at least 3 million Zimbabweans fled abroad to seek stability, primarily relocating to neighboring South Africa. 

Following a brief stabilization period when Mugabe was compelled to share power with the opposition during a 2009–2013 coalition government, the economy floundered once more, driven this time by severe shortages of U.S. dollars. By October, monthly inflation surged past 50 percent according to certain economists, placing basic provisions out of reach for a population facing 90 percent unemployment. 

Mugabe’s sole public appearance since the military takeover occurred during a university graduation ceremony on Friday morning. Dressed in blue and yellow academic regalia, he looked fatigued and appeared to fall asleep in his seat at one point. 

A high-ranking ZANU-PF official noted that his departure was inevitable. 

"If he becomes stubborn, we will arrange for him to be fired on Sunday," the source said. "When that is done, it's impeachment on Tuesday."

Tennessee's Republican governor gave his approval on Wednesday to legislation permitting mental health therapists to turn away clients based on "sincerely held principles," marking the latest addition to a wave of state-level policies facing criticism for perceived discrimination against the LGBT community. 

Governor Bill Haslam enacted the measure into law right away, coming three weeks after the state legislature gave it the green light. In a released statement, Haslam argued that the legislation does not target any specific group, issue, or belief system. Instead, he explained, it grants counselors the same ability given to other professionals like attorneys and physicians to direct a client elsewhere if the client's behaviors or goals conflict with a deeply held personal belief. 

While the legislation initially included explicit references to religion, lawmakers amended the text to remove those mentions before final passage. Even without direct religious wording, the statute shields therapists from facing legal consequences when they turn down clients due to their personal convictions, putting state law at odds with the American Counseling Association's ethical code, which strictly forbids denying care in such a manner.

Criticism came swiftly from organizations like the American Civil Liberties Union of Tennessee. Hedy Weinberg, the executive director of the group, issued a statement condemning the policy as being built on the hazardous notion that religious beliefs can serve as permission to discriminate. She categorized the enactment as another assault on the lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender population, arriving in the wake of the previous year's landmark Supreme Court decision that invalidated state-level prohibitions on same-sex marriage.

Prior to signing, Haslam had mentioned to Nashville Public Radio that he was evaluating the potential fallout for the state and its inhabitants, especially as various states faced intense examination over measures deemed biased against LGBT individuals. The governor pointed to developments in North Carolina, where corporations such as Deutsche Bank and PayPal Holdings scrapped expansion plans and job creation efforts after that state enacted a rule mandating that individuals use public and school restrooms corresponding to the biological sex listed on their birth certificates rather than their gender identity.

Ultimately, Haslam noted that a key factor in his decision to approve the counseling measure was a specific exception ensuring therapists cannot turn away patients who pose an immediate threat of harming themselves or someone else. Earlier in the month, Haslam drew backlash from some local Christians when he exercised his veto power against a bill that sought to designate the Bible as the official state book, concluding that the proposal ran afoul of the United States Constitution.

Bob Krist of Omaha stated on Monday that the Legislature needs to consider censuring, expelling, or impeaching Kintner over the cybersex controversy to allow the governing body to return to legislative business. ROME (Reuters) — According to statements from U.N. officials on Friday, the United Nations is making preparations to send between 150 and 250 personnel—primarily from Nepal—to safeguard its facility in the Libyan capital. This deployment is a key component of a broader strategy to resume operations within the country. With the backing of Western nations, the organization is working to bridge the divide among Libya's competing factions to bring stability, combat terrorism, and curb human trafficking originating from the nation's northern shoreline.

Ever since 2014, when clashes between competing local brigades prompted the evacuation of the majority of foreign diplomatic personnel, the U.N. mission has operated out of Tunis. However, it has slowly expanded its footprint inside Libya and spent months organizing a permanent comeback. Jean-Pierre Lacroix, the U.N. Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations, indicated during a Geneva press briefing that the security contingent would likely number around 150 individuals, with the majority hailing from Nepal. 

Lacroix explained that to ensure the safety of personnel during their rollout in Tripoli, a guard unit comprised fundamentally of U.N. military troops from Nepal would be established. Meanwhile, the head of the U.N. Libya mission, Ghassan Salame—who took the helm in June—told the Italian publication La Stampa that a figure slightly below 250 might arrive over the next few weeks. Salame noted that placing these guards at the Tripoli compound would allow a major portion of their operations to resume inside the country around the start of October. A mission spokesperson clarified that there are no intentions to dispatch U.N. peacekeepers to the nation.

The security situation across Tripoli and other sections of western Libya remains precarious, with power largely wielded by independent armed factions. The capital's airport was severely damaged during intense factional combat in 2014, prompting foreign embassies to shutter their doors and evacuate personnel. This marked the most severe violence seen since the 2011 ouster and death of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi, an event that plunged the country into chaos following a NATO-backed revolt. Although a U.N.-supported administration was established in Tripoli last year, it has faced difficulties establishing control and confronts opposition from groups holding sway in the east of the country.

During talks in Paris in July, opposing leaders committed to pursuing a conditional ceasefire and holding elections in the upcoming year. Salame emphasized the necessity of drafting electoral and constitutional frameworks to guarantee that any upcoming ballot yields enduring reforms, stressing the importance of universal acceptance of the outcome, particularly given that the nation has never previously held presidential elections.

Salame additionally voiced annoyance regarding the overlapping diplomatic efforts by various European and regional governments competing for influence in Libya, stating that an abundance of mediators and initiatives is counterproductive. Conversely, French Foreign Minister Jean-Yves Le Drian expressed optimism during a trip to Moscow that French diplomatic efforts might lead to an overhaul of the 2015 U.N.-brokered agreement that established the Tripoli administration, operating under Salame's leadership. These talks have primarily focused on restructuring the governance and command over military assignments. Le Drian remarked to reporters in Moscow that the various diplomatic tracks appear to be aligning.

Responsible Gun Owner Shoots Himself After ‘Accidentally’ Killing Friend (VIDEO)

Justin Lowrie, a self-described responsible gun owner, opted to bypass a scheduled Alcoholics Anonymous meeting on the night of January 7, 2016, choosing instead to consume alcohol with companions. Reporting indicates that Lowrie possessed significant familiarity with weapons. Just two months prior, the 32-year-old, struggling with alcoholism, had obtained a concealed carry authorization issued by Wisconsin authorities. This license legally permitted Lowrie to bring his 9 mm firearm to a social gathering involving drinking.

As the evening drew to a close at approximately 10:30 p.m., Lowrie and several acquaintances were congregated within an apartment complex situated in Rice Lake, with his handgun in his hand. Standing close by were Cheri Fullarton and Laura Polichnia, linked arm-in-arm. At that moment, Lowrie fired his weapon, striking Fullarton in the face and resulting in her death.

An apartment building resident, Melissa Leland, recounted the aftermath to WQOW, stating they heard a shot followed by immediate screams and weeping, prompting her to step into the hallway after a brief interval to investigate. According to Leland, a neighbor rushed toward her in tears exclaiming that someone had been shot, which led to a 911 call from someone in the building. 

Prior to the arrival of law enforcement, Lowrie departed the gathering space and went back to his own residence situated two doors down from the unit where the fatal shooting occurred. Inside his apartment, he placed the firearm against his head and fired, taking his own life amidst intoxicated despair.

The Leader-Telegram characterized Lowrie as an individual burdened by a difficult history and substance abuse. In a discussion with the publication, Lowrie's father mentioned that his son had suffered from emotional distress following his wife's departure and the 2014 death of his mother from cancer. Meanwhile, the NRA maintains that firearm ownership is an inherent right for all individuals, irrespective of their emotional and mental well-being, while framing any regulatory measures aimed at averting such incidents as a malicious liberal conspiracy to confiscate firearms and confine citizens to FEMA camps.

Cheri Fullarton was 37 years old and raised three children. Roger Miller, her brother, expressed in an interview with the Leader-Telegram that his relatives are grappling with the devastation, remembering her as an intelligent and attractive woman devoted to her kids, while remaining fiercely angry about the reckless handling of a firearm, regardless of whether it was mistakenly assumed to be empty.

Reflecting on the tragedy, Lowrie's grieving father told the Leader-Telegram that his son acted out of his own volition while intoxicated and is no longer available to explain his actions. He also expressed hope that the Lord might save others through the situation, noting that while the events cannot be undone and second chances do not exist, acknowledging the reality can foster better decisions and potentially alter someone else's path for the better—an outcome that right-wing Christian narratives of a gun-toting Jesus would supposedly never permit. Additional coverage of the incident was provided by WQOW.

KABUL (Reuters) - Military data indicates that the volume of munitions dropped by American aircraft in Afghanistan has reached levels not recorded since the peak of the 2010 U.S. troop surge. This uptick follows President Donald Trump’s unveiling of a revised strategy in August, which relaxed restrictions on attacks and broadened the scope of targets among militant factions. 

According to Air Force statistics, the U.S. military released 751 bombs in September, marking a nearly 50 percent jump from the 503 recorded in August and representing the highest monthly total in seven years. 

An Air Force monthly report noted that the surge stems from the president's approach to more aggressively confront extremist networks that endanger the security and well-being of the Afghan population. To support these operations, the military dispatched six additional F-16 fighter bombers to Bagram air field, located north of Kabul, while also assigning more heavy B-52 bombers to conduct strikes in Afghanistan from locations in the Persian Gulf. 

These figures provided by the Air Force do not account for operations carried out by the U.S. Army, which operates armed helicopters and other aircraft within the country. 

The South Asia policy introduced by Trump involved commitments to grant U.S. forces greater leeway in pursuing militants. During his August address introducing the framework, Trump asserted that these individuals must understand they have no safe havens and that no location escapes the reach of American military power, promising swift and potent retribution. 

Under the previous administration, former President Barack Obama had sought to wind down the U.S. commitment in Afghanistan, often restricting American forces to engaging the Taliban strictly under specific conditions, including self-defense. Secretary of Defense James Mattis affirmed to lawmakers this month that the Trump administration has removed those previous limitations.

21st Century Wire reports that while mainstream journalists and political figures rail against a December 22nd tweet from Donald Trump concerning the enhancement of American nuclear strength—claiming he is sparking an arms race—the Obama administration has quietly implemented a historic shift in policies regarding space-based weaponry, hiding the move behind the label of missile defense. Why has the major media largely ignored Obama's recent actions? Critics warn this could strain ties with major military competitors like Russia and China while also driving a tremendous financial loss. Prominent defense scientists have characterized the concept that space-based architecture could shield the nation from a nuclear strike as pure fantasy.

As the political establishment and dominant news outlets condemn Trump's supposedly provocative statements on nuclear arsenals, President Obama has quietly signed a bill that alters long-standing United States nuclear defense strategy by removing just a single word. Observers note the profound irony, as this move risks escalating friction with Beijing and Moscow while initiating a costly push toward space-based defensive capabilities.

Following Trump's December 22, 2016 message on Twitter declaring that the United States must significantly build up and broaden its nuclear power until global sanity prevails regarding atomic weapons, mainstream platforms sharply criticized the incoming commander-in-chief for threatening global safety and igniting a renewed nuclear arms race. Yet, those same outlets have remained largely silent about Obama's concurrent legislative move.

The National Defense Authorization Act, an omnibus policy package covering nearly every facet of the American armed forces, included a pair of clauses carrying potentially profound ramifications. According to the Associated Press, the first clause removed the word "limited" from the text defining the scope of the nation's homeland missile defense network. Previously, the system was framed as a defense against modest strikes originating from non-superpowers such as Iran or North Korea. 

A companion clause directs the Pentagon to initiate research, testing, development, and evaluation concerning space-based missile defense infrastructure. Combined, these measures indicate the United States intends to pursue advanced technological means capable of countering both limited and extensive nuclear aggression. Such a shift threatens to destabilize the long-standing strategic equilibrium among the world's primary nuclear powers.

Massive bipartisan majorities in both chambers of Congress passed these policy adjustments over the preceding month with virtually no public discussion. Although the White House had initially voiced objections to the modifications, it ultimately refrained from issuing a veto threat, and Obama signed the measure into law on a Friday.

Experts in defense science argue that relying on space-based networks for nuclear protection is completely unrealistic. L. David Montague, a retired president of Lockheed's missile systems division and co-chair of a congressional panel studying missile defense at the National Academy of Sciences, stated that the idea ignores the laws of physics and lacks any scientific foundation. Montague explained in an interview that even if the skies were crowded with hundreds or thousands of interceptors and satellites, a determined attack could never be reliably blocked, making the endeavor an opportunity to squander massive sums of money. He labeled the congressional provisions as absolute insanity.

Republican Representative Trent Franks, who championed and pushed the policy changes through the House, acknowledged that his efforts were inspired by Ronald Reagan's 1980s Strategic Defense Initiative. That program, designed to employ lasers and other space-based armaments to render nuclear weapons obsolete, was popularly known as "Star Wars" and cost taxpayers $30 billion without ever deploying an operational system.

Philip E. Coyle III, a former assistant secretary of defense and past head of the Pentagon's weapons testing office, labeled the notion of a space-based nuclear shield a sham. Coyle remarked that the undertaking would cost astronomical sums of money, noting that neither the necessary technology nor the required funding exists, and expressed regret that Congress failed to recognize this. He further warned that both Russia and China would seize upon the initiative as a pretext to advance their own desired actions.

Nearly half of the U.S. public now rejects the Republican-backed tax proposal currently making its way through Congress, reflecting a notable uptick in negative sentiment since October. Findings from a Wednesday Reuters/Ipsos survey indicate that 49% of respondents familiar with the legislation are against it, marking an increase from the 41% opposition recorded previously. Meanwhile, Republican lawmakers are pushing to hold a vote on the Senate floor before the week concludes, while President Donald Trump remains a firm advocate of the package, aiming to enact it into law before the year is out. 

The poll, which gathered responses from 1,257 adults between Thursday and Monday, also showed that 29% of participants back the plan, while 22% are undecided. Asked about the primary beneficiaries of the legislation, over 50% of the surveyed population pointed to major corporations or the wealthy. Only 14% believed the advantages would go to "all Americans," while 6% named the middle class and just 2% selected lower-income households. The ongoing legislative effort in the Senate involves lowering the corporate tax rate, removing specific levies currently paid exclusively by wealthy citizens, and providing temporary or mixed tax reductions for various families and individuals. 

Data compiled by Reuters/Ipsos demonstrates that public resistance has steadily climbed as the legislative debate has progressed, a trend that began after Trump introduced a brief nine-page outline on Sept. 27 to kick off the discussions. For instance, an Oct. 24 survey of individuals familiar with the Republican tax initiative found that 41% were opposed, 31% were unsure, and 28% expressed support. 

Securing a major overhaul of the tax code represents a primary legislative goal for Trump and his party, who took control of the presidency and both congressional chambers in January. Following the House of Representatives' passage of its own version on Nov. 16, the Senate prepared to vote on Wednesday on whether to open formal debate on its measure, setting the stage for a critical floor vote later in the week. Any final legislation must ultimately be harmonized between the two chambers before reaching the White House for the president's signature. 

Partisan divides remain sharp regarding the package. According to the Nov. 23-27 survey, 59% of self-identified Republicans endorse the bill, with 15% opposed and 26% uncertain. Conversely, 82% of Democrats are against the measure, with only 8% in favor and 11% stating they did not know. The internet-based survey carries a credibility interval of three percentage points.

text:
BERLIN (Reuters) - Pressured from all sides, Germany’s Social Democrats decided on Friday to open discussions with Chancellor Angela Merkel about reviving their departing governing alliance, though they promised that any potential agreement would require the approval of the party rank-and-file. 

This reversal by the center-left party—which previously insisted on moving to the opposition benches following its worst electoral defeat in seven decades during the September vote—might prevent a destabilizing new election in the continent’s leading economic and political engine. 

Addressing a press conference, SPD chief Martin Schulz explained that the leadership arrived at this choice out of duty to both the nation and the broader continent. This shift follows the breakdown on Sunday of Merkel's negotiations to build a government with two smaller factions: the pro-business Free Democrats and the environmentalist Greens.

"There is nothing automatic about the direction we are moving in," Schulz stated, adding that if talks lead to any form of government participation, the final outcome will be submitted to a membership ballot. 

Speaking to approximately 300 members of the party’s youth wing in Saarbruecken—where youth delegates had just voted against another "grand coalition"—Schulz maintained that no final choice had been made. Nonetheless, he argued that holding power might provide a stronger platform to fulfill his core objective of bettering lives domestically and internationally. 

"From which position is that best possible? What is more important? The radiance of our decisions, or the improvement of the everyday lives of people?" he posed to the audience, noting their previous election support while calling for loyalty and constructive backing regardless of the leadership's ultimate direction. 

According to SPD deputy chief Ralf Stegner, supporting a fresh administration could involve a formal coalition pact, a pledge not to block a minority government led by Merkel, or alternative arrangements yet to be examined. Stegner, who remains doubtful about renewing the grand coalition, noted on ZDF television that the party intends to drive a hard bargain, remarking that the SPD "won't go cheaply."

Meanwhile, Rainer Haseloff, leader of the Christian Democrats in Saxony-Anhalt and a member of Merkel’s center-right bloc, told Reuters that sentiment seemed to be shifting toward a renewed grand coalition. While conservatives are prepared to examine SPD proposals, he stressed they will not accept any attempts to oust Merkel. 

Juergen Trittin, a prominent figure in the Green party, told the RND newspaper network that the question of the SPD entering coalition talks with conservatives was "a question of when, not if." 

Following an event in Brussels, Merkel addressed reporters but chose to take no questions. 

Polling conducted by infratest dimap for ARD prior to the latest SPD announcements revealed that half the public backed the party's initial refusal to enter a new grand coalition, whereas 44 percent favored continuing the partnership that has governed for the past four years. At the same time, 60 percent expressed support for holding fresh elections. 

Throughout her dozen years in office, Merkel has repeatedly partnered with coalitions whose members subsequently experienced severe voter backlash. A visual published by Cicero magazine portrayed the SPD as a mouse lured from its hiding spot by a waiting cat representing Merkel. 

Looking ahead, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier plans to bring together Schulz, Merkel, and Horst Seehofer—head of the CDU’s traditional Bavarian sister party—for discussions next Thursday. Steinmeier, a former SPD foreign minister, has strongly encouraged his former colleagues to reconsider their opposition stance, having previously designated new elections as an option of last resort. 

The current political deadlock stems from the September election, which saw losses for Merkel's conservatives alongside the entry of the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany into parliament. With the SPD reeling from its defeat, a complicated three-way alliance with smaller factions had initially seemed like the sole remaining path for the diminished chancellor.

text:
LONDON (Reuters) - David Davis, the minister responsible for Brexit, acknowledged on Wednesday that Britain has not yet carried out formal, industry-by-industry evaluations regarding how departing the European Union will affect the national economy, maintaining that such studies are premature. This admission sparked fresh outrage among detractors of the administration's management of the intricate separation negotiations, particularly as discussions with Brussels have hit an impasse over post-Brexit arrangements for the Irish border. 

For some time, Davis has been locked in a dispute with members of parliament—including figures within his own Conservative ranks—concerning the nature of the government's preparations and the transparency surrounding them. Appearing before a parliamentary panel, Davis stated that he is unaware of any systematic impact study, adding that undertaking such evaluations would be better suited for a later stage in the exit proceedings. 

These admissions immediately provoked pushback from committee members, who pointed out that Davis had previously claimed the administration possessed exhaustive, highly detailed sectoral analyses. Wera Hobhouse, a Liberal Democrat sitting on the Brexit committee, accused Davis of misleading parliament from the beginning, attributing the situation either to incompetence or insincerity, and expressed astonishment that these much-touted reports apparently do not exist, leaving officials blind to the domestic consequences of their strategy. 

Opposition politicians have continuously pushed for the release of summaries concerning these studies. During Wednesday's session, they voiced frustration that the materials provided thus far were lacking in detail and demanded more comprehensive disclosures. Even so, the panel tasked with monitoring the exit strategy acknowledged that the administration had met its publication requirements. Meanwhile, Labour's pro-EU politician Chuka Umunna announced he had reached out to the House of Commons speaker to investigate whether parliament had been deliberately misled. 

Previously, Davis and his departmental colleagues argued that their internal industry breakdowns do not constitute formal impact assessments—which are specific technical papers presented to lawmakers—and maintained that revealing these working documents could weaken the nation's leverage at the negotiating table. 

Looking ahead, Davis explained that officials will eventually attempt to measure the consequences of various potential negotiation results as those milestones approach, noting that the second phase of talks centered on trade has not yet commenced. He confirmed that future evaluations will examine potential outcomes for specific fields such as agriculture, manufacturing, and financial services.

In response to the claims, Spacey posted a tweet stating he genuinely has no recollection of the incident, noting it would have taken place over three decades ago, while adding that if he acted the way the accuser claims, he offers his sincerest apologies for what would have constituted deeply inappropriate drunken conduct and feels sorry for the lasting impact the accuser describes. In a collaborative statement released today, Netflix and Media Rights Capital expressed profound concern over the previous evening's reports regarding Kevin Spacey, noting that company executives traveled to Baltimore this afternoon to confer with the cast and crew, ensuring their continued safety and support, and pointing out that Spacey was already not scheduled to be working on set.

text: OSLO/MOSCOW (Reuters) - Norwegian search and rescue teams think they might have found the remains of a Russian helicopter that vanished Thursday carrying eight individuals near the Arctic Svalbard archipelago. Tore Hongset, who heads Norway's rescue coordination center, told Reuters that authorities spotted air bubbles and oil slicking the water's surface, while a boat in the vicinity spotted a submerged form that could potentially be the aircraft. He mentioned that a mini submarine operated remotely was being rushed to the location and was expected to be sent down early Friday morning to confirm the find, adding that efforts to find survivors would press on, with the reminder that the chopper carried life rafts. According to Russia's Emergency Ministry, all five crew members and three passengers were Russian citizens. The missing aircraft, a Russian-built Mil Mi-8, had sent its last signal around 1335 GMT. A statement from the Russian Energy Ministry clarified that the trio of passengers were employees of the nation's Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute. The flight was traveling from the deserted settlement of Pyramiden toward the Barentsburg coal mining port, though it was later verified to have crashed into the sea a short distance away from where it was supposed to land. Marinetraffic.com vessel tracking information showed multiple ships operating in the zone, with the governor of Svalbard's vessel, the Polarsyssel, leading the search coordination. The Barentsburg mine, operated by the Russian firm Arktikugol, employs a workforce of both Russians and Ukrainians. A representative for Convers Avia Air informed Reuters that the company owned the missing aircraft and had dropped contact with it. Prior to that update, Hongset shared with Norwegian network TV2 that the danger of fatality and hypothermia increases with every passing minute. Positioned roughly 700 kilometers (435 miles) north of the European mainland, Svalbard operates under an agreement giving Norway, a NATO member, sovereignty, while granting other participating nations the right to commercial activity and resource extraction. The treaty has signatories numbering over 40. For many years, Moscow has kept a presence on the archipelago, viewing it as a key strategic outpost in the far north.

text:
An intense wave of backlash has hit National Geographic following the reveal of their upcoming magazine cover, which features a nine-year-old transgender child. 

For readers wishing to voice their thoughts or terminate their subscriptions, a phone number has been circulated: 1-800-647-5463. The January issue cover has triggered widespread anger across the internet by highlighting children who question their gender and promoting what the publication describes as a "gender revolution." 

According to an official press release, the entire first edition for 2017 focuses exclusively on the evolving terrain of gender, featuring pieces named "Rethinking Gender," "Dangerous Lives of Girls," and "Making a man." The announcement notes that gender identity has moved into the public square to an extent that would have been completely unexpected ten years ago, with the print edition scheduled to arrive on newsstands on December 27, as cited by Infowars.

National Geographic shared a post on Twitter on December 16, 2016, stating they dedicated their whole January 2017 Special Issue to exploring gender, accompanied by a link and a promotional image. 

Social media users quickly flooded the replies to the official post. Susan Scott announced her decision to cancel her subscription, expressing regret over the perceived decline of a formerly respected publication. Another user, Raymond Luxury-Yacht, stated support for LGBT rights while calling the feature irresponsible, arguing that developing children lack the maturity for such choices. Additional commentary argued that biological sex at birth is unrelated to actual gender, with one user asserting that physical anatomy does not define being a man or a woman. Meanwhile, another user accused National Geographic of abandoning science in favor of what they termed culture-rotting fantasy.

text:
Rapist Cop Daniel Holtzclaw Disappears From Prison Database (IMAGES)

Back in December 2015, an Oklahoma City police officer named Daniel Holtzclaw was convicted by a jury on 18 separate counts involving rape and sexual assault. Judge Timothy Henderson handed down a 263-year consecutive prison sentence to the serial rapist a month afterward on January 21, 2016. However, KFOR, the NBC affiliate in Oklahoma City, reported on a Friday that Holtzclaw's name was no longer visible on the Oklahoma Department of Corrections website. Information regarding Holtzclaw was still visible in the database on Tuesday, according to KFOR images. By January 29, which was three days later, the database displayed zero records for Holtzclaw, as shown in KFOR images. When KFOR reached out to the state Department of Corrections, a spokesperson declined to comment, citing security reasons. Holtzclaw received convictions for sexually assaulting seven women, though he is suspected of targeting numerous others. Nearly all of his victims were Black women. The youngest person he victimized was 17 years old, and the oldest was a 57-year-old grandmother of 12. Victims in Oklahoma hold specific legal rights, which include being informed of an offender's whereabouts. Law enforcement agencies and the state Attorney General's office make this data available through the VINELink website, designed to receive daily updates regarding offender statuses. While Holtzclaw remains listed in the VINELink system, his current location is marked as unknown, based on KFOR imagery. KFOR noted that the women abused by Holtzclaw received no notification regarding any shifts in his status or location, despite Oklahoma regulations mandating that crime victims be alerted to such updates. Alex Gerszewski, speaking for the Oklahoma Department of Corrections, declined to disclose details about Holtzclaw's location to KFOR, stating merely that he underwent processing at Lexington identically to any other inmate. Gerszewski reiterated the security justification, stating that his location cannot be disclosed due to the safety of both the facility and the inmate. The state Department of Corrections along with VINELink publicly display details for all prisoners, encompassing child abductors, pedophiles, serial killers, and numerous others convicted of severe and violent offenses. It is safe to assume that these criminals would also prefer the removal of their details from the Department of Corrections site. Keeping their locations confidential for security purposes would undoubtedly appeal to them, given that such convictions frequently lead to targeted violence, assault, or death behind bars. One key factor distinguishes Holtzclaw from every other incarcerated serial rapist in Oklahoma: he used to be a police officer. By scrubbing his details from the database and hiding his whereabouts, the Oklahoma Department of Corrections appears to believe it is permissible to break the law and infringe upon the rights of the women Holtzclaw assaulted and raped. This situation is entirely unallowable. Protecting crime victims remains the obligation of the Oklahoma Department of Corrections, rather than shielding serial rapists who happen to be former law enforcement officers.Featured image credit: VINELink

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Citing suspicious timing, a senior Republican congressman reached out to Secretary of State John Kerry on Wednesday to demand answers regarding a $1.7 billion financial settlement transferred to Iran concurrently with the freeing of detained Americans last month. Ed Royce, who heads the House Foreign Affairs Committee, stated in a letter that because the payout coincided with the prisoner release and lawmakers were kept in the dark, critics are worried the funds were essentially a ransom payment for the captives. 

Royce set a deadline of February 17 for Kerry to deliver various documents and details, which include the names of American officials involved in the talks surrounding the payout, the hostage exchange, and the July nuclear accord. Additionally, the lawmaker requested legal evaluations of the conflict, a chronological breakdown of the discussions, and a breakdown showing how the accrued interest was computed. 

The State Department announced on January 17 that a historic dispute through the Iran-U.S. Claims Tribunal had been resolved, resulting in the transfer of $400 million in assets that had been frozen since 1981, alongside $1.3 billion in interest payments. 

John Kirby, a spokesman for the State Department, indicated that Kerry plans to reply to the inquiry, though he declined to provide a timeline or format for the response. Acknowledging that the correspondence had arrived from Chairman Royce, Kirby noted that the agency handles messages from Congress through standard, appropriate channels. 

GOP legislators, who have consistently opposed President Barack Obama's approach to Iran, have raised doubts about the transaction for several weeks. When Congress reviewed the nuclear deal last year, it did not receive a single Republican vote. Following the public disclosure of the settlement, President Obama defended the move, arguing it was preferable to letting the interest continue to mount while awaiting a final court ruling.

text:
The debut of the Smithsonian’s Museum of African-American History was met with widespread celebration, alongside backlash from critics who view the institution as an attack on white heritage and a form of reverse discrimination. In the wake of Donald Trump's presidential victory, reported incidents of hate crimes have surged, culminating in an individual—or multiple perpetrators—bringing their bigotry directly into the museum itself by displaying a noose.

Over a four-day span, a noose was hung inside the Museum of African-American History on two separate occasions. The item carries a heavy, painful historical weight, serving as a direct reminder of the era of widespread lynchings directed at Black individuals. 

This symbolism is the exact motivation behind such actions, according to a representative from the Southern Poverty Law Center, who noted the current climate of hostility: "We haven't seen such mainstream support for hate in decades, not since the Civil Rights era 50 years ago. We're witnessing a moment when there are tremendous challenges to the country that we built on pluralism and democracy. The civil rights accorded every American are firmly under threat." 

For certain segments of the population, marginalized communities—including people of color, women, and the LGBTQ community—are perceived as a direct challenge to the traditional demographic, and the recent election has emboldened individuals to act under the banner of reclaiming the nation from political correctness.

In response to the incidents, the Smithsonian released a formal reaction condemning the behavior. David Skorton, the secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, addressed staff in an organization-wide message: "The Smithsonian family stands together in condemning this act of hatred and intolerance, especially repugnant in a museum that affirms and celebrates the American values of inclusion and diversity. We will not be intimated. Cowardly acts like these will not, for one moment, prevent us from the vital work we do."

text:
WASHINGTON (Reuters) - U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson admitted during a Tuesday briefing that he and President Donald Trump hold differing opinions regarding the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement, noting that they talk about ways to leverage the international accord to further administration goals. Throughout his 2016 campaign, Trump frequently promised to scrap the pact, which was brokered by the United States, China, Russia, and three European nations to restrict Iran's nuclear activities in exchange for the removal of the majority of Western sanctions. Despite his stated objections, Trump has kept the agreement in place thus far, though he has made it known that he only did so grudgingly after receiving counsel from Tillerson. 

Using the formal name Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), Tillerson remarked at the State Department that he and the president hold divergent perspectives on the pact and how it should be handled. According to Tillerson, the administration faces a choice between abandoning the agreement entirely or remaining a party to it while holding Tehran strictly accountable to its provisions, which he noted includes expecting Iran to behave as a cooperative neighbor. Opponents of the accord argue that it fails to adequately address Tehran's backing of militant groups in Syria and Iraq, its regional weapons proliferation, and its ballistic missile testing. The White House declined to provide an immediate response when asked for comment regarding Tillerson's statements. 

In a previous interview with the Wall Street Journal last month, Trump stated that he expects Tehran to be found in noncompliance when the upcoming October review deadline arrives, adding that he would have preferred to reach that conclusion earlier. By contrast, Tillerson offered a more measured perspective on Tuesday regarding the pact's potential advantages. He explained that the agreement provides various alternative tools for shaping policy and managing relations with Iran, which is typically the focus of his discussions with the president. 

Meanwhile, European diplomats would likely hesitate to reinstate sanctions, particularly the sweeping economic penalties that originally compelled Iran to the negotiating table. Furthermore, a prominent Iranian lawmaker stated that recent U.S. sanctions enacted in July violated the nuclear accord, prompting Tehran to file a formal grievance with the organization responsible for monitoring the pact's execution. Tillerson conceded that America's capacity to pressure Iran unilaterally is constrained, emphasizing that working alongside the other signatories is essential. He concluded that the most effective leverage to alter Iranian conduct is collective pressure applied by all parties involved.

Senate passes bill to boost travel security after Brussels

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Following the recent attacks in Brussels, the Senate gave its overwhelming approval on Tuesday to a measure designed to enhance domestic travel safety while extending Federal Aviation Administration programs through September 2017. With a 95-3 tally, the legislation now heads over to the House of Representatives. Members of the House have previously stalled on their own version of an FAA bill due to disagreements regarding a proposal that would spin off the nation's air traffic control system into a private entity. 

By steering clear of the privatization debate, the bipartisan Senate package introduces numerous travel security initiatives that Republican senators are labeling the most far-reaching upgrade to airport protection seen in almost ten years. Among these additions are an expansion—doubling the presence—of bomb-sniffing canine units across U.S. airports, enhanced background checks for aviation workers, and heightened safeguards around ticketing and luggage retrieval zones. Furthermore, the legislation funds FAA administration, infrastructure upgrades for airports, and aviation research studies, while mandating that commercial carriers reimburse travelers for misplaced luggage and issue refunds when paid services fail to be rendered. 

John Thune, who leads the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee, remarked that the act will enhance safety and security while improving the overall experience for flyers. In addition, the Senate bill features extensive provisions concerning drones, mandating updated regulatory frameworks for commercial unmanned aircraft regarding privacy, design, safety measures, identification protocols, and the handling of information collected by the devices.
